impossible to touch.  Dead!  He could not hear or bear the word.  The
slightest hint of it would throw him into a paroxysm, like that he had
had when it was first spoken.  In what [[concepts/hope|hope]] he lived, no man could
tell; but that he had some [[concepts/hope|hope]] of finding her again--some faint and
shadowy [[concepts/hope|hope]], deferred from day to day, and making him from day to day
more sick and sore at heart--was plain to all.

They bethought them of a removal from the scene of this last sorrow; of
trying whether change of place would rouse or cheer him.  His brother
sought the advice of those who were accounted skilful in such matters,
and they came and saw him.  Some of the number staid upon the spot,
conversed with him when he would converse, and watched him as he
wandered up and down, alone and silent.  Move him where they might,
they said, he would ever seek to get back there.  His mind would run
upon that spot.  If they confined him closely, and kept a strict guard
upon him, they might hold him prisoner, but if he could by any means
escape, he would surely wander back to that place, or die upon the [[motifs/road|road]].

The boy, to whom he had submitted at first, had no longer any influence
with him.  At times he would suffer the [[archetypes/child|child]] to walk by his side, or
would even take such notice of his presence as giving him his hand, or
would stop to kiss his cheek, or pat him on the head.  At other times,
he would entreat him--not unkindly--to be gone, and would not brook him
near.  But, whether alone, or with this pliant friend, or with those
who would have given him, at any cost or sacrifice, some consolation or
some peace of mind, if happily the means could have been devised; he
was at all times the same--with no [[motifs/love|love]] or care for anything in life--a
broken-hearted man.

At length, they found, one day, that he had risen early, and, with his
knapsack on his back, his staff in hand, her own straw hat, and little
basket full of such things as she had been used to carry, was gone.  As
they were making ready to pursue him far and wide, a frightened
schoolboy came who had seen him, but a moment before, sitting in the
church--upon her [[motifs/grave|grave]], he said.

They hastened there, and going softly to the door, espied him in the
attitude of one who waited patiently.  They did not disturb him then,
but kept a watch upon him all that day.  When it grew quite dark, he
[[motifs/rose|rose]] and returned [[motifs/home|home]], and went to bed, murmuring to himself, ‘She
will come to-morrow!’

Upon the morrow he was there again from sunrise until [[motifs/night|night]]; and still
at [[motifs/night|night]] he laid him down to rest, and murmured, ‘She will come
to-morrow!’

And thenceforth, every day, and all day long, he waited at her [[motifs/grave|grave]],
for her.  How many pictures of new journeys over pleasant country, of
resting-places under the free broad sky, of rambles in the fields and
woods, and paths not often trodden--how many tones of that one
[[motifs/well|well]]-remembered voice, how many glimpses of the form, the fluttering
dress, the hair that waved so gaily in the [[motifs/wind|wind]]--how many visions of
what had been, and what he hoped was yet to be--[[motifs/rose|rose]] up before him, in
the old, dull, silent church!  He never told them what he thought, or
where he went.  He would sit with them at [[motifs/night|night]], pondering with a
secret satisfaction, they could see, upon the flight that he and she
would take before [[motifs/night|night]] came again; and still they would hear him
whisper in his prayers, ‘Lord!  Let her come to-morrow!’

The last [[motifs/time|time]] was on a genial day in [[motifs/spring|spring]].  He did not return at the
usual hour, and they went to seek him.  He was lying dead upon the
stone.

They laid him by the side of her whom he had loved so [[motifs/well|well]]; and, in the
church where they had often prayed, and mused, and lingered hand in
hand, the [[archetypes/child|child]] and the old man slept together.




CHAPTER 73

The magic reel, which, rolling on before, has led the chronicler thus
far, now slackens in its pace, and stops.  It lies before the goal; the
pursuit is at an end.

It remains but to dismiss the leaders of the little crowd who have
borne us company upon the [[motifs/road|road]], and so to close the [[motifs/journey|journey]].

Foremost among them, smooth [[characters/sampson-brass|Sampson Brass]] and Sally, arm in arm, claim
our polite attention.

Mr Sampson, then, being detained, as already has been shown, by the
justice upon whom he called, and being so strongly pressed to protract
his stay that he could by no means refuse, remained under his
protection for a considerable [[motifs/time|time]], during which the great attention of
his entertainer kept him so extremely close, that he was quite lost to
society, and never even went abroad for exercise saving into a small
paved yard.  So [[motifs/well|well]], indeed, was his modest and retiring temper
understood by those with whom he had to deal, and so jealous were they
of his absence, that they required a kind of friendly bond to be
entered into by two substantial housekeepers, in the sum of fifteen
hundred pounds a-piece, before they would suffer him to quit their
hospitable roof--doubting, it appeared, that he would return, if once
let loose, on any other terms.  Mr Brass, struck with the humour of
this jest, and carrying out its spirit to the utmost, sought from his
wide connection a pair of friends whose joint possessions fell some
halfpence short of fifteen pence, and proffered them as bail--for that
was the merry word agreed upon both sides.  These gentlemen being
rejected after twenty-four hours’ pleasantry, Mr Brass consented to
remain, and did remain, until a club of choice spirits called a Grand
jury (who were in the joke) summoned him to a trial before twelve other
wags for perjury and fraud, who in their turn found him guilty with a
most facetious joy,--nay, the very populace entered into the whim, and
when Mr Brass was moving in a hackney-coach towards the building where
these wags assembled, saluted him with rotten eggs and carcases of
kittens, and feigned to wish to tear him into shreds, which greatly
increased the comicality of the thing, and made him relish it the more,
no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]].

To work this sportive vein still further, Mr Brass, by his counsel,
moved in arrest of judgment that he had been led to criminate himself,
by assurances of safety and promises of pardon, and claimed the
leniency which the law extends to such confiding natures as are thus
deluded.  After solemn argument, this point (with others of a technical
[[concepts/nature|nature]], whose humorous extravagance it would be difficult to
exaggerate) was referred to the judges for their decision, Sampson
being meantime removed to his former quarters.  Finally, some of the
points were given in Sampson’s favour, and some against him; and the
upshot was, that, instead of being desired to travel for a [[motifs/time|time]] in
foreign parts, he was permitted to grace the mother country under
certain insignificant restrictions.

These were, that he should, for a term of years, reside in a spacious
mansion where several other gentlemen were lodged and boarded at the
public charge, who went clad in a sober uniform of grey turned up with
yellow, had their hair cut extremely short, and chiefly lived on gruel
and light soup.  It was also required of him that he should partake of
their exercise of constantly ascending an endless flight of stairs;
and, lest his legs, unused to such exertion, should be weakened by it,
that he should wear upon one ankle an amulet or charm of iron.  These
conditions being arranged, he was removed one evening to his new abode,
and enjoyed, in common with nine other gentlemen, and two ladies, the
privilege of being taken to his place of retirement in one of Royalty’s
own carriages.

Over and above these trifling penalties, his name was erased and
blotted out from the roll of attorneys; which erasure has been always
held in these latter times to be a great degradation and reproach, and
to imply the commission of some amazing villany--as indeed it would
seem to be the case, when so many worthless names remain among its
better records, unmolested.

Of [[characters/sally-brass|Sally Brass]], conflicting rumours went abroad.  Some said with
confidence that she had gone down to the docks in male attire, and had
become a female sailor; others darkly whispered that she had enlisted
as a private in the second regiment of Foot Guards, and had been seen
in uniform, and on duty, to wit, leaning on her musket and looking out
of a sentry-box in St James’s Park, one evening.  There were many such
whispers as these in circulation; but the [[concepts/truth|truth]] appears to be that,
after the lapse of some five years (during which there is no direct
evidence of her having been seen at all), two wretched people were more
than once observed to crawl at dusk from the inmost recesses of St
Giles’s, and to take their way along the streets, with shuffling steps
and cowering shivering forms, looking into the roads and kennels as
they went in search of refuse food or disregarded offal.  These forms
were never beheld but in those nights of cold and gloom, when the
terrible spectres, who lie at all other times in the obscene
hiding-places of [[settings/london|London]], in archways, dark vaults and cellars, venture
to creep into the streets; the embodied spirits of Disease, and Vice,
and Famine.  It was whispered by those who should have known, that
these were Sampson and his sister Sally; and to this day, it is said,
they sometimes pass, on bad nights, in the same loathsome guise, close
at the elbow of the shrinking passenger.

The [[concepts/body|body]] of Quilp being found--though not until some days had
elapsed--an inquest was held on it near the spot where it had been
washed ashore.  The general supposition was that he had committed
[[concepts/suicide|suicide]], and, this appearing to be favoured by all the circumstances of
his [[motifs/death|death]], the verdict was to that effect.  He was left to be buried
with a stake through his heart in the centre of four lonely roads.

It was rumoured afterwards that this horrible and barbarous ceremony
had been dispensed with, and that the remains had been secretly given
up to Tom Scott.  But even here, opinion was divided; for some said Tom
dug them up at midnight, and carried them to a place indicated to him
by the widow.  It is probable that both these stories may have had
their origin in the simple fact of Tom’s shedding [[motifs/tears|tears]] upon the
inquest--which he certainly did, extraordinary as it may appear.  He
manifested, besides, a strong [[motifs/desire|desire]] to assault the jury; and being
restrained and conducted out of [[settings/court|court]], darkened its only [[motifs/window|window]] by
standing on his head upon the sill, until he was dexterously tilted
upon his feet again by a cautious beadle.

Being cast upon the world by his master’s [[motifs/death|death]], he determined to go
through it upon his head and hands, and accordingly began to tumble for
his bread.  Finding, however, his English birth an insurmountable
obstacle to his advancement in this pursuit (notwithstanding that his
art was in high repute and favour), he assumed the name of an Italian
image lad, with whom he had become acquainted; and afterwards tumbled
with extraordinary success, and to overflowing audiences.

Little Mrs Quilp never quite forgave herself the one deceit that lay so
heavy on her [[concepts/conscience|conscience]], and never spoke or thought of it but with
bitter [[motifs/tears|tears]]. Her husband had no relations, and she was rich.  He had
made no will, or she would probably have been poor.  Having married the
first [[motifs/time|time]] at her mother’s instigation, she consulted in her second
choice nobody but herself.  It fell upon a smart young fellow enough;
and as he made it a preliminary condition that Mrs Jiniwin should be
thenceforth an out-pensioner, they lived together after [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] with no
more than the average amount of quarrelling, and led a merry life upon
the dead [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]]’s money.

Mr and Mrs Garland, and Mr Abel, went out as usual (except that there
was a change in their household, as will be seen presently), and in due
[[motifs/time|time]] the latter went into partnership with his friend the notary, on
which occasion there was a dinner, and a ball, and great extent of
dissipation.  Unto this ball there happened to be invited the most
bashful young lady that was ever seen, with whom Mr Abel happened to
fall in [[motifs/love|love]].  HOW it happened, or how they found it out, or which of
them first communicated the discovery to the other, nobody knows.  But
certain it is that in course of [[motifs/time|time]] they were married; and equally
certain it is that they were the happiest of the happy; and no less
certain it is that they deserved to be so.  And it is pleasant to write
down that they reared a family; because any propagation of goodness and
benevolence is no small addition to the aristocracy of [[concepts/nature|nature]], and no
small subject of rejoicing for mankind at large.

The pony preserved his character for independence and principle down to
the last moment of his life; which was an unusually long one, and
caused him to be looked upon, indeed, as the very Old Parr of ponies.
He often went to and fro with the little phaeton between Mr Garland’s
and his son’s, and, as the old people and the young were frequently
together, had a stable of his own at the new establishment, into which
he would walk of himself with surprising dignity.  He condescended to
play with the children, as they grew old enough to cultivate his
[[concepts/friendship|friendship]], and would run up and down the little paddock with them like
a dog; but though he relaxed so far, and allowed them such small
freedoms as caresses, or even to look at his shoes or hang on by his
tail, he never permitted any one among them to mount his back or drive
him; thus showing that even their familiarity must have its limits, and
that there were points between them far too serious for trifling.

He was not unsusceptible of warm attachments in his later life, for
when the good bachelor came to live with Mr Garland upon the
clergyman’s decease, he conceived a great [[concepts/friendship|friendship]] for him, and
amiably submitted to be driven by his hands without the least
resistance.  He did no work for two or three years before he died, but
lived in clover; and his last act (like a choleric old gentleman) was
to kick his doctor.

Mr Swiveller, recovering very slowly from his illness, and entering
into the receipt of his annuity, bought for the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] a handsome
stock of clothes, and put her to school forthwith, in redemption of the
vow he had made upon his fevered bed.  After casting about for some
[[motifs/time|time]] for a name which should be worthy of her, he decided in favour of
Sophronia Sphynx, as being euphonious and genteel, and furthermore
indicative of mystery.  Under this title the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] repaired, in
[[motifs/tears|tears]], to the school of his selection, from which, as she soon
distanced all competitors, she was removed before the lapse of many
quarters to one of a higher grade.  It is but bare justice to Mr
Swiveller to say, that, although the expenses of her [[concepts/education|education]] kept him
in straitened circumstances for half a dozen years, he never slackened
in his zeal, and always held himself sufficiently repaid by the
accounts he heard (with great gravity) of her advancement, on his
monthly visits to the governess, who looked upon him as a literary
gentleman of eccentric habits, and of a most prodigious talent in
quotation.

In a word, Mr Swiveller kept the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] at this establishment
until she was, at a moderate guess, full nineteen years of age--
good-looking, clever, and good-humoured; when he began to consider
seriously what was to be done next.  On one of his periodical visits,
while he was revolving this question in his mind, the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] came
down to him, alone, looking more smiling and more fresh than ever.
Then, it occurred to him, but not for the first [[motifs/time|time]], that if she would
marry him, how comfortable they might be!  So [[characters/richard|Richard]] asked her;
whatever she said, it wasn’t No; and they were married in good earnest
that day week.  Which gave Mr Swiveller frequent occasion to remark at
divers subsequent periods that there had been a young lady saving up
for him after all.

A little cottage at Hampstead being to let, which had in its [[motifs/garden|garden]] a
smoking-box, the envy of the civilised world, they agreed to become its
tenants, and, when the honey-[[motifs/moon|moon]] was over, entered upon its
occupation.  To this retreat Mr Chuckster repaired regularly every
[[characters/sunday|Sunday]] to spend the day--usually beginning with breakfast--and here he
was the great purveyor of general news and fashionable intelligence.
For some years he continued a deadly foe to Kit, protesting that he had
a better opinion of him when he was supposed to have stolen the
five-pound note, than when he was shown to be perfectly free of the
crime; inasmuch as his [[concepts/guilt|guilt]] would have had in it something daring and
bold, whereas his innocence was but another proof of a sneaking and
crafty disposition.  By slow degrees, however, he was reconciled to him
in the end; and even went so far as to [[concepts/honour|honour]] him with his patronage,
as one who had in some measure reformed, and was therefore to be
forgiven.  But he never forgot or pardoned that circumstance of the
shilling; holding that if he had come back to get another he would have
done [[motifs/well|well]] enough, but that his returning to work out the former gift
was a stain upon his moral character which no penitence or contrition
could ever wash away.

Mr Swiveller, having always been in some measure of a philosophic and
reflective turn, grew immensely contemplative, at times, in the
smoking-box, and was accustomed at such periods to debate in his own
mind the mysterious question of Sophronia’s parentage.  Sophronia
herself supposed she was an [[archetypes/orphan|orphan]]; but Mr Swiveller, putting various
slight circumstances together, often thought Miss Brass must know
better than that; and, having heard from his wife of her strange
interview with Quilp, entertained sundry misgivings whether that
person, in his lifetime, might not also have been able to solve the
[[forms/riddle|riddle]], had he chosen.  These speculations, however, gave him no
uneasiness; for Sophronia was ever a most cheerful, affectionate, and
provident wife to him; and Dick (excepting for an occasional outbreak
with Mr Chuckster, which she had the good sense rather to encourage
than oppose) was to her an attached and domesticated husband.  And they
played many hundred thousand games of cribbage together.  And let it be
added, to Dick’s [[concepts/honour|honour]], that, though we have called her Sophronia, he
called her the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] from first to last; and that upon every
anniversary of the day on which he found her in his sick room, Mr
Chuckster came to dinner, and there was great glorification.

The gamblers, Isaac List and Jowl, with their trusty confederate Mr
James Groves of unimpeachable [[motifs/memory|memory]], pursued their course with varying
success, until the failure of a spirited enterprise in the way of their
profession, dispersed them in various directions, and caused their
career to receive a sudden check from the long and strong arm of the
law.  This defeat had its origin in the untoward detection of a new
associate--young Frederick Trent--who thus became the unconscious
instrument of their punishment and his own.

For the young man himself, he rioted abroad for a brief term, living by
his wits--which means by the abuse of every faculty that worthily
employed raises man above the beasts, and so degraded, sinks him far
below them.  It was not long before his [[concepts/body|body]] was recognised by a
stranger, who chanced to visit that hospital in [[settings/paris|Paris]] where the drowned
are laid out to be owned; despite the bruises and disfigurements which
were said to have been occasioned by some previous scuffle.  But the
stranger kept his own counsel until he returned [[motifs/home|home]], and it was never
claimed or cared for.

The younger brother, or the single gentleman, for that designation is
more familiar, would have drawn the poor schoolmaster from his lone
retreat, and made him his companion and friend.  But the humble village
teacher was timid of venturing into the noisy world, and had become
fond of his dwelling in the old churchyard.  Calmly happy in his
school, and in the spot, and in the attachment of Her little mourner,
he pursued his quiet course in peace; and was, through the righteous
gratitude of his friend--let this brief mention suffice for that--a
POOR school-master no more.

That friend--single gentleman, or younger brother, which you will--had
at his heart a heavy sorrow; but it bred in him no [[concepts/misanthropy|misanthropy]] or
monastic gloom.  He went forth into the world, a [[archetypes/lover|lover]] of his kind.
For a long, long [[motifs/time|time]], it was his chief delight to travel in the steps
of the old man and the [[archetypes/child|child]] (so far as he could trace them from her
last narrative), to halt where they had halted, sympathise where they
had suffered, and rejoice where they had been made glad.  Those who had
been kind to them, did not escape his search.  The sisters at the
school--they who were her friends, because themselves so
friendless--Mrs Jarley of the wax-work, Codlin, Short--he found them
all; and trust me, the man who fed the furnace [[motifs/fire|fire]] was not forgotten.

Kit’s story having got abroad, raised him up a host of friends, and
many offers of provision for his future life.  He had no idea at first
of ever quitting Mr Garland’s service; but, after serious remonstrance
and advice from that gentleman, began to contemplate the possibility of
such a change being brought about in [[motifs/time|time]].  A good post was procured
for him, with a rapidity which took away his breath, by some of the
gentlemen who had believed him guilty of the offence laid to his
charge, and who had acted upon that belief.  Through the same kind
agency, his mother was secured from want, and made quite happy.  Thus,
as Kit often said, his great misfortune turned out to be the source of
all his subsequent prosperity.

Did Kit live a single man all his days, or did he marry?  Of course he
married, and who should be his wife but Barbara?  And the best of it
was, he married so soon that little Jacob was an uncle, before the
calves of his legs, already mentioned in this [[concepts/history|history]], had ever been
encased in broadcloth pantaloons,--though that was not quite the best
either, for of necessity the baby was an uncle too.  The delight of
Kit’s mother and of Barbara’s mother upon the great occasion is past
all telling; finding they agreed so [[motifs/well|well]] on that, and on all other
subjects, they took up their abode together, and were a most harmonious
pair of friends from that [[motifs/time|time]] forth.  And hadn’t Astley’s cause to
bless itself for their all going together once a quarter--to the
pit--and didn’t Kit’s mother always say, when they painted the outside,
that Kit’s last treat had helped to that, and [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] what the manager
would feel if he but knew it as they passed his house!

When Kit had children six and seven years old, there was a Barbara
among them, and a pretty Barbara she was.  Nor was there wanting an
exact facsimile and copy of little Jacob, as he appeared in those
remote times when they taught him what oysters meant.  Of course there
was an Abel, own godson to the Mr Garland of that name; and there was a
Dick, whom Mr Swiveller did especially favour.  The little group would
often gather round him of a [[motifs/night|night]] and beg him to tell again that story
of good Miss Nell who died.  This, Kit would do; and when they cried to
hear it, wishing it longer too, he would teach them how she had gone to
Heaven, as all good people did; and how, if they were good, like her,
they might [[concepts/hope|hope]] to be there too, one day, and to see and know her as he
had done when he was quite a boy.  Then, he would relate to them how
needy he used to be, and how she had taught him what he was otherwise
too poor to learn, and how the old man had been used to say ‘she always
laughs at Kit;’ at which they would brush away their [[motifs/tears|tears]], and laugh
themselves to think that she had done so, and be again quite merry.

He sometimes took them to the street where she had lived; but new
improvements had altered it so much, it was not like the same.  The old
house had been long ago pulled down, and a fine broad [[motifs/road|road]] was in its
place.  At first he would draw with his stick a square upon the ground
to show them where it used to stand.  But he soon became uncertain of
the spot, and could only say it was thereabouts, he thought, and these
alterations were confusing.

Such are the changes which a few years bring about, and so do things
pass away, like a tale that is told!




<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_01" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 1 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/city,motif/death,motif/dreams,motif/flowers,motif/garden,motif/home,motif/love,motif/night,motif/noon,motif/pain,motif/road,motif/spring,motif/summer,motif/time,motif/water,motif/window,concept/hope,concept/poverty,concept/suicide,concept/truth,concept/wonder,setting/castle,setting/court"></span>


CHAPTER 1

Although I am an old man, [[motifs/night|night]] is generally my [[motifs/time|time]] for walking. In the
[[motifs/summer|summer]] I often leave [[motifs/home|home]] early in the morning, and roam about fields
and lanes all day, or even escape for days or weeks together; but,
saving in the country, I seldom go out until after dark, though, Heaven
be thanked, I [[motifs/love|love]] its light and feel the cheerfulness it sheds upon the
earth, as much as any creature living.

I have fallen insensibly into this habit, both because it favours my
infirmity and because it affords me greater opportunity of speculating
on the characters and occupations of those who fill the streets. The
glare and hurry of broad [[motifs/noon|noon]] are not adapted to idle pursuits like
mine; a glimpse of passing faces caught by the light of a street-lamp
or a shop [[motifs/window|window]] is often better for my purpose than their full
revelation in the daylight; and, if I must add the [[concepts/truth|truth]], [[motifs/night|night]] is
kinder in this respect than day, which too often destroys an air-built
[[settings/castle|castle]] at the moment of its completion, without the least ceremony or
remorse.

That constant pacing to and fro, that never-ending restlessness, that
incessant tread of feet wearing the rough stones smooth and glossy--is
it not a [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] how the dwellers in narrows ways can bear to hear it!
Think of a sick man in such a place as Saint Martin’s [[settings/court|Court]], listening
to the footsteps, and in the midst of [[motifs/pain|pain]] and weariness obliged,
despite himself (as though it were a task he must perform) to detect
the [[archetypes/child|child]]’s step from the man’s, the slipshod beggar from the booted
exquisite, the lounging from the busy, the dull heel of the sauntering
outcast from the quick tread of an expectant pleasure-seeker--think of
the hum and noise always being present to his sense, and of the stream
of life that will not stop, pouring on, on, on, through all his
restless [[motifs/dreams|dreams]], as if he were condemned to lie, dead but conscious, in
a noisy churchyard, and had no [[concepts/hope|hope]] of rest for centuries to come.

Then, the crowds forever passing and repassing on the bridges (on
those which are free of toll at least), where many stop on fine evenings
looking listlessly down upon the [[motifs/water|water]] with some vague idea that by and
by it runs between green banks which grow wider and wider until at last
it joins the broad vast sea--where some halt to rest from heavy loads
and think as they look over the parapet that to smoke and lounge away
one’s life, and lie sleeping in the sun upon a hot tarpaulin, in a
dull, slow, sluggish barge, must be happiness unalloyed--and where
some, and a very different class, pause with heavier loads than they,
remembering to have heard or read in old [[motifs/time|time]] that drowning was not a
hard [[motifs/death|death]], but of all means of [[concepts/suicide|suicide]] the easiest and best.

Covent [[motifs/garden|Garden]] Market at sunrise too, in the [[motifs/spring|spring]] or [[motifs/summer|summer]], when the
fragrance of sweet [[motifs/flowers|flowers]] is in the air, over-powering even the
unwholesome streams of last [[motifs/night|night]]’s debauchery, and driving the dusky
thrush, whose cage has hung outside a garret [[motifs/window|window]] all [[motifs/night|night]] long,
half mad with joy! Poor bird! the only neighbouring thing at all akin
to the other little captives, some of whom, shrinking from the hot
hands of drunken purchasers, lie drooping on the path already, while
others, soddened by close contact, await the [[motifs/time|time]] when they shall be
watered and freshened up to please more sober company, and make old
clerks who pass them on their [[motifs/road|road]] to business, [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] what has filled
their breasts with visions of the country.

But my present purpose is not to expatiate upon my walks. The story I
am about to relate, and to which I shall recur at intervals,  arose out
of one of these rambles; and thus I have been led to speak of them by
way of preface.

One [[motifs/night|night]] I had roamed into the [[motifs/city|City]], and was walking slowly on in my
usual way, musing upon a great many things, when I was arrested by an
inquiry, the purport of which did not reach me, but which seemed to be
addressed to myself, and was preferred in a soft sweet voice that
struck me very pleasantly. I turned hastily round and found at my elbow
a pretty little girl, who begged to be directed to a certain street at
a considerable distance, and indeed in quite another quarter of the
town.

‘It is a very long way from here,’ said I, ‘my [[archetypes/child|child]].’

‘I know that, sir,’ she replied timidly. ‘I am afraid it is a very long
way, for I came from there to-[[motifs/night|night]].’

‘[[works/alone-(poe)|Alone]]?’ said I, in some surprise.

‘Oh, yes, I don’t mind that, but I am a little frightened now, for I
had lost my [[motifs/road|road]].’

‘And what made you ask it of me? Suppose I should tell you wrong?’

‘I am sure you will not do that,’ said the little creature,’ you are
such a very old gentleman, and walk so slow yourself.’

I cannot describe how much I was impressed by this appeal and the
energy with which it was made, which brought a tear into the [[archetypes/child|child]]’s
clear eye, and made her slight figure tremble as she looked up into my
face.

‘Come,’ said I, ‘I’ll take you there.’

She put her hand in mine as confidingly as if she had known me from her
cradle, and we trudged away together; the little creature accommodating
her pace to mine, and rather seeming to lead and take care of me than I
to be protecting her. I observed that every now and then she stole a
curious look at my face, as if to make quite sure that I was not
deceiving her, and that these glances (very sharp and keen they were
too) seemed to increase her confidence at every repetition.

For my part, my curiosity and interest were at least equal to the
[[archetypes/child|child]]’s, for [[archetypes/child|child]] she certainly was, although I thought it probably
from what I could make out, that her very small and delicate frame
imparted a peculiar youthfulness to her appearance. Though more
scantily attired than she might have been she was dressed with perfect
neatness, and betrayed no marks of [[concepts/poverty|poverty]] or neglect.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 1

Anche se sono un vecchio, la [[motifs/night|notte]] è generalmente il mio [[motifs/time|tempo]] per passeggiare. In [[motifs/summer|estate]] spesso lascio [[motifs/home|casa]] all'alba e vago per campi e stradine tutto il giorno, o addirittura mi assento per giorni o settimane di seguito; ma, salvo che in campagna, raramente esco dopo il tramonto, anche se, grazie al cielo, [[motifs/love|amo]] la sua luce e ne sento la gioia che diffonde sulla terra, tanto quanto qualsiasi creatura vivente.

Sono caduto senza accorgermene in questa abitudine, sia perché favorisce la mia debolezza che perché mi offre maggiori opportunità di riflettere sui caratteri e sulle occupazioni di coloro che affollano le strade. Lo splendore e l'affanno del pieno [[motifs/noon|mezzogiorno]] non sono adatti a passatempi oziosi come i miei; uno sguardo fugace ai volti che passano, catturato dalla luce di un lampione o della vetrina di un negozio, è spesso più utile al mio scopo della loro piena rivelazione alla luce del giorno; e, se devo aggiungere la [[concepts/truth|verità]], la [[motifs/night|notte]] è in questo senso più gentile del giorno, che troppo spesso distrugge un [[settings/castle|castello]] di aria nel momento del suo completamento, senza il minimo cerimoniale o rimorso.

Quel continuo camminare avanti e indietro, quella irrequieta incessante, quel passo che consuma le pietre ruvide fino a renderle lisce e lucide: non è strano che gli abitanti di quei vicoli ristretti riescano a sopportarne il rumore? Pensate a un uomo malato in un luogo come Saint Martin’s [[settings/court|Court]], costretto ad ascoltare i passi, e nel mezzo del [[motifs/pain|dolore]] e della stanchezza obbligato, suo malgrado (come se fosse un compito che deve assolvere) a distinguere il passo di un [[archetypes/child|bambino]] da quello di un uomo, lo straccione in pantofole dal damerino con gli stivali, chi si aggira senza meta da chi ha fretta, il tallone pesante del fuorilegge che gironzola da quello veloce di chi cerca piaceri: pensate al brusio e al rumore sempre presenti ai suoi sensi, e alla corrente della vita che non si ferma mai, che scorre avanti, avanti, avanti attraverso tutti i suoi inquieti [[motifs/dreams|sogni]], come se fosse condannato a giacere morto ma cosciente in un cimitero rumoroso e non avesse alcuna [[concepts/hope|speranza]] di riposo per i prossimi secoli.

Poi le folle che passano e ripassano per sempre sui ponti (almeno su quelli esenti da pedaggio), dove molti si fermano nelle belle serate a guardare con aria svogliata l'[[motifs/water|acqua]] sotto di loro, con la vaga idea che presto scorra tra rive verdi sempre più ampie fino a unirsi infine al vasto e immenso mare; dove alcuni si fermano per riposarsi dai pesanti carichi e pensano mentre guardano oltre il parapetto che fumare e trascorrere la vita in ozio, dormendo al sole su una calda tela cerata, in un battello lento, pigro e indolente, debba essere pura felicità; e dove alcuni, di classe ben diversa, si fermano con carichi più pesanti dei loro, ricordando di aver sentito o letto nei vecchi [[motifs/time|tempi]] che l'annegamento non era una [[motifs/death|morte]] dolorosa, ma il mezzo di [[concepts/suicide|suicidio]] più facile e migliore.

Il mercato di Covent [[motifs/garden|Garden]] all'alba anche in [[motifs/spring|primavera]] o [[motifs/summer|estate]], quando il profumo dei dolci [[motifs/flowers|fiori]] è nell'aria, soverchiando persino i flussi malsani della sbronza di ieri [[motifs/night|sera]], e facendo impazzire di gioia l'usignolo scuro, la cui gabbia è appesa fuori da una [[motifs/window|finestra]] del solaio tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]] lunga! Povero uccello! L'unica cosa vicina che abbia qualcosa in comune con gli altri piccoli prigionieri, alcuni dei quali, ritraendosi dalle mani calde degli acquirenti ubriachi, giacciono già appassiti sul sentiero, mentre altri, intrisi dal contatto ravvicinato, attendono il [[motifs/time|momento]] in cui saranno innaffiati e rinfrescati per compiacere compagnie più sobrie, e far [[concepts/wonder|meravigliare]] i vecchi impiegati che li superano sulla loro [[motifs/road|strada]] verso gli affari, chiedendosi cosa abbia riempito il loro petto di visioni della campagna.

Ma il mio scopo attuale non è di dilungarmi sulle mie passeggiate. La storia che sto per raccontare e a cui tornerò di tanto in tanto, nacque da una di queste escursioni; ed ecco perché sono stato indotto a parlarne come preambolo.

Una [[motifs/night|notte]] ero vagabondato fino alla [[motifs/city|Città]], e stavo camminando lentamente come al solito,
riflettendo su molte cose, quando fui fermato da una domanda, il cui significato non mi giunse chiaro,
ma che sembrava rivolta a me e fu pronunciata con una voce dolce e melodiosa
che mi colpì molto piacevolmente. Mi voltai in fretta e scoprii al mio fianco
una graziosa bambina, la quale chiedeva indicazioni per raggiungere una certa strada a notevole distanza,
e anzi in un'altra zona della città.

«È un viaggio molto lungo da qui», dissi io, «mio [[archetypes/child|piccolo]].»

«Lo so, signore», rispose timorosamente. «Temo che sia un viaggio molto lungo, perché sono venuta da lì [[motifs/night|questa]] notte».

«Solo?», dissi io, con un certo stupore.

«Oh, sì, non mi preoccupo di questo, ma ora ho un po' paura perché avevo perso la mia [[motifs/road|strada]].»

"E cosa ti ha spinto a chiedermelo? E se ti dicessi una bugia?"

«Sono sicura che non lo farete», disse la piccola creatura «siete un signore così anziano e camminate con tanta lentezza.»

Non posso descrivere quanto fossi colpito da questo appello e dalla
energia con cui fu fatto, che portò una lacrima nell'occhio limpido del [[archetypes/child|bambino]],
e fece tremare la sua esile figura mentre alzava lo sguardo verso il mio viso.

'Vieni,' dissi io, 'ti accompagno lì.'

Lei mi mise la mano nella mia con fiducia come se mi avesse conosciuto dalla sua culla e ci allontanammo insieme; la piccola creatura adattava il suo passo al mio, sembrando piuttosto lei a guidarmi e prendersi cura di me che io a proteggerla. Notai che ogni tanto mi lanciava un'occhiata curiosa sul viso, come se volesse assicurarsi che non la stessi ingannando, e che queste occhiate (erano molto acute e penetranti) sembravano aumentare la sua fiducia ad ogni ripetizione.

Per quanto mi riguarda, la mia curiosità e il mio interesse erano almeno pari a quelli del [[archetypes/child|bambino]], perché tale era certamente lei, anche se pensavo che probabilmente, da quello che potevo capire, il suo fisico molto piccolo e delicato le conferiva un aspetto particolarmente giovanile. Sebbene fosse vestita più modestamente di quanto avrebbe potuto essere, era comunque abbigliata con perfetta cura e non mostrava segni di [[concepts/poverty|povertà]] o trascuratezza.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_02" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 1 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/dreams,motif/fire,motif/ghosts,motif/home,motif/love,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/road,motif/time,concept/fear,concept/jealousy,concept/nature,concept/truth,form/riddle"></span>


‘Who has sent you so far by yourself?’ said I.

‘Someone who is very kind to me, sir.’

‘And what have you been doing?’

‘That, I must not tell,’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]] firmly.

There was something in the manner of this reply which caused me to look
at the little creature with an involuntary expression of surprise; for
I wondered what kind of errand it might be that occasioned her to be
prepared for questioning. Her quick eye seemed to read my thoughts, for
as it met mine she added that there was no harm in what she had been
doing, but it was a great secret--a secret which she did not even know
herself.

This was said with no appearance of cunning or deceit, but with an
unsuspicious frankness that bore the impress of [[concepts/truth|truth]]. She walked on as
before, growing more familiar with me as we proceeded and talking
cheerfully by the way, but she said no more about her [[motifs/home|home]], beyond
remarking that we were going quite a new [[motifs/road|road]] and asking if it were a
short one.

While we were thus engaged, I revolved in my mind a hundred different
explanations of the [[forms/riddle|riddle]] and rejected them every one. I really felt
ashamed to take advantage of the ingenuousness or grateful feeling of
the [[archetypes/child|child]] for the purpose of gratifying my curiosity. I [[motifs/love|love]] these
little people; and it is not a slight thing when they, who are so fresh
from God, [[motifs/love|love]] us. As I had felt pleased at first by her confidence I
determined to deserve it, and to do credit to the [[concepts/nature|nature]] which had
prompted her to repose it in me.

There was no reason, however, why I should refrain from seeing the
person who had inconsiderately sent her to so great a distance by [[motifs/night|night]]
and alone, and as it was not improbable that if she found herself near
[[motifs/home|home]] she might take farewell of me and deprive me of the opportunity, I
avoided the most frequented ways and took the most intricate, and thus
it was not until we arrived in the street itself that she knew where we
were. Clapping her hands with pleasure and running on before me for a
short distance, my little acquaintance stopped at a door and remaining
on the step till I came up knocked at it when I joined her.

A part of this door was of glass unprotected by any shutter, which I
did not observe at first, for all was very dark and silent within, and
I was anxious (as indeed the [[archetypes/child|child]] was also) for an answer to our
summons. When she had knocked twice or thrice there was a noise as if
some person were moving inside, and at length a faint light appeared
through the glass which, as it approached very slowly, the bearer
having to make his way through a great many scattered articles, enabled
me to see both what kind of person it was who advanced and what kind of
place it was through which he came.

It was an old man with long grey hair, whose face and figure as he held
the light above his head and looked before him as he approached, I
could plainly see. Though much altered by age, I fancied I could
recognize in his spare and slender form something of that delicate
mould which I had noticed in the [[archetypes/child|child]]. Their bright blue eyes were
certainly alike, but his face was so deeply furrowed and so very full
of care, that here all resemblance ceased.

The place through which he made his way at leisure was one of those
receptacles for old and curious things which seem to crouch in odd
corners of this town and to hide their musty treasures from the public
eye in [[concepts/jealousy|jealousy]] and distrust. There were suits of mail standing like
[[motifs/ghosts|ghosts]] in armour here and there, fantastic carvings brought from
monkish cloisters, rusty weapons of various kinds, distorted figures in
china and wood and iron and ivory: tapestry and strange furniture that
might have been designed in [[motifs/dreams|dreams]]. The haggard aspect of the little
old man was wonderfully suited to the place; he might have groped among
old churches and tombs and deserted houses and gathered all the spoils
with his own hands. There was nothing in the whole collection but was
in keeping with himself nothing that looked older or more worn than he.

As he turned the key in the lock, he surveyed me with some astonishment
which was not diminished when he looked from me to my companion. The
door being opened, the [[archetypes/child|child]] addressed him as grandfather, and told him
the little story of our companionship.

‘Why, bless thee, [[archetypes/child|child]],’ said the old man, patting her on the head,
‘how couldst thou miss thy way? What if I had lost thee, Nell!’

‘I would have found my way back to YOU, grandfather,’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]]
boldly; ‘never [[concepts/fear|fear]].’

The old man kissed her, then turning to me and begging me to walk in, I
did so. The door was closed and locked. Preceding me with the light, he
led me through the place I had already seen from without, into a small
sitting-room behind, in which was another door opening into a kind of
closet, where I saw a little bed that a fairy might have slept in, it
looked so very small and was so prettily arranged. The [[archetypes/child|child]] took a
candle and tripped into this little room, leaving the old man and me
together.

‘You must be tired, sir,’ said he as he placed a chair near the [[motifs/fire|fire]],
‘how can I thank you?’

‘By taking more care of your grandchild another [[motifs/time|time]], my good friend,’
I replied.

‘More care!’ said the old man in a shrill voice, ‘more care of Nelly!
Why, who ever loved a [[archetypes/child|child]] as I [[motifs/love|love]] Nell?’

He said this with such evident surprise that I was perplexed what
answer to make, and the more so because coupled with something feeble
and wandering in his manner, there were in his face marks of deep and
anxious thought which convinced me that he could not be, as I had been
at first inclined to suppose, in a state of dotage or imbecility.

‘I don’t think you consider--’ I began.

‘I don’t consider!’ cried the old man interrupting me, ‘I don’t
consider her! Ah, how little you know of the [[concepts/truth|truth]]! Little Nelly,
little Nelly!’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

«Chi vi ha mandato così lontano da solo?» dissi io.

'Qualcuno che è molto gentile con me, signore.'

E cosa hai fatto?

«Questo non devo dirlo», disse il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] con fermezza.

C'era qualcosa nel modo di questa risposta che mi fece guardare la piccola creatura con un'espressione involontaria di sorpresa; perché mi chiedevo quale genere di missione potesse averla portata a prepararsi per essere interrogata. Il suo sguardo rapido sembrava leggere i miei pensieri, perché quando incontrò il mio aggiunse che non c'era niente di male in quello che aveva fatto, ma era un grande segreto--un segreto che lei stessa non conosceva.

Questo fu detto senza alcun'apparenza di astuzia o inganno, ma con una franchezza spontanea che portava l'impronta della [[concepts/truth|verità]]. Camminò come prima, diventando più familiare con me man mano che procedevamo e parlando allegramente lungo il cammino, ma non disse altro riguardo alla sua [[motifs/home|casa]], se non osservando che stavamo percorrendo una [[motifs/road|strada]] completamente nuova e chiedendo se fosse breve.

Mentre eravamo così impegnati, ho vagliato nella mia mente cento diverse spiegazioni dell'[[forms/riddle|enigma]] e le ho scartate tutte. Mi sentivo davvero in colpa a sfruttare l'ingenuità o il senso di gratitudine del [[archetypes/child|bambino]] per soddisfare la mia curiosità. [[motifs/love|Amo]] questi piccoli; e non è cosa da poco quando loro, che sono così freschi da Dio, ci [[motifs/love|amano]]. Poiché mi ero sentito lusingato inizialmente dalla sua fiducia ho deciso di meritarmela, e di onorare la [[concepts/nature|natura]] che le aveva suggerito di riporre in me tale fiducia.

Non c'era tuttavia motivo per cui dovessi astenermi dal vedere la persona che l'aveva inviata in modo sconsiderato a una così grande distanza di [[motifs/night|notte]] e sola, e poiché non era improbabile che, se si fosse trovata vicino a [[motifs/home|casa]], avrebbe potuto salutarmi e privarmi dell'opportunità, evitai le vie più frequentate e ne scelsi delle più intricate; così fu solo quando arrivammo nella strada stessa che lei seppe dove ci trovavamo. Battendo le mani per la gioia e correndo davanti a me per una breve distanza, la mia piccola conoscente si fermò davanti a una porta e rimase sul gradino fino al mio arrivo; quando mi unii a lei, bussò alla porta.

Una parte di questa porta era in vetro non protetto da nessuna persiana, cosa che non notai subito perché all'interno tutto era molto buio e silenzioso, ed ero ansioso (come lo era anche il [[archetypes/child|bambino]]) di ricevere una risposta al nostro richiamo. Quando ebbe bussato due o tre volte si udì un rumore come se qualcuno stesse muovendosi all'interno e infine apparve una luce fioca attraverso il vetro che, avvicinandosi molto lentamente perché chi la portava doveva farsi strada tra molti oggetti sparsi, mi permise di vedere sia che tipo di persona si avvicinasse sia che tipo di luogo fosse quello in cui si trovava.

Era un vecchio con lunghi capelli grigi; potevo vedere chiaramente il suo volto e la sua figura mentre teneva la luce sopra la testa e guardava davanti a sé avvicinandosi. Anche se molto cambiato dall'età, mi sembrò di riconoscere nella sua forma magra e snella qualcosa di quella delicata struttura che avevo notato nel [[archetypes/child|bambino]]. I loro luminosi occhi blu erano certamente simili, ma il suo volto era così profondamente segnato e così pieno di preoccupazioni che qui ogni somiglianza cessava.

Il luogo attraverso il quale si fece strada con calma era uno di quei
receptacoli per cose vecchie e curiose che sembrano accovacciarsi in angoli
strani di questa città e nascondere i loro tesori muffosi dall'occhio pubblico
in [[concepts/jealousy|gelosia]] e sfiducia. C'erano armature che stavano lì come
[[motifs/ghosts|fantasmi]] in armatura qua e là, intagli fantastici portati da
chiostri monastici, armi arrugginite di vario genere, figure distorte in
ceramica e legno e ferro e avorio: arazzi e mobili strani che
avrebbero potuto essere stati progettati in [[motifs/dreams|sogni]]. L'aspetto emaciato del piccolo
vecchietto si adattava meravigliosamente al luogo; avrebbe potuto aver frugato tra
vecchie chiese e tombe e case deserte e raccolto tutti i bottini
con le sue stesse mani. Non c'era nulla in tutta la collezione che non fosse
in armonia con lui, niente che sembrasse più vecchio o più consumato di lui.

Mentre girava la chiave nella serratura, mi osservò con un certo stupore,
che non diminuì quando passò lo sguardo da me al mio compagno.
Aperta la porta, il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] lo chiamò nonno e gli raccontò
la breve storia della nostra compagnia.

«Ma benedetta te, [[archetypes/child|bambina]]», disse il vecchio accarezzandole la testa,
«come hai potuto perdere la strada? E se ti avessi persa io, Nell!»

«Sarei riuscito a tornare da VOI, nonno», disse il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] con coraggio;
«non avete mai motivo di [[concepts/fear|temere]].»

Il vecchio la baciò e poi si rivolse a me pregandomi di entrare; lo feci.
La porta fu chiusa e sbarrata. Precedendomi con la luce, mi condusse attraverso il luogo che avevo già visto dall'esterno fino ad una piccola sala da soggiorno sul retro, in cui si apriva un'altra porta su di una specie di ripostiglio dove vidi un lettino così minuscolo e graziosamente apparecchiato che avrebbe potuto ospitare una fata. La [[archetypes/child|bambina]] prese una candela ed entrò in questa piccola stanza, lasciando il vecchio e me soli insieme.

«Dovete essere stanco, signore», disse mentre metteva una sedia vicino al [[motifs/fire|fuoco]], «come posso ringraziarvi?»

«Prendendosi più cura di suo nipote un'altra [[motifs/time|volta]], mio buon amico», replicai.

«Più attenzione!» disse il vecchio con voce stridula «più attenzione per Nellie! Chi mai ha amato un [[archetypes/child|bambino]] come io [[motifs/love|amo]] Nell?»

Lo disse con tale evidente sorpresa che rimasi perplesso su quale risposta dare,
e ancor più perché accoppiato a qualcosa di debole e vagante nel suo comportamento,
c'erano sul suo volto i segni di un pensiero profondo e ansioso, il che mi convinse
che non poteva essere, come inizialmente avevo supposto, in uno stato di demenza o imbecillità.

«Non credo che tu consideri --» cominciai.

«Non la considero!» gridò il vecchio interrompendomi «non la considero!
Ah, quanto poco conosci la [[concepts/truth|verità]]! Povera piccola Nell, povera piccola Nell!»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_03" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 1 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/childhood,motif/fire,motif/love,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,form/comedy"></span>


It would be impossible for any man, I care not what his form of speech
might be, to express more affection than the dealer in curiosities did,
in these four words. I waited for him to speak again, but he rested his
chin upon his hand and shaking his head twice or thrice fixed his eyes
upon the [[motifs/fire|fire]].

While we were sitting thus in [[motifs/silence|silence]], the door of the closet opened,
and the [[archetypes/child|child]] returned, her light brown hair hanging loose about her
neck, and her face flushed with the haste she had made to rejoin us.
She busied herself immediately in preparing supper, and while she was
thus engaged I remarked that the old man took an opportunity of
observing me more closely than he had done yet. I was surprised to see
that all this [[motifs/time|time]] everything was done by the [[archetypes/child|child]], and that there
appeared to be no other persons but ourselves in the house. I took
advantage of a moment when she was absent to venture a hint on this
point, to which the old man replied that there were few grown persons
as trustworthy or as careful as she.

‘It always grieves me,’ I observed, roused by what I took to be his
selfishness, ‘it always grieves me to contemplate the initiation of
children into the ways of life, when they are scarcely more than
infants. It checks their confidence and simplicity--two of the best
qualities that Heaven gives them--and demands that they share our
sorrows before they are capable of entering into our enjoyments.’

‘It will never check hers,’ said the old man looking steadily at me,
‘the springs are too deep. Besides, the children of the poor know but
few pleasures. Even the cheap delights of [[motifs/childhood|childhood]] must be bought and
paid for.’

‘But--forgive me for saying this--you are surely not so very
poor’--said I.

‘She is not my [[archetypes/child|child]], sir,’ returned the old man. ‘Her mother was, and
she was poor. I save nothing--not a penny--though I live as you see,
but’--he laid his hand upon my arm and leant forward to whisper--‘she
shall be rich one of these days, and a fine lady. Don’t you think ill
of me because I use her help. She gives it cheerfully as you see, and
it would break her heart if she knew that I suffered anybody else to do
for me what her little hands could undertake. I don’t consider!’--he
cried with sudden querulousness, ‘why, God knows that this one [[archetypes/child|child]] is
the thought and object of my life, and yet he never prospers me--no,
never!’

At this juncture, the subject of our conversation again returned, and
the old man motioning to me to approach the table, broke off, and said
no more.

We had scarcely begun our repast when there was a knock at the door by
which I had entered, and Nell bursting into a hearty laugh, which I was
rejoiced to hear, for it was childlike and full of hilarity, said it
was no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] dear old Kit coming back at last.

‘Foolish Nell!’ said the old man fondling with her hair. ‘She always
laughs at poor Kit.’

The [[archetypes/child|child]] laughed again more heartily than before, and I could not help
smiling from pure sympathy. The little old man took up a candle and
went to open the door. When he came back, Kit was at his heels.

Kit was a shock-headed, shambling, awkward lad with an uncommonly wide
mouth, very red cheeks, a turned-up nose, and certainly the most
comical expression of face I ever saw. He stopped short at the door on
seeing a stranger, twirled in his hand a perfectly round old hat
without any vestige of a brim, and resting himself now on one leg and
now on the other and changing them constantly, stood in the doorway,
looking into the parlour with the most extraordinary leer I ever
beheld. I entertained a grateful feeling towards the boy from that
minute, for I felt that he was the [[forms/comedy|comedy]] of the [[archetypes/child|child]]’s life.

‘A long way, wasn’t it, Kit?’ said the little old man.

‘Why, then, it was a goodish stretch, master,’ returned Kit.

‘Of course you have come back hungry?’

‘Why, then, I do consider myself rather so, master,’ was the answer.

The lad had a remarkable manner of standing sideways as he spoke, and
thrusting his head forward over his shoulder, as if he could not get at
his voice without that accompanying action. I think he would have
amused one anywhere, but the [[archetypes/child|child]]’s exquisite enjoyment of his oddity,
and the relief it was to find that there was something she associated
with merriment in a place that appeared so unsuited to her, were quite
irresistible. It was a great point too that Kit himself was flattered
by the sensation he created, and after several efforts to preserve his
gravity, burst into a loud roar, and so stood with his mouth wide open
and his eyes nearly shut, laughing violently.

The old man had again relapsed into his former abstraction and took no
notice of what passed, but I remarked that when her laugh was over, the
[[archetypes/child|child]]’s bright eyes were dimmed with [[motifs/tears|tears]], called forth by the
fullness of heart with which she welcomed her uncouth favourite after
the little anxiety of the [[motifs/night|night]]. As for Kit himself (whose laugh had
been all the [[motifs/time|time]] one of that sort which very little would change into
a cry) he carried a large slice of bread and meat and a mug of beer
into a corner, and applied himself to disposing of them with great
voracity.

‘Ah!’ said the old man turning to me with a sigh, as if I had spoken to
him but that moment, ‘you don’t know what you say when you tell me that
I don’t consider her.’

‘You must not attach too great weight to a remark founded on first
appearances, my friend,’ said I.

‘No,’ returned the old man thoughtfully, ‘no. Come hither, Nell.’

The little girl hastened from her seat, and put her arm about his neck.

‘Do I [[motifs/love|love]] thee, Nell?’ said he. ‘Say--do I [[motifs/love|love]] thee, Nell, or no?’

The [[archetypes/child|child]] only answered by her caresses, and laid her head upon his
breast.

‘Why dost thou sob?’ said the grandfather, pressing her closer to him
and glancing towards me. ‘Is it because thou know’st I [[motifs/love|love]] thee, and
dost not like that I should seem to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] it by my question? [[motifs/well|Well]],
[[motifs/well|well]]--then let us say I [[motifs/love|love]] thee dearly.’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Sarebbe impossibile per un uomo, non importa quale fosse il suo modo di parlare,
esprimere più affetto di quanto abbia fatto il commerciante di curiosità in queste quattro parole. Aspettai che riparlasse, ma si appoggiò il mento sulla mano e scuotendo la testa due o tre volte fissò gli occhi sul [[motifs/fire|fuoco]].

Mentre stavamo seduti così in [[motifs/silence|silenzio]], la porta dell'armadio si aprì,
e la [[archetypes/child|bambina]] tornò, con i suoi capelli castano chiari che le cadevano sciolti sul collo e il viso arrossato per l'affanno di essersi affrettata a raggiungerci.
Si mise subito all'opera per preparare la cena, e mentre era così impegnata notai che il vecchio approfittava dell'occasione per osservarmi più da vicino di quanto avesse fatto finora. Fui sorpreso nel vedere che in tutto questo [[motifs/time|tempo]] tutto veniva fatto dalla [[archetypes/child|bambina]], e che non sembravano esserci altre persone oltre a noi nella casa. Approfittai di un momento in cui era assente per fare una timida osservazione su questo punto, alla quale il vecchio rispose che pochi adulti erano affidabili o attenti quanto lei.

«Mi addolora sempre», osservai, spinto da quello che consideravo il suo egoismo, «mi addolora sempre vedere i bambini iniziati ai modi della vita quando sono appena più che infanti. Questo reprime la loro fiducia e semplicità - due delle migliori qualità che Dio gli dona - e pretende che condividano le nostre pene prima di essere capaci di partecipare alle nostre gioie».

«Non riuscirà mai a frenare la sua», disse il vecchio guardandomi fisso negli occhi,
«le molla sono troppo profonde. Inoltre, i figli dei poveri conoscono solo poche gioie.
Anche le modeste delizie dell'[[motifs/childhood|infanzia]] devono essere acquistate e pagate».

«Ma, perdoni se glielo dico, lei non è certamente così povero» -- dissi io.

«Non è mia [[archetypes/child|figlia]], signore», rispose il vecchio. «Lo era sua madre, e lei era povera. Non metto da parte nulla -- neanche un centesimo -- anche se vivo come vedete, ma» -- mi posò la mano sul braccio e si chinò in avanti per sussurrarmi -- «un giorno sarà ricca e una gran dama. Non pensate male di me perché accetto il suo aiuto. Lo offre con gioia, come vedete, e le spezzerebbe il cuore sapere che lascio fare a qualcun altro quello che le sue piccole mani possono fare. Io non ci penso!» -- esclamò con improvvisa querulosità -- «perché, Dio sa che questa [[archetypes/child|figlia]] è l'oggetto e il pensiero della mia vita, eppure lui non mi fa mai prosperare -- no, mai!»

In quel momento il soggetto della nostra conversazione tornò di nuovo in ballo e l'anziano signore, facendomi cenno di avvicinarmi al tavolo, si interruppe e non disse altro.

Avevamo appena iniziato il nostro pasto quando qualcuno bussò alla porta da cui ero entrato e Nell scoppiò in una risata sincera, che mi fece piacere sentire perché era infantile e piena di allegria, dicendo che non c'erano [[concepts/doubt|dubbi]]: il caro vecchio Kit stava finalmente tornando.

'Povera Nell!' disse il vecchio accarezzandole i capelli. 'Ride sempre di povero Kit.'

Il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] rise di nuovo più cordialmente che prima e io non potei fare a meno di sorridere per pura simpatia. Il vecchietto prese una candela e andò ad aprire la porta. Quando tornò, Kit era alle sue calcagna.

Kit era un ragazzo con i capelli arruffati, goffo e maldestro, con una bocca straordinariamente larga,
le guance molto rosse, il naso all'insù e certamente l'espressione facciale più
comica che io abbia mai visto. Si fermò di colpo sulla porta alla vista di uno sconosciuto, fece girare in mano un vecchio cappello perfettamente rotondo senza alcun segno di tesa, e appoggiandosi ora su una gamba e ora sull'altra, cambiandole costantemente, rimase sulla soglia,
guardando nel salotto con il ghigno più straordinario che io abbia mai
visto. Da quel momento provai un sentimento di gratitudine verso quel ragazzo, perché sentivo che lui era la [[forms/comedy|commedia]] della vita del [[archetypes/child|bambino]].

«Una lunga strada, non è vero, Kit?» disse il vecchietto.

«Ebbene, allora era un bel tratto, padrone», rispose Kit.

'Naturalmente siete tornati affamati?'

«Allora, sì, mi ritengo piuttosto tale, signore», fu la risposta.

Il ragazzo aveva un modo straordinario di stare in piedi di lato mentre parlava,
sporgendo la testa oltre la spalla, come se non potesse trovare la sua voce senza quell'azione accompagnatoria.
Penso che avrebbe divertito chiunque ovunque, ma il [[archetypes/child|bambino]]’s squisita gioia per la sua stranezza,
e il sollievo di scoprire che c'era qualcosa con cui associava la allegria in un luogo che sembrava così inadatto a lei,
erano davvero irresistibili. Fu anche molto importante che Kit stesso fosse lusingato
dalla sensazione che creava, e dopo diversi tentativi di mantenere la sua gravità,
scoppiò in una forte risata, e così rimase con la bocca spalancata
e gli occhi quasi chiusi, ridendo violentemente.

Il vecchio era di nuovo caduto nella sua precedente astrazione e non si accorgeva di ciò che succedeva intorno a lui, ma notai che quando la risata della [[archetypes/child|bambina]] finì i suoi occhi luminosi erano offuscati da [[motifs/tears|lacrime]], provocate dalla pienezza del cuore con cui aveva accolto il suo strano preferito dopo l'ansia della [[motifs/night|notte]]. Quanto a Kit (la cui risata era stata tutto quel [[motifs/time|tempo]] di un tipo che ben poco mancava dal trasformarsi in pianto) portò una grande fetta di pane e carne e una boccale di birra in un angolo, e si dedicò a consumarli con grande voracità.

«Ah!», disse il vecchio rivolgendosi a me con un sospiro, come se gli avessi appena parlato in quel momento, «non sai cosa dici quando mi fai presente che non la considero.»

«Non dovete attribuire troppo peso ad un'osservazione basata sulle prime impressioni, mio caro amico», dissi io.

'No,' rispose l'uomo anziano pensieroso, 'no. Vieni qui, Nell.'

La bambina si affrettò ad alzarsi dal suo posto e gli mise un braccio intorno al collo.

«Ti [[motifs/love|amo]], Nell?» disse lui. «Dimmi: ti [[motifs/love|amo]], Nell, o no?»

La [[archetypes/child|bambina]] rispose solo con le sue carezze e posò la testa sul suo petto.

«Perché piangi?» disse il nonno, stringendola più vicino a sé e guardandomi. «È perché sai che ti [[motifs/love|amo]] e non vuoi che io sembri [[concepts/doubt|dubitare]] di questo con la mia domanda? [[motifs/well|Bene]], [[motifs/well|bene]]--allora diciamo che ti [[motifs/love|amo]] teneramente.»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_01--part_04" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 1 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 01" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/fool,motif/home,motif/night,motif/pain,motif/rose,motif/silence,motif/sleep,motif/time,motif/well,concept/beauty"></span>


‘Indeed, indeed you do,’ replied the [[archetypes/child|child]] with great earnestness, ‘Kit
knows you do.’

Kit, who in despatching his bread and meat had been swallowing
two-thirds of his knife at every mouthful with the coolness of a
juggler, stopped short in his operations on being thus appealed to, and
bawled ‘Nobody isn’t such a [[archetypes/fool|fool]] as to say he doosn’t,’ after which he
incapacitated himself for further conversation by taking a most
prodigious sandwich at one bite.

‘She is poor now’--said the old man, patting the [[archetypes/child|child]]’s cheek, ‘but I
say again that the [[motifs/time|time]] is coming when she shall be rich. It has been a
long [[motifs/time|time]] coming, but it must come at last; a very long [[motifs/time|time]], but it
surely must come. It has come to other men who do nothing but waste and
riot. When WILL it come to me!’

‘I am very happy as I am, grandfather,’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]].

‘Tush, tush!’ returned the old man, ‘thou dost not know--how should’st
thou!’ then he muttered again between his teeth, ‘The [[motifs/time|time]] must come, I
am very sure it must. It will be all the better for coming late’; and
then he sighed and fell into his former musing state, and still holding
the [[archetypes/child|child]] between his knees appeared to be insensible to everything
around him. By this [[motifs/time|time]] it wanted but a few minutes of midnight and I
[[motifs/rose|rose]] to go, which recalled him to himself.

‘One moment, sir,’ he said, ‘Now, Kit--near midnight, boy, and you
still here! Get [[motifs/home|home]], get [[motifs/home|home]], and be true to your [[motifs/time|time]] in the
morning, for there’s work to do. Good [[motifs/night|night]]! There, bid him good [[motifs/night|night]],
Nell, and let him be gone!’

‘Good [[motifs/night|night]], Kit,’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]], her eyes lighting up with merriment
and kindness.

‘Good [[motifs/night|night]], Miss Nell,’ returned the boy.

‘And thank this gentleman,’ interposed the old man, ‘but for whose care
I might have lost my little girl to-[[motifs/night|night]].’

‘No, no, master,’ said Kit, ‘that won’t do, that won’t.’

‘What do you mean?’ cried the old man.

‘I’d have found her, master,’ said Kit, ‘I’d have found her. I’ll bet
that I’d find her if she was above ground, I would, as quick as
anybody, master. Ha, ha, ha!’

Once more opening his mouth and shutting his eyes, and laughing like a
stentor, Kit gradually backed to the door, and roared himself out.

Free of the room, the boy was not slow in taking his departure; when he
had gone, and the [[archetypes/child|child]] was occupied in clearing the table, the old man
said:

‘I haven’t seemed to thank you, sir, for what you have done to-[[motifs/night|night]],
but I do thank you humbly and heartily, and so does she, and her thanks
are better worth than mine. I should be sorry that you went away, and
thought I was unmindful of your goodness, or careless of her--I am not
indeed.’

I was sure of that, I said, from what I had seen. ‘But,’ I added, ‘may
I ask you a question?’

‘Ay, sir,’ replied the old man, ‘What is it?’

‘This delicate [[archetypes/child|child]],’ said I, ‘with so much [[concepts/beauty|beauty]] and
intelligence--has she nobody to care for her but you? Has she no other
companion or advisor?’

‘No,’ he returned, looking anxiously in my face, ‘no, and she wants no
other.’

‘But are you not fearful,’ said I, ‘that you may misunderstand a charge
so tender? I am sure you mean [[motifs/well|well]], but are you quite certain that you
know how to execute such a trust as this? I am an old man, like you,
and I am actuated by an old man’s concern in all that is young and
promising. Do you not think that what I have seen of you and this
little creature to-[[motifs/night|night]] must have an interest not wholly free from
[[motifs/pain|pain]]?’

‘Sir,’ rejoined the old man after a moment’s [[motifs/silence|silence]]. ‘I have no right
to feel hurt at what you say. It is true that in many respects I am the
[[archetypes/child|child]], and she the grown person--that you have seen already. But waking
or sleeping, by [[motifs/night|night]] or day, in sickness or health, she is the one
object of my care, and if you knew of how much care, you would look on
me with different eyes, you would indeed. Ah! It’s a weary life for an
old man--a weary, weary life--but there is a great end to gain and that
I keep before me.’

Seeing that he was in a state of excitement and impatience, I turned to
put on an outer coat which I had thrown off on entering the room,
purposing to say no more. I was surprised to see the [[archetypes/child|child]] standing
patiently by with a cloak upon her arm, and in her hand a hat, and
stick.

‘Those are not mine, my dear,’ said I.

‘No,’ returned the [[archetypes/child|child]], ‘they are grandfather’s.’

‘But he is not going out to-[[motifs/night|night]].’

‘Oh, yes, he is,’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]], with a smile.

‘And what becomes of you, my pretty one?’

‘Me! I stay here of course. I always do.’

I looked in astonishment towards the old man, but he was, or feigned to
be, busied in the arrangement of his dress. From him I looked back to
the slight gentle figure of the [[archetypes/child|child]]. [[works/alone-(poe)|Alone]]! In that gloomy place all
the long, dreary [[motifs/night|night]].

She evinced no consciousness of my surprise, but cheerfully helped the
old man with his cloak, and when he was ready took a candle to light us
out. Finding that we did not follow as she expected, she looked back
with a smile and waited for us.  The old man showed by his face that he
plainly understood the cause of my hesitation, but he merely signed to
me with an inclination of the head to pass out of the room before him,
and remained silent. I had no resource but to comply.

When we reached the door, the [[archetypes/child|child]] setting down the candle, turned to
say good [[motifs/night|night]] and raised her face to kiss me. Then she ran to the old
man, who folded her in his arms and bade God bless her.

‘[[motifs/sleep|Sleep]] soundly, Nell,’ he said in a low voice, ‘and angels guard thy
bed! Do not forget thy prayers, my sweet.’

‘No, indeed,’ answered the [[archetypes/child|child]] fervently, ‘they make me feel so
happy!’

‘That’s [[motifs/well|well]]; I know they do; they should,’ said the old man. ‘Bless
thee a hundred times! Early in the morning I shall be [[motifs/home|home]].’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

«Sì, sì che lo fate», rispose il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] con grande serietà, «Kit sa che lo fate.»

Kit, che nel consumare il suo pane e carne aveva inghiottito due terzi del coltello ad ogni boccone con la freddezza di un giocoliere, si fermò bruscamente nelle sue operazioni quando fu così interpellato e gridò: «Nessuno non è così [[archetypes/fool|stupido]] da dire che non lo fa», dopo di che si rese incapace di ulteriori conversazioni prendendo un panino enorme in un solo morso.

«È povera adesso» -- disse il vecchio, accarezzando la guancia del [[archetypes/child|bambino]], «ma ripeto che sta arrivando il [[motifs/time|momento]] in cui sarà ricca. È un momento che tarda da molto [[motifs/time|tempo]] a venire, ma alla fine deve pur arrivare; un momento davvero lungo, ma sicuramente arriverà. È arrivato ad altri uomini che non fanno altro che sprecare e vivere nel lusso. Quando ARRIVERÀ per me!»

«Sono molto felice così com'è, nonno», disse il [[archetypes/child|bambino]].

«Bah, bah!» rispose il vecchio «tu non sai, come potresti saperlo?», poi borbottò tra i denti: «Il [[motifs/time|momento]] deve arrivare, ne sono sicuro. Sarà ancora meglio se arriverà tardi»; e quindi sospirò e ricadde nel suo precedente stato di meditazione, continuando a tenere il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] tra le ginocchia senza sembrare accorgersi di nulla intorno. A quell'[[motifs/time|ora]] mancavano solo pochi minuti alla mezzanotte e io mi [[motifs/rose|alzai]] per andarmene, il che lo riportò in sé.

«Un momento, signore», disse, «Ora, Kit, quasi mezzanotte, ragazzo, e tu ancora qui! Vai a [[motifs/home|casa]], vai a [[motifs/home|casa]] e rispetta il tuo [[motifs/time|orario]] domattina, perché c'è del lavoro da fare. Buona [[motifs/night|notte]]! Ecco, salutalo con un buon [[motifs/night|anotte]], Nell, e lascia che se ne vada!»

«Buona [[motifs/night|notte]], Kit», disse la [[archetypes/child|bambina]], con gli occhi che si illuminavano di allegria e gentilezza.

«Buona [[motifs/night|notte]], signorina Nell», rispose il ragazzo.

«E ringraziate questo signore», intervenne il vecchio, «se non fosse stato per la sua premura,
avrei potuto perdere mia figlia questa [[motifs/night|sera]].»

'No, no, padrone', disse Kit, 'questo non va bene, questo no'.

«Cosa intendete dire?» gridò il vecchio.

«L’avrei trovata, padrone», disse Kit, «l’avrei trovata. Scommetto che la troverei se fosse in giro per il mondo, sì, più in fretta di chiunque altro, padrone. Ha, ha, ha!»

Aprì di nuovo la bocca e strizzò gli occhi, ridendo come un Stentore, e Kit si ritirò lentamente verso la porta, urlando fino a uscire.

Uscito dalla stanza, il ragazzo non si fece pregare per andarsene; quando se ne fu andato e la [[archetypes/child|bambina]] era intenta a sparecchiare, l'anziano disse:

«Non sembra che io le abbia ringraziato, signore, per quello che ha fatto [[motifs/night|questa]] sera,
ma glielo ringrazio umilmente e con tutto il cuore, e lo fa anche lei, e i suoi ringraziamenti
valgono più dei miei. Mi dispiacerebbe se andasse via pensando che io non abbia apprezzato la sua gentilezza,
o che sia indifferente nei suoi confronti -- in realtà non lo sono».

Ne ero sicuro, dissi, per quello che avevo visto. «Ma», aggiunsi,
«posso farle una domanda?»

«Sì, signore», rispose il vecchio, «Cosa c'è?»

«Questa delicata [[archetypes/child|bambina]],» dissi io, «con tanta [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]] e intelligenza -- non ha nessuno che si prenda cura di lei se non voi? Non ha altri compagni o consiglieri?»

'No', rispose lui, guardandomi ansiosamente in faccia, 'no, e lei non ne vuole altri'.

«Ma non temete», dissi, «di fraintendere un incarico così delicato? Sono certo che avete [[motifs/well|bene]] intenzioni, ma siete proprio sicuro di sapere come portare a termine una responsabilità del genere? Anch'io sono un vecchio, come voi, e mi muove la preoccupazione di un vecchio per tutto ciò che è giovane e promettente. Non pensate che quanto ho visto tra voi e questa piccola creatura stasera debba suscitare un interesse non del tutto privo di [[motifs/pain|dolore]]?»

«Signore», riprese il vecchio dopo un momento di [[motifs/silence|silenzio]]. «Non ho diritto di offendermi per quello che dice. È vero che in molti aspetti io sono il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] e lei la persona adulta, come ha già visto. Ma sveglio o addormentato, di [[motifs/night|notte]] o giorno, in salute o in malattia, è l'unico oggetto della mia cura, e se sapessi quanto mi preoccupo per lei, mi guarderebbe con occhi diversi, davvero. Ah! È una vita stancante per un vecchio, una vita stancante, ma c'è un grande scopo da raggiungere e lo tengo sempre presente».

Vedendo che era in uno stato di agitazione e impazienza, mi voltai per indossare un soprabito che avevo tolto entrando nella stanza, deciso a non dire altro. Fui sorpreso nel vedere la [[archetypes/child|bambina]] che stava pazientemente lì accanto con uno scialle sul braccio e in mano un cappello e un bastone.

«Quelle non sono mie, mia cara», dissi io.

«No», rispose il [[archetypes/child|bambino]], «sono del nonno».

«Ma lui non esce stasera [[motifs/night|stasera]].»

«Oh, sì, lo è», disse il [[archetypes/child|bambino]], con un sorriso.

'E cosa ne sarà di te, mia bella?'

'Noi! Certo che ci restiamo. Lo facciamo sempre.'

Guardai con stupore verso il vecchio, ma lui era, o fingeva di essere,
impegnato nell'aggiustare i suoi vestiti. Da lui guardai indietro alla
snella e gentile figura del [[archetypes/child|bambino]]. Solo! In quel luogo tetro per tutta la lunga, monotona [[motifs/night|notte]].

Non diede segno di accorgersi della mia sorpresa, ma allegra aiutò il vecchio con la sua giacca e quando fu pronto prese una candela per illuminarci la strada. Vedendo che non la seguivamo come si aspettava, si voltò sorridente ad attenderci. Il vecchio mostrò in volto di aver capito benissimo il motivo della mia esitazione, ma mi fece solo cenno con un inchino del capo di uscire dalla stanza prima di lui e rimase in silenzio. Non avevo altra scelta che obbedire.

Quando raggiungemmo la porta, il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] posò la candela e si voltò per augurarmi una buona [[motifs/night|notte]], alzando il viso per darmi un bacio. Poi corse dal vecchio che l'abbracciò forte e chiese a Dio di benedirla.

«Dormi tranquilla, Nell», disse con voce bassa, «e che gli angeli veglino sul tuo letto! Non dimenticare le tue preghiere, mia dolce.»

«No, davvero», rispose il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] con fervore, «mi fanno sentire così felice!»

«È [[motifs/well|bene]]; so che lo fanno; dovrebbero», disse il vecchio. «Ti benedico cento volte! Domattina presto sarò a [[motifs/home|casa]].»
