mates of East Indiamen, smoked his smuggled cigars under the very nose
of the Custom House, and made appointments on ‘Change with men in
glazed hats and round jackets pretty [[motifs/well|well]] every day. On the Surrey side
of the [[motifs/river|river]] was a small rat-infested dreary yard called ‘Quilp’s
Wharf,’ in which were a little wooden counting-house burrowing all awry
in the [[motifs/dust|dust]] as if it had fallen from the clouds and ploughed into the
ground; a few fragments of rusty anchors; several large iron rings;
some piles of rotten wood; and two or three heaps of old sheet copper,
crumpled, cracked, and battered. On Quilp’s Wharf, [[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]] was a
[[motifs/ship|ship]]-breaker, yet to judge from these appearances he must either have
been a [[motifs/ship|ship]]-breaker on a very small scale, or have broken his ships up
very small indeed. Neither did the place present any extraordinary
aspect of life or activity, as its only human occupant was an
amphibious boy in a canvas suit, whose sole change of occupation was
from sitting on the head of a pile and throwing stones into the mud
when the tide was out, to standing with his hands in his pockets gazing
listlessly on the motion and on the bustle of the [[motifs/river|river]] at high-[[motifs/water|water]].

The [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]]’s lodging on Tower [[motifs/hill|hill]] comprised, besides the needful
accommodation for himself and Mrs Quilp, a small sleeping-closet for
that lady’s mother, who resided with the couple and waged perpetual war
with Daniel; of whom, notwithstanding, she stood in no slight dread.
Indeed, the ugly creature contrived by some means or other--whether by
his ugliness or his ferocity or his natural cunning is no great
matter--to impress with a wholesome [[concepts/fear|fear]] of his anger, most of those
with whom he was brought into daily contact and communication. Over
nobody had he such complete ascendance as Mrs Quilp herself--a pretty
little, mild-spoken, blue-eyed woman, who having allied herself in
wedlock to the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]] in one of those strange infatuations of which
examples are by no means scarce, performed a sound practical penance
for her folly, every day of her life.

It has been said that Mrs Quilp was pining in her bower. In her bower
she was, but not alone, for besides the old lady her mother of whom
mention has recently been made, there were present some half-dozen
ladies of the neighborhood who had happened by a strange accident (and
also by a little understanding among themselves) to drop in one after
another, just about tea-[[motifs/time|time]]. This being a season favourable to
conversation, and the room being a cool, shady, lazy kind of place,
with some plants at the open [[motifs/window|window]] shutting out the [[motifs/dust|dust]], and
interposing pleasantly enough between the tea table within and the old
Tower without, it is no [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] that the ladies felt an inclination to
talk and linger, especially when there are taken into account the
additional inducements of fresh butter, new bread, shrimps, and
watercresses.

Now, the ladies being together under these circumstances, it was
extremely natural that the discourse should turn upon the propensity of
mankind to tyrannize over the weaker sex, and the duty that developed
upon the weaker sex to resist that tyranny and assert their rights and
dignity. It was natural for four reasons: firstly, because Mrs Quilp
being a young woman and notoriously under the dominion of her husband
ought to be excited to [[archetypes/rebel|rebel]]; secondly, because Mrs Quilp’s parent was
known to be laudably shrewish in her disposition and inclined to resist
male authority; thirdly, because each visitor wished to show for
herself how superior she was in this respect to the generality of her
sex; and fourthly, because the company being accustomed to scandalise
each other in pairs, were deprived of their usual subject of
conversation now that they were all assembled in close [[concepts/friendship|friendship]], and
had consequently no better employment than to attack the common enemy.

Moved by these considerations, a stout lady opened the proceedings by
inquiring, with an air of great concern and sympathy, how Mr Quilp was;
whereunto Mr Quilp’s wife’s mother replied sharply, ‘Oh! He was [[motifs/well|well]]
enough--nothing much was ever the matter with him--and ill weeds were
sure to thrive.’ All the ladies then sighed in concert, shook their
heads gravely, and looked at Mrs Quilp as a martyr.

‘Ah!’ said the spokeswoman, ‘I wish you’d give her a little of your
advice, Mrs Jiniwin’--Mrs Quilp had been a Miss Jiniwin it should be
observed--‘nobody knows better than you, ma’am, what us women owe to
ourselves.’

‘Owe indeed, ma’am!’ replied Mrs Jiniwin. ‘When my poor husband, her
dear father, was alive, if he had ever ventured a [[motifs/cross|cross]] word to me, I’d
have--’ The good old lady did not finish the sentence, but she twisted
off the head of a shrimp with a vindictiveness which seemed to imply
that the action was in some degree a substitute for words. In this
light it was clearly understood by the other party, who immediately
replied with great approbation, ‘You quite enter into my feelings,
ma’am, and it’s jist what I’d do myself.’

‘But you have no call to do it,’ said Mrs Jiniwin. ‘Luckily for you,
you have no more occasion to do it than I had.’

‘No woman need have, if she was true to herself,’ rejoined the stout
lady.

‘Do you hear that, Betsy?’ said Mrs Jiniwin, in a warning voice.  ‘How
often have I said the same words to you, and almost gone down my knees
when I spoke ‘em!’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 4

Il signor e la signora Quilp risiedevano su Tower [[motifs/hill|Hill]]; e nel suo boudoir su Tower [[motifs/hill|Hill]] la signora Quilp fu lasciata a languire per l'assenza del suo sposo, quando egli la abbandonò per occuparsi di quella faccenda che aveva già visto a conclusione.

Non si poteva dire che il signor Quilp esercitasse un mestiere o una professione particolare, sebbene le sue attività fossero varie e i suoi impieghi numerosi. Riscuoteva gli affitti di interi quartieri di strade e vicoli luridi lungo il [[motifs/river|fiume]], prestava denaro ai marinai e agli ufficiali minori delle navi mercantili, aveva una quota nelle imprese di vari capitani delle navi per le Indie Orientali, fumava i suoi sigari di contrabbando sotto al naso della Dogana, e si dava appuntamento alla Borsa con uomini in cappelli lucidi e giacche a quadri praticamente ogni giorno. Sulla riva del Surrey c'era un piccolo cortile desolato infestato dai topi chiamato "Molo di Quilp", dove si trovavano una piccola contabilità in legno che scavava nel [[motifs/dust|polvere]] come se fosse caduta dalle nuvole e avesse arato il terreno; alcuni frammenti di ancore arrugginite; diversi grandi anelli di ferro; alcune pile di legname marcio; e due o tre mucchi di vecchie lamiere di rame, accartocciate, crepate e ammaccate. Al Molo di Quilp, [[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]] era un demolitore di [[motifs/ship|navi]], ma a giudicare da queste apparenze doveva essere o un demolitore di navi su scala molto ridotta, o aver smantellato le sue navi in pezzi davvero piccoli. Né il posto presentava un aspetto straordinario di vita o attività, poiché il suo unico occupante umano era un ragazzo anfibio in tuta di tela cerata, la cui unica variazione di occupazione consisteva nel passare dal sedere sulla testa di una pila e lanciare sassi nel fango quando la marea era bassa, a stare in piedi con le mani nelle tasche fissando apaticamente il movimento e l'attività del [[motifs/river|fiume]] all'alta [[motifs/water|marea]].

L’alloggio del [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]] su Tower [[motifs/hill|hill]] comprendeva, oltre al necessario
spazio per lui e la signora Quilp, un piccolo ripostiglio da letto per
la madre di quella signora, che risiedeva con la coppia e combatteva una guerra perpetua
con Daniel; di cui, nonostante ciò, aveva una certa paura.
Infatti, la brutta creatura riusciva in qualche modo -- se fosse grazie
alla sua bruttezza o alla sua ferocia o al suo naturale inganno non ha molta importanza -- a imporre un sano [[concepts/fear|timore]] della sua ira su gran parte di coloro
con cui veniva quotidianamente in contatto e comunicazione. Su nessuno aveva un tale ascendente come sulla stessa signora Quilp -- una donna graziosa, dal parlare mite e dagli occhi azzurri, che avendo unito in matrimonio il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]] in uno di quegli strani capricci dei quali gli esempi non sono affatto rari, si pentiva ogni giorno della propria follia.

Si è detto che la signora Quilp languisse nel suo boudoir. Nel suo boudoir era, ma non da sola, perché oltre alla vecchia signora sua madre di cui si è recentemente parlato, erano presenti una mezza dozzina circa di signore del vicinato che per un strano caso (e anche grazie a qualche accordo tra loro) erano entrate una dopo l'altra proprio verso l'[[motifs/time|ora]] del tè. Essendo questa un'occasione propizia alla conversazione, e la stanza essendo un luogo fresco, ombreggiato e pigro, con alcune piante all'[[motifs/window|aperta finestra]] che tenevano lontana la [[motifs/dust|polvere]] e si interponessero in modo gradevole tra il tavolino del tè dentro e la vecchia Torre fuori, non c'è da [[concepts/wonder|stupirsi]] se le signore sentivano una certa inclinazione a chiacchierare e indugiare, specialmente quando si tengono in considerazione gli ulteriori incentivi del burro fresco, il pane nuovo, i gamberetti e i crescioni.

Ora che le signore si trovavano insieme in tali circostanze, era del tutto naturale che il discorso cadesse sulla propensione dell'umanità a tiranneggiare il sesso debole e sul dovere di quest'ultimo di resistere a tale tirannia e rivendicare i propri diritti e dignità. Era naturale per quattro ragioni: in primo luogo, perché la signora Quilp, essendo una giovane donna notoriamente sotto il dominio del marito, avrebbe dovuto essere incoraggiata ad [[archetypes/rebel|insorgere]]; in secondo luogo, perché si sapeva che la madre della signora Quilp era lodevolmente irascibile nel suo carattere e incline a resistere all'autorità maschile; in terzo luogo, perché ogni visitatrice desiderava dimostrare di essere superiore sotto questo aspetto alla maggior parte del proprio sesso; e in quarto luogo, perché le signore, abituate a scandalizzarsi l'una con l'altra a coppie, erano ora private dell'argomento di conversazione consueto, dato che si trovavano tutte riunite in stretta [[concepts/friendship|amicizia]], e non avevano quindi altro da fare se non attaccare il nemico comune.

Mossa da queste considerazioni, una signora robusta aprì i lavori chiedendo,
con un'aria di grande preoccupazione e simpatia, come stesse il signor Quilp;
alla quale la madre della moglie del signor Quilp rispose bruscamente: «Oh! Era [[motifs/well|bene]]
abbastanza - non c'era mai molto da dire su di lui - e le erbacce sono
sicuramente destinate a prosperare». Tutte le signore sospirarono all'unisono, scossero gravemente la testa e guardarono la signora Quilp come una martire.

«Ah!» disse la portavoce «vorrei che le dessi un po' dei tuoi consigli,
signora Jiniwin» -- va osservato che la signora Quilp era stata una certa miss Jiniwin --
«nessuno lo sa meglio di te, signora, cosa noi donne dobbiamo a
noi stesse.»

«Debito davvero, signora!» rispose la signora Jiniwin. «Quando mio povero marito, suo caro padre, era in vita, se avesse mai osato rivolgermi una parola [[motifs/cross|sgradevole]], io, » La buona vecchia non finì la frase, ma strappò via la testa di un gamberetto con tale vendicatività che sembrava voler dire che quell'azione fosse in qualche modo un sostituto delle parole. Questo fu chiaramente compreso dall'altra parte, che rispose subito con grande approvazione: «Entrate perfettamente nei miei sentimenti, signora, ed è esattamente quello che farei io stessa».

«Ma non hai motivo di farlo», disse la signora Jiniwin, «per fortuna tua, non hai più motivo di farlo di quelli che avevo io».

«Nessuna donna dovrebbe averne bisogno, se fosse fedele a sé stessa», replicò la signora robusta.

«Avete sentito, Betsy?» disse la signora Jiniwin con voce ammonitrice «Quante volte vi ho detto le stesse parole e quasi mi sono messa in ginocchio mentre le pronunciavo!»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_04--part_02" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 4 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 04" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/tyrant,motif/cross,motif/death,motif/lamb,motif/love,motif/marriage,motif/night,motif/silence,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,character/daniel_quilp"></span>


Poor Mrs Quilp, who had looked in a state of helplessness from one face
of condolence to another, coloured, smiled, and shook her head
doubtfully. This was the signal for a general clamour, which beginning
in a low murmur gradually swelled into a great noise in which everybody
spoke at once, and all said that she being a young woman had no right
to set up her opinions against the experiences of those who knew so
much better; that it was very wrong of her not to take the advice of
people who had nothing at heart but her good; that it was next door to
being downright ungrateful to conduct herself in that manner; that if
she had no respect for herself she ought to have some for other women,
all of whom she compromised by her meekness; and that if she had no
respect for other women, the [[motifs/time|time]] would come when other women would
have no respect for her; and she would be very sorry for that, they
could tell her. Having dealt out these admonitions, the ladies fell to
a more powerful assault than they had yet made upon the  mixed tea, new
bread, fresh butter, shrimps, and watercresses, and said that their
vexation was so great to see her going on like that, that they could
hardly bring themselves to eat a single morsel.

It’s all very fine to talk,’ said Mrs Quilp with much simplicity, ‘but
I know that if I was to die to-morrow, Quilp could marry anybody he
pleased--now that he could, I know!’

There was quite a scream of indignation at this idea. Marry whom he
pleased! They would like to see him dare to think of marrying any of
them; they would like to see the faintest approach to such a thing.
One lady (a widow) was quite certain she should stab him if he hinted
at it.

‘Very [[motifs/well|well]],’ said Mrs Quilp, nodding her head, ‘as I said just now,
it’s very easy to talk, but I say again that I know--that I’m
sure--Quilp has such a way with him when he likes, that the best
looking woman here couldn’t refuse him if I was dead, and she was free,
and he chose to make [[motifs/love|love]] to her. Come!’

Everybody bridled up at this remark, as much as to say, ‘I know you
mean me. Let him try--that’s all.’ and yet for some hidden reason they
were all angry with the widow, and each lady whispered in her
neighbour’s ear that it was very plain that said widow thought herself
the person referred to, and what a puss she was!

‘Mother knows,’ said Mrs Quilp, ‘that what I say is quite correct, for
she often said so before we were married. Didn’t you say so, mother?’

This inquiry involved the respected lady in rather a delicate position,
for she certainly had been an active party in making her daughter Mrs
Quilp, and, besides, it was not supporting the family credit to
encourage the idea that she had married a man whom nobody else would
have. On the other hand, to exaggerate the captivating qualities of her
son-in-law would be to weaken the cause of revolt, in which all her
energies were deeply engaged. Beset by these opposing considerations,
Mrs Jiniwin admitted the powers of insinuation, but denied the right to
govern, and with a timely compliment to the stout lady brought back the
discussion to the point from which it had strayed.

‘Oh! It’s a sensible and proper thing indeed, what Mrs George has
said!’ exclaimed the old lady. ‘If women are only true to
themselves!--But Betsy isn’t, and more’s the shame and pity.’

‘Before I’d let a man order me about as Quilp orders her,’ said Mrs
George, ‘before I’d consent to stand in awe of a man as she does of
him, I’d--I’d kill myself, and write a letter first to say he did it!’

This remark being loudly commended and approved of, another lady (from
the Minories) put in her word:

‘Mr Quilp may be a very nice man,’ said this lady, ‘and I supposed
there’s no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] he is, because Mrs Quilp says he is, and Mrs Jiniwin
says he is, and they ought to know, or nobody does. But still he is not
quite a--what one calls a handsome man, nor quite a young man neither,
which might be a little excuse for him if anything could be; whereas
his wife is young, and is good-looking, and is a woman--which is the
greatest thing after all.’

This last clause being delivered with extraordinary pathos, elicited a
corresponding murmer from the hearers, stimulated by which the lady
went on to remark that if such a husband was [[motifs/cross|cross]] and unreasonable
with such a wife, then--

‘If he is!’ interposed the mother, putting down her tea-cup and
brushing the crumbs out of her lap, preparatory to making a solemn
declaration. ‘If he is! He is the greatest [[archetypes/tyrant|tyrant]] that every lived, she
daren’t call her [[motifs/soul|soul]] her own, he makes her tremble with a word and
even with a look, he frightens her to [[motifs/death|death]], and she hasn’t the spirit
to give him a word back, no, not a single word.’

Notwithstanding that the fact had been notorious beforehand to all the
tea-drinkers, and had been discussed and expatiated on at every
tea-drinking in the neighbourhood for the last twelve months, this
official communication was no sooner made than they all began to talk
at once and to vie with each other in vehemence and volubility.  Mrs
George remarked that people would talk, that people had often said this
to her before, that Mrs Simmons then and there present had told her so
twenty times, that she had always said, ‘No, Henrietta Simmons, unless
I see it with my own eyes and hear it with my own ears, I never will
believe it.’ Mrs Simmons corroborated this testimony and added strong
evidence of her own. The lady from the Minories recounted a successful
course of treatment under which she had placed her own husband, who,
from manifesting one month after [[motifs/marriage|marriage]] unequivocal symptoms of the
tiger, had by this means become subdued into a perfect [[motifs/lamb|lamb]]. Another
lady recounted her own personal struggle and final triumph, in the
course whereof she had found it necessary to call in her mother and two
aunts, and to weep incessantly [[motifs/night|night]] and day for six weeks. A third,
who in the general confusion could secure no other listener, fastened
herself upon a young woman still unmarried who happened to be amongst
them, and conjured her, as she valued her own peace of mind and
happiness to profit by this solemn occasion, to take example from the
weakness of Mrs Quilp, and from that [[motifs/time|time]] forth to direct her whole
thoughts to taming and subduing the rebellious spirit of man. The noise
was at its height, and half the company had elevated their voices into
a perfect shriek in order to drown the voices of the other half, when
Mrs Jiniwin was seen to change colour and shake her forefinger
stealthily, as if exhorting them to [[motifs/silence|silence]]. Then, and not until then,
[[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]] himself, the cause and occasion of all this clamour, was
observed to be in the room, looking on and listening with profound
attention.




<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_04--part_03" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 4 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 04" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/night,motif/ship,motif/stars,motif/time,motif/window,concept/fear,concept/hope,setting/ship,character/dwarf"></span>


‘Go on, ladies, go on,’ said Daniel. ‘Mrs Quilp, pray ask the ladies to
stop to supper, and have a couple of lobsters and something light and
palatable.’

‘I--I--didn’t ask them to tea, Quilp,’ stammered his wife. ‘It’s quite
an accident.’

‘So much the better, Mrs Quilp; these accidental parties are always the
pleasantest,’ said the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]], rubbing his hands so hard that he seemed
to be engaged in manufacturing, of the dirt with which they were
encrusted, little charges for popguns. ‘What! Not going, ladies, you
are not going, surely!’

His fair enemies tossed their heads slightly as they sought their
respective bonnets and shawls, but left all verbal contention to Mrs
Jiniwin, who finding herself in the position of champion, made a faint
struggle to sustain the character.

‘And why not stop to supper, Quilp,’ said the old lady, ‘if my daughter
had a mind?’

‘To be sure,’ rejoined Daniel. ‘Why not?’

‘There’s nothing dishonest or wrong in a supper, I [[concepts/hope|hope]]?’ said Mrs
Jiniwin.

‘Surely not,’ returned the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]]. ‘Why should there be? Nor anything
unwholesome, either, unless there’s lobster-salad or prawns, which I’m
told are not good for digestion.’

‘And you wouldn’t like your wife to be attacked with that, or anything
else that would make her uneasy would you?’ said Mrs Jiniwin.

‘Not for a score of worlds,’ replied the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]] with a grin. ‘Not even
to have a score of mothers-in-law at the same [[motifs/time|time]]--and what a blessing
that would be!’

‘My daughter’s your wife, Mr Quilp, certainly,’ said the old lady with
a giggle, meant for satirical and to imply that he needed to be
reminded of the fact; ‘your wedded wife.’

‘So she is, certainly. So she is,’ observed the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]].

‘And she has a right to do as she likes, I [[concepts/hope|hope]], Quilp,’ said the
old lady trembling, partly with anger and partly with a secret [[concepts/fear|fear]] of
her impish son-in-law.

‘[[concepts/hope|Hope]] she has!’ he replied. ‘Oh! Don’t you know she has? Don’t you know
she has, Mrs Jiniwin?

‘I know she ought to have, Quilp, and would have, if she was of my way
of thinking.’

‘Why an’t you of your mother’s way of thinking, my dear?’ said the
[[characters/dwarf|dwarf]], turing round and addressing his wife, ‘why don’t you always
imitate your mother, my dear? She’s the ornament of her sex--your
father said so every day of his life. I am sure he did.’

‘Her father was a blessed creetur, Quilp, and worthy twenty thousand of
some people,’ said Mrs Jiniwin; ‘twenty hundred million thousand.’

‘I should like to have known him,’ remarked the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]]. ‘I dare say he
was a blessed creature then; but I’m sure he is now. It was a happy
release. I believe he had suffered a long [[motifs/time|time]]?’

The old lady gave a gasp, but nothing came of it; Quilp resumed, with
the same malice in his eye and the same sarcastic politeness on his
tongue.

‘You look ill, Mrs Jiniwin; I know you have been exciting yourself too
much--talking perhaps, for it is your weakness. Go to bed. Do go to
bed.’

‘I shall go when I please, Quilp, and not before.’

‘But please to do now. Do please to go now,’ said the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]].

The old woman looked angrily at him, but retreated as he advanced, and
falling back before him, suffered him to shut the door upon her and
bolt her out among the guests, who were by this [[motifs/time|time]] crowding
downstairs. Being left along with his wife, who sat trembling in a
corner with her eyes fixed upon the ground, the little man planted
himself before her, and folding his arms looked steadily at her for a
long [[motifs/time|time]] without speaking.

‘Mrs Quilp,’ he said at last.

‘Yes, Quilp,’ she replead meekly.

Instead of pursuing the theme he had in his mind, Quilp folded his arms
again, and looked at her more sternly than before, while she averted
her eyes and kept them on the ground.

‘Mrs Quilp.’

‘Yes, Quilp.’

‘If ever you listen to these beldames again, I’ll bite you.’

With this laconic threat, which he accompanied with a snarl that gave
him the appearance of being particularly in earnest, Mr Quilp bade her
clear the teaboard away, and bring the rum. The spirit being set before
him in a huge case-bottle, which had originally come out of some [[motifs/ship|ship]]’s
locker, he settled himself in an arm-chair with his large head and face
squeezed up against the back, and his little legs planted on the table.

‘Now, Mrs Quilp,’ he said; ‘I feel in a smoking humour, and shall
probably blaze away all [[motifs/night|night]]. But sit where you are, if you please, in
case I want you.’

His wife returned no other reply than the necessary ‘Yes, Quilp,’ and
the small lord of the creation took his first cigar and mixed his first
glass of grog. The sun went down and the [[motifs/stars|stars]] peeped out, the Tower
turned from its own proper colours to grey and from grey to black, the
room became perfectly dark and the end of the cigar a deep fiery red,
but still Mr Quilp went on smoking and drinking in the same position,
and staring listlessly out of [[motifs/window|window]] with the doglike smile always on
his face, save when Mrs Quilp made some involuntary movement of
restlessness or fatigue; and then it expanded into a grin of delight.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

«Avanti, signore, avanti», disse Daniel. «Signora Quilp, la prego di chiedere alle signore di fermarsi per cena e di procurare un paio di aragoste e qualcosa di leggero e gustoso».

«Non li ho invitati a prendere il tè, Quilp», balbettò sua moglie. «È stato un puro caso».

«Tanto meglio, signora Quilp; queste feste casuali sono sempre le più piacevoli», disse il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]], strofinandosi le mani così forte che sembrava impegnato a fabbricare, dalla sporcizia con cui erano incrostate, piccole cariche per pistole giocattolo. «Che cosa! Non ve ne andate, signore, non ve ne andrete mica, spero!»

Le sue avversarie gentili scossero leggermente la testa mentre cercavano i rispettivi cappelli e scialli, ma lasciarono ogni contesa verbale alla signora Jiniwin, che trovandosi nella posizione di campionessa, fece un debole tentativo per sostenere il personaggio.

"E perché non fermarsi a cena, Quilp," disse la vecchia signora, "se mia figlia avesse voglia?"

«Certo», replicò Daniel. «Perché no?»

«Non c'è nulla di disonesto o sbagliato in una cena, lo [[concepts/hope|spero]]?» disse la signora Jiniwin.

«Certo che no», rispose il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]]. «Perché dovrebbe esserci? E nemmeno niente di nocivo, a meno che non ci siano insalate di aragosta o gamberetti, e mi hanno detto che non sono buoni per la digestione.»

«E non vorreste che vostra moglie fosse aggredita con quello o con qualsiasi altra cosa che la rendesse inquieta, vero?» disse la signora Jiniwin.

«Non per un centinaio di mondi», rispose il [[characters/dwarf|n nano]] con una smorfia. «Neanche per avere un centinaio di suocere nello stesso [[motifs/time|momento]]--e che benedizione sarebbe!»

«La mia figlia è sua moglie, signor Quilp, certamente», disse la vecchia signora con una risatina che intendeva essere sarcastica e implicava che lui aveva bisogno di ricordare quel fatto; «sua legittima sposa.»

«E infatti lo è, certamente. E infatti lo è», osservò il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]].

«E ha il diritto di fare ciò che vuole, lo [[concepts/hope|spero]], Quilp», disse la vecchia signora tremando, in parte per rabbia e in parte per un segreto [[concepts/fear|timore]] del suo diabolico genero.

«Ha [[concepts/hope|speranza]]!» rispose lui. «Oh! Non lo sapeva che l'ha? Non lo sapeva,
signora Jiniwin?

'So avrebbe dovuto fare, Quilp, e lo avrebbe fatto se pensasse come me.'

«Perché non sei dello stesso modo di pensare di tua madre, mia cara?» disse il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]], girandosi e rivolgendosi a sua moglie «perché non imiti sempre tua madre, mia cara? È l'ornamento del suo sesso: tuo padre lo diceva ogni giorno della sua vita. Ne sono sicuro».

«Suo padre era una creatura benedetta, Quilp, e valeva ventimila volte più di certa gente», disse la signora Jiniwin; «venti milioni di miliardi».

«Mi sarebbe piaciuto conoscerlo», osservò il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]]. «Immagino che fosse una creatura benedetta allora; ma sono sicuro che lo è adesso. È stata una liberazione felice. Credo abbia sofferto a lungo per un bel [[motifs/time|pezzo]]?»

La vecchia signora emise un gemito soffocato, ma non ne venne fuori nulla; Quilp riprese con la stessa malizia negli occhi e lo stesso sarcasmo cortese nella voce.

«Avete un'aria malaticcia, signora Jiniwin; so che vi siete agitata troppo,
parlando probabilmente, perché è il vostro punto debole. Andate a letto.
Andate a letto».

'Andrò quando mi pare, Quilp, e non prima.'

«Ma per favore fatelo ora. Per piacere andatevene ora», disse il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]].

La vecchia lo guardò con rabbia ma si ritirò mentre lui avanzava e,
indietreggiando davanti a lui, gli permise di chiudere la porta su di lei e
di sbatterla fuori tra gli ospiti che in quel [[motifs/time|momento]] affollavano le scale. Rimaso solo con sua moglie, che sedeva tremante in un angolo con lo sguardo fisso a terra, l'uomo si piantò davanti a lei e, incrociando le braccia, la guardò attentamente per un lungo [[motifs/time|periodo]] senza parlare.

«Signora Quilp», disse alla fine.

«Sì, Quilp», replicò mansueta.

Invece di proseguire con il tema che aveva in mente, Quilp si incrociò nuovamente le braccia e la guardò più severamente del prima, mentre lei distoglieva lo sguardo e lo teneva fisso a terra.

'La signora Quilp.'

'Sì, Quilp.'

'Non ascoltare mai più queste vecchie streghe, altrimenti ti mordo.'

Con questa laconica minaccia, che accompagnò con un ringhio che gli conferiva l'aspetto di essere particolarmente serio, il signor Quilp le ordinò di sparecchiare il vassoio del tè e portare il rum. Lo spirito fu messo davanti a lui in una enorme bottiglia da viaggio, che era originariamente uscita dal cassettone di qualche [[motifs/ship|nave]], si sistemò su una poltrona con la sua grande testa e viso schiacciati contro lo schienale e le sue piccole gambe appoggiate sul tavolo.

«Ora, signora Quilp», disse lui, «mi sento nell'umore di fumare e probabilmente continuerò a farlo tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]]. Ma resti dove è, per favore, nel caso avessi bisogno di lei.»

Sua moglie non rispose altro che il necessario “Sì, Quilp”, e il piccolo signore della creazione accese il suo primo sigaro e preparò la sua prima coppa di grog. Il sole tramontò e le [[motifs/stars|stelle]] apparvero, la Torre cambiò dai suoi colori naturali al grigio e dal grigio al nero, la stanza divenne completamente buia e l'estremità del sigaro si tinse di un rosso fuoco intenso; ma il signor Quilp continuava a fumare e bere nella stessa posizione, fissando senza interesse dalla [[motifs/window|finestra]] con quel sorriso da cane sempre sul volto, tranne quando la signora Quilp faceva qualche movimento involontario di inquietudine o affaticamento; allora si trasformava in una smorfia di piacere.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_05--part_01" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 5 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 05" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/monster,archetype/tyrant,archetype/villain,motif/city,motif/desire,motif/mirror,motif/night,motif/river,motif/sleep,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/water,concept/doubt,concept/grotesque,character/dwarf"></span>


CHAPTER 5

Whether Mr Quilp took any [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] by snatches of a few winks at a [[motifs/time|time]],
or whether he sat with his eyes wide open all [[motifs/night|night]] long, certain it is
that he kept his cigar alight, and kindled every fresh one from the
ashes of that which was nearly consumed, without requiring the
assistance of a candle. Nor did the striking of the clocks, hour after
hour, appear to inspire him with any sense of drowsiness or any natural
[[motifs/desire|desire]] to go to rest, but rather to increase his wakefulness, which he
showed, at every such indication of the progress of the [[motifs/night|night]], by a
suppressed cackling in his throat, and a motion of his shoulders, like
one who laughs heartily but the same [[motifs/time|time]] slyly and by stealth.

At length the day broke, and poor Mrs Quilp, shivering with cold of
early morning and harassed by fatigue and want of [[motifs/sleep|sleep]], was discovered
sitting patiently on her chair, raising her eyes at intervals in mute
appeal to the compassion and clemency of her lord, and gently reminding
him by an occasion cough that she was still unpardoned and that her
penance had been of long duration. But her dwarfish spouse still smoked
his cigar and drank his rum without heeding her; and it was not until
the sun had some [[motifs/time|time]] risen, and the activity and noise of [[motifs/city|city]] day
were rife in the street, that he deigned to recognize her presence by
any word or sign. He might not have done so even then, but for certain
impatient tapping at the door he seemed to denote that some pretty hard
knuckles were actively engaged upon the other side.

‘Why dear me!’ he said looking round with a malicious grin, ‘it’s day.
Open the door, sweet Mrs Quilp!’

His obedient wife withdrew the bolt, and her lady mother entered.

Now, Mrs Jiniwin bounced into the room with great impetuosity; for,
supposing her son-in-law to be still a-bed, she had come to relieve her
feelings by pronouncing a strong opinion upon his general conduct and
character. Seeing that he was up and dressed, and that the room
appeared to have been occupied ever since she quitted it on the
previous evening, she stopped short, in some embarrassment.

Nothing escaped the hawk’s eye of the ugly little man, who, perfectly
understanding what passed in the old lady’s mind, turned uglier still
in the fulness of his satisfaction, and bade her good morning, with a
leer or triumph.

‘Why, Betsy,’ said the old woman, ‘you haven’t been--you don’t mean to
say you’ve been a--’

‘Sitting up all [[motifs/night|night]]?’ said Quilp, supplying the conclusion of the
sentence. ‘Yes she has!’

‘All [[motifs/night|night]]?’ cried Mrs Jiniwin.

‘Ay, all [[motifs/night|night]]. Is the dear old lady deaf?’ said Quilp, with a smile of
which a frown was part. ‘Who says man and wife are bad company?  Ha ha!
The [[motifs/time|time]] has flown.’

‘You’re a brute!’ exclaimed Mrs Jiniwin.

‘Come come,’ said Quilp, wilfully misunderstanding her, of course, ‘you
mustn’t call her names. She’s married now, you know. And though she did
beguile the [[motifs/time|time]] and keep me from my bed, you must not be so tenderly
careful of me as to be out of humour with her.  Bless you for a dear
old lady. Here’s to your health!’

‘I am much obliged to you,’ returned the old woman, testifying by a
certain restlessness in her hands a vehement [[motifs/desire|desire]] to shake her
matronly fist at her son-in-law. ‘Oh! I’m very much obliged to you!’

‘Grateful [[motifs/soul|soul]]!’ cried the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]]. ‘Mrs Quilp.’

‘Yes, Quilp,’ said the timid sufferer.

‘Help your mother to get breakfast, Mrs Quilp. I am going to the wharf
this morning--the earlier the better, so be quick.’

Mrs Jiniwin made a faint demonstration of rebellion by sitting down in
a chair near the door and folding her arms as if in a resolute
determination to do nothing. But a few whispered words from her
daughter, and a kind inquiry from her son-in-law whether she felt
faint, with a hint that there was abundance of cold [[motifs/water|water]] in the next
apartment, routed these symptoms effectually, and she applied herself
to the prescribed preparations with sullen diligence.

While they were in progress, Mr Quilp withdrew to the adjoining room,
and, turning back his coat-collar, proceeded to smear his countenance
with a damp towel of very unwholesome appearance, which made his
complexion rather more cloudy than it was before.  But, while he was
thus engaged, his caution and inquisitiveness did not forsake him, for
with a face as sharp and cunning as ever, he often stopped, even in
this short process, and stood listening for any conversation in the
next room, of which he might be the theme.

‘Ah!’ he said after a short effort of attention, ‘it was not the towel
over my ears, I thought it wasn’t. I’m a little hunchy [[archetypes/villain|villain]] and a
[[archetypes/monster|monster]], am I, Mrs Jiniwin? Oh!’

The pleasure of this discovery called up the old doglike smile in full
force. When he had quite done with it, he shook himself in a very
doglike manner, and rejoined the ladies.

Mr Quilp now walked up to front of a looking-glass, and was standing
there putting on his neckerchief, when Mrs Jiniwin happening to be
behind him, could not resist the inclination she felt to shake her fist
at her [[archetypes/tyrant|tyrant]] son-in-law. It was the gesture of an instant, but as she
did so and accompanied the action with a menacing look, she met his eye
in the glass, catching her in the very act. The same glance at the
[[motifs/mirror|mirror]] conveyed to her the reflection of a horribly [[concepts/grotesque|grotesque]] and
distorted face with the tongue lolling out; and the next instant the
[[characters/dwarf|dwarf]], turning about with a perfectly bland and placid look, inquired
in a tone of great affection.

‘How are you now, my dear old darling?’

Slight and ridiculous as the incident was, it made him appear such a
little fiend, and withal such a keen and knowing one, that the old
woman felt too much afraid of him to utter a single word, and suffered
herself to be led with extraordinary politeness to the breakfast-table.
Here he by no means diminished the impression he had just produced, for
he ate hard eggs, shell and all, devoured gigantic prawns with the
heads and tails on, chewed tobacco and [[motifs/water|water]]-cresses at the same [[motifs/time|time]]
and with extraordinary greediness, drank boiling tea without winking,
bit his fork and spoon till they bent again, and in short performed so
many horrifying and uncommon acts that the women were nearly frightened
out of their wits, and began to [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] if he were really a human
creature. At last, having gone through these proceedings and many
others which were equally a part of his system, Mr Quilp left them,
reduced to a very obedient and humbled state, and betook himself to the
[[motifs/river|river]]-side, where he took boat for the wharf on which he had bestowed
his name.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 5

Che il signor Quilp dormisse di un [[motifs/sleep|sonno]] spezzato da pochi battiti di ciglia alla volta,
o che se ne stesse seduto con gli occhi spalancati tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]], è certo
che mantenne acceso il suo sigaro, e accese ogni nuovo sigaro dalle
ceneri di quello quasi consumato, senza aver bisogno dell'aiuto di una candela. Né i rintocchi degli orologi, ora dopo ora,
sembravano ispirargli alcun senso di sonnolenza o naturale [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di andare a riposare, ma piuttosto aumentarono la sua veglia, che mostrò
ad ogni tale indicazione del progredire della [[motifs/night|notte]], con un gorgoglio represso in gola e un movimento delle spalle, come uno che ride di gusto ma allo stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]] furtivamente e di nascosto.

Alla fine il giorno sorse e la povera signora Quilp, tremante dal freddo del primo mattino e tormentata dalla fatica e dalla mancanza di [[motifs/sleep|sonno]], fu scoperta seduta pazientemente sulla sua sedia, alzando gli occhi a intervalli in un muto appello alla compassione e alla clemenza del suo signore, e ricordandogli gentilmente con una tosse occasionale che era ancora non perdonata e che la sua penitenza era stata di lunga durata. Ma il suo marito nano continuava a fumare il suo sigaro e bere il suo rum senza badarle; e non fu fino a quando il sole era già sorto da qualche [[motifs/time|tempo]] e l'attività e il rumore della giornata di [[motifs/city|città]] erano vivaci in strada, che si degnò di riconoscere la sua presenza con una parola o un segno. Forse non lo avrebbe fatto nemmeno allora, se non fosse stato per alcuni colpi impazienti alla porta che sembravano indicare che alcune abbastanza dure nocche erano attivamente impegnate dall'altra parte.

«Perbacco!» disse guardandosi intorno con un ghigno malizioso «è giorno. Apra la porta, cara signora Quilp!»

La moglie obbediente tolse il chiavistello e la madre della signora entrò.

In quel momento la signora Jiniwin entrò nella stanza con grande impeto; infatti,
pensando che il genero fosse ancora a letto, era venuta per sfogare i suoi sentimenti esprimendo un'opinione decisa sulla sua condotta e sul suo carattere in generale. Vedendo che lui si era alzato e vestito, e che la stanza sembrava essere stata occupata da quando l'aveva lasciata la sera precedente, si fermò di colpo, un po' imbarazzata.

Nulla sfuggiva all’occhio di falco dell’uomo brutto e piccolo che,
comprendendo perfettamente ciò che passava nella mente della vecchia signora,
diventò ancora più brutto per la pienezza del suo compiacimento, e le augurò buongiorno
con un ghigno di trionfo.

«Ma, Betsy», disse la vecchia signora, «non siete stata, non vorrete dire che siete stata una, »

«Rimane in piedi tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]]?» disse Quilp, fornendo la conclusione della frase. «Sì che lo ha fatto!»

«Tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]]?» esclamò la signora Jiniwin.

«Sì, tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]]. La cara vecchietta è sorda?» disse Quilp con un sorriso in cui si mescolava una smorfia. «Chi dice che marito e moglie non fanno buona compagnia? Ah ah! Il [[motifs/time|tempo]] è volato.»

«Sei un bruto!» esclamò la signora Jiniwin.

«Dai, dai», disse Quilp, fingendo di non capirla, naturalmente, «non dovete chiamarla con quei nomi. Ora è sposata, sapete. E anche se ha ingannato il [[motifs/time|tempo]] e mi ha tenuto lontano dal mio letto, non dovete essere così teneramente premurosi nei miei confronti da arrabbiarvi con lei.  Dio vi benedica, cara vecchia signora. Alla vostra salute!»

«Sono molto obbligata», rispose la vecchia, dimostrando con una certa irrequietezza delle mani un vivace [[motifs/desire|desiderio]] di scuotere il suo pugno matronale contro il genero. «Oh! Sono davvero molto obbligata!»

«Grata [[motifs/soul|anima]]!» gridò il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]]. «Signora Quilp.»

«Sì, Quilp», disse la timida vittima.

«Aiuta tua madre a preparare la colazione, signora Quilp. Questa mattina vado al molo: prima è meglio, quindi sbrigati».

La signora Jiniwin fece un debole tentativo di ribellione sedendosi su una sedia vicino alla porta e incrociando le braccia come se fosse determinata a non fare nulla. Ma poche parole sussurrate da sua figlia, e la gentile domanda del genero se si sentisse male, con l'accenno che c'era abbondante [[motifs/water|acqua]] fredda nella stanza accanto, misero in fuga efficacemente questi sintomi, e lei si dedicò alle prescritte preparazioni con diligente malumore.

Mentre tutto ciò era in corso, il signor Quilp si ritirò nella stanza attigua e,
voltandosi di spalle, procedette a strofinare il suo volto con un asciugamano umido dall'aspetto piuttosto poco salubre, che rese la sua carnagione ancora più scura di prima. Ma mentre era così impegnato, la sua cautela e curiosità non lo abbandonarono, poiché spesso si fermava, anche in questo breve processo, e rimaneva in ascolto per cogliere eventuali conversazioni nella stanza accanto, delle quali lui potesse essere l'argomento.

«Ah!» disse dopo un breve sforzo di attenzione «non era l'asciugamano sopra le mie orecchie, pensavo che non lo fosse. Sono un piccolo gobbo [[archetypes/villain|villain]] e una [[archetypes/monster|mostro]], vero signora Jiniwin? Oh!»

Il piacere di questa scoperta fece riapparire il vecchio sorriso da cane con tutta la sua forza.
Quando ebbe finito, si scrollò in modo molto canino e tornò dalle signore.

Il signor Quilp si avvicinò ora allo specchio e stava lì mettendosi il fazzoletto al collo quando la signora Jiniwin, trovandosi per caso dietro di lui, non seppe resistere alla voglia che provava di mostrargli il pugno chiuso contro quel [[archetypes/tyrant|tiranno]] di genero. Fu un gesto istantaneo, ma mentre lo faceva e accompagnava l'azione con uno sguardo minaccioso, incrociò i suoi occhi nello specchio che la coglievano sul fatto. La stessa occhiata allo [[motifs/mirror|specchio]] le mostrò il riflesso di un volto orribilmente [[concepts/grotesque|grottesco]] e distorto con la lingua fuori; e nel momento successivo lo stesso [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]], voltandosi con uno sguardo perfettamente mite e placido, le chiese in tono di grande affetto.

'Come stai ora, mia cara vecchia tesoro?'

Leggero e ridicolo com'era l'accaduto, lo fece apparire così diabolico,
e al tempo stesso così acuto e scaltro, che la vecchia si sentì troppo spaventata per dire una sola parola, e si lasciò condurre con straordinaria cortesia fino alla tavola della colazione.
Qui egli non fece altro che rafforzare l'impressione appena prodotta,
perché mangiava uova dure, guscio e tutto, divorava enormi gamberetti
con teste e code, masticava tabacco e [[motifs/water|acqua]]-crescia nello stesso [[motifs/time|tempo]]
e con straordinaria golosità, beveva tè bollente senza batter ciglio,
mordicchiava forchetta e cucchiaio fino a piegarli, e in breve compiva
tanti atti orribili e insoliti che le donne erano quasi fuori di sé dalla paura,
e cominciarono a [[concepts/doubt|dubitare]] se fosse davvero un essere umano.
Alla fine, dopo aver portato a termine queste operazioni e molte
altre che facevano ugualmente parte del suo sistema, il signor Quilp li lasciò,
ridotti in uno stato di grande obbedienza e umiltà, e si recò sulle rive del [[motifs/river|fiume]],
dove prese una barca per il molo a cui aveva dato il proprio nome.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_05--part_02" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 5 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 05" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/monster,motif/clock,motif/cross,motif/night,motif/pain,motif/river,motif/sleep,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,motif/window,concept/doubt,character/daniel_quilp,character/dwarf"></span>


It was flood tide when [[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]] sat himself down in the ferry to
[[motifs/cross|cross]] to the opposite shore. A fleet of barges were coming lazily on,
some sideways, some head first, some stern first; all in a
wrong-headed, dogged, obstinate way, bumping up against the larger
craft, running under the bows of steamboats, getting into every kind of
nook and corner where they had no business, and being crunched on all
sides like so many walnut-shells; while each with its pair of long
sweeps struggling and splashing in the [[motifs/water|water]] looked like some lumbering
fish in [[motifs/pain|pain]]. In some of the vessels at anchor all hands were busily
engaged in coiling ropes, spreading out sails to dry, taking in or
discharging their cargoes; in others no life was visible but two or
three tarry boys, and perhaps a barking dog running to and fro upon the
deck or scrambling up to look over the side and bark the louder for the
view. Coming slowly on through the forests of masts was a great
steamship, beating the [[motifs/water|water]] in short impatient strokes with her heavy
paddles as though she wanted room to breathe, and advancing in her huge
bulk like a sea [[archetypes/monster|monster]] among the minnows of the Thames. On either hand
were long black tiers of colliers; between them vessels slowly working
out of harbour with sails glistening in the sun, and creaking noise on
board, re-echoed from a hundred quarters. The [[motifs/water|water]] and all upon it was
in active motion, dancing and buoyant and bubbling up; while the old
grey Tower and piles of building on the shore, with many a church-spire
shooting up between, looked coldly on, and seemed to disdain their
chafing, restless neighbour.

[[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]], who was not much affected by a bright morning save in so
far as it spared him the trouble of carrying an umbrella, caused
himself to be put ashore hard by the wharf, and proceeded thither
through a narrow lane which, partaking of the amphibious character of
its frequenters, had as much [[motifs/water|water]] as mud in its composition, and a
very liberal supply of both. Arrived at his destination, the first
object that presented itself to his view was a pair of very imperfectly
shod feet elevated in the air with the soles upwards, which remarkable
appearance was referable to the boy, who being of an eccentric spirit
and having a natural taste for tumbling, was now standing on his head
and contemplating the aspect of the [[motifs/river|river]] under these uncommon
circumstances. He was speedily brought on his heels by the sound of his
master’s voice, and as soon as his head was in its right position, Mr
Quilp, to speak expressively in the absence of a better verb, ‘punched
it’ for him.

‘Come, you let me alone,’ said the boy, parrying Quilp’s hand with both
his elbows alternatively. ‘You’ll get something you won’t like if you
don’t and so I tell you.’

‘You dog,’ snarled Quilp, ‘I’ll beat you with an iron rod, I’ll scratch
you with a rusty nail, I’ll pinch your eyes, if you talk to me--I will.’

With these threats he clenched his hand again, and dexterously diving
in between the elbows and catching the boy’s head as it dodged from
side to side, gave it three or four good hard knocks. Having now
carried his point and insisted on it, he left off.

‘You won’t do it agin,’ said the boy, nodding his head and drawing
back, with the elbows ready in case of the worst; ‘now--’

‘Stand still, you dog,’ said Quilp. ‘I won’t do it again, because I’ve
done it as often as I want. Here. Take the key.’

‘Why don’t you hit one of your size?’ said the boy approaching very
slowly.

‘Where is there one of my size, you dog?’ returned Quilp. ‘Take the
key, or I’ll brain you with it’--indeed he gave him a smart tap with
the handle as he spoke. ‘Now, open the counting-house.’

The boy sulkily complied, muttering at first, but desisting when he
looked round and saw that Quilp was following him with a steady look.
And here it may be remarked, that between this boy and the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]] there
existed a strange kind of mutual liking. How born or bred, and or
nourished upon blows and threats on one side, and retorts and defiances
on the other, is not to the purpose. Quilp would certainly suffer
nobody to contract him but the boy, and the boy would assuredly not
have submitted to be so knocked about by anybody but Quilp, when he had
the power to run away at any [[motifs/time|time]] he chose.

‘Now,’ said Quilp, passing into the wooden counting-house, ‘you mind
the wharf. Stand upon your head agin, and I’ll cut one of your feet
off.’

The boy made no answer, but directly Quilp had shut himself in, stood
on his head before the door, then walked on his hands to the back and
stood on his head there, and then to the opposite side and repeated the
performance. There were indeed four sides to the counting-house, but he
avoided that one where the [[motifs/window|window]] was, deeming it probable that Quilp
would be looking out of it. This was prudent, for in point of fact, the
[[characters/dwarf|dwarf]], knowing his disposition, was lying in wait at a little distance
from the sash armed with a large piece of wood, which, being rough and
jagged and studded in many parts with broken nails, might possibly have
hurt him.

It was a dirty little box, this counting-house, with nothing in it but
an old ricketty desk and two stools, a hat-peg, an ancient almanack, an
inkstand with no ink, and the stump of one pen, and an eight-day [[motifs/clock|clock]]
which hadn’t gone for eighteen years at least, and of which the
minute-hand had been twisted off for a tooth-pick. [[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]] pulled
his hat over his brows, climbed on to the desk (which had a flat top)
and stretching his short length upon it went to [[motifs/sleep|sleep]] with ease of an
old practitioner; intending, no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], to compensate himself for the
deprivation of last [[motifs/night|night]]’s rest, by a long and sound nap.

Sound it might have been, but long it was not, for he had not been
asleep a quarter of an hour when the boy opened the door and thrust in
his head, which was like a bundle of badly-picked oakum. Quilp was a
light sleeper and started up directly.

‘Here’s somebody for you,’ said the boy.

‘Who?’

‘I don’t know.’

‘Ask!’ said Quilp, seizing the trifle of wood before mentioned and
throwing it at him with such dexterity that it was [[motifs/well|well]] the boy
disappeared before it reached the spot on which he had stood. ‘Ask, you
dog.’

Not caring to venture within range of such missles again, the boy
discreetly sent in his stead the first cause of the interruption, who
now presented herself at the door.

‘What, Nelly!’ cried Quilp.

‘Yes,’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]], hesitating whether to enter or retreat, for the
[[characters/dwarf|dwarf]] just roused, with his dishevelled hair hanging all about him and
a yellow handkerchief over his head, was something fearful to behold;
it’s only me, sir.’

‘Come in,’ said Quilp, without getting off the desk. ‘Come in. Stay.
Just look out into the yard, and see whether there’s a boy standing on
his head.’

‘No, sir,’ replied Nell. ‘He’s on his feet.’

‘You’re sure he is?’ said Quilp. ‘[[motifs/well|Well]]. Now, come in and shut the door.
What’s your message, Nelly?’

The [[archetypes/child|child]] handed him a letter. Mr Quilp, without changing his position
further than to turn over a little more on his side and rest his chin
on his hand, proceeded to make himself acquainted with its contents.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Era alta marea quando [[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]] si sedette sulla barca traghettatrice per
[[motifs/cross|attraversare]] fino alla riva opposta. Una flottiglia di chiatte stava arrivando pigramente,
alcune di traverso, altre prua avanti, altre poppa avanti; tutte in un modo
testardo e ostinato, sbattendo contro le imbarcazioni più grandi,
passando sotto la prua delle navi a vapore, infilandosi in ogni sorta di
angolo dove non avevano nulla da fare, e venendo schiacciate da tutte le
parti come tante gusci di noce; mentre ognuna con il suo paio di lunghi
remi che si agitavano e facevano schiuma nell'[[motifs/water|acqua]] sembrava un pesce goffo in
[[motifs/pain|agonia]]. In alcune delle navi all'ancora tutti erano impegnati a riavvolgere le corde,
stendere le vele ad asciugare, caricare o scaricare i loro carichi; in altre non si vedeva vita se non due o
tre ragazzini sporchi di catrame e forse un cane che abbaiava correndo avanti e indietro sul
ponte o arrampicandosi per guardare oltre il parapetto e abbaiare più forte alla vista. Avanzando lentamente attraverso le foreste di alberi comparve una grande nave a vapore, che batteva l'[[motifs/water|acqua]] con brevi colpi impazienti delle sue pesanti pale come se volesse spazio per respirare, e avanzava nella sua enorme mole come un [[archetypes/monster|mostro]] marino tra i piccoli pesci del Tamigi. Da entrambi i lati si allungavano file di navi carbone; tra loro altre imbarcazioni che uscivano lentamente dal porto con le vele che brillavano al sole, e il rumore scricchiolante a bordo, riecheggiato da centinaia di direzioni. L'[[motifs/water|acqua]] e tutto ciò che vi era sopra erano in movimento attivo, danzando e galleggiando e formando bolle; mentre la vecchia Torre grigia e i cumuli di edifici sulla riva, con molte guglie di chiese che spuntavano tra loro, guardavano freddamente e sembravano disdegnare il loro vicino agitato e irrequieto.

[[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]], che non era molto influenzato da una mattina luminosa se non per il fatto che gli risparmiava la fatica di portare un ombrello, fece sì che lo mettessero a terra vicino al molo e si diresse lì attraverso un vicolo stretto che, condividendo il carattere anfibio dei suoi frequentatori, aveva nella sua composizione tanto [[motifs/water|acqua]] quanto fango e una generosa quantità di entrambi. Giunto a destinazione, il primo oggetto che gli si presentò alla vista fu un paio di piedi molto imperfettamente calzati sollevati in aria con le suole rivolte verso l'alto, un'apparenza notevole attribuibile al ragazzo, che essendo di spirito eccentrico e avendo una naturale propensione per le capriole, ora stava in piedi sulla testa e contemplava l'aspetto del [[motifs/river|fiume]] sotto queste circostanze insolite. Fu rapidamente riportato sui talloni dal suono della voce del suo padrone, e non appena la sua testa fu nella posizione corretta, il signor Quilp, per esprimersi in modo efficace in assenza di un verbo migliore, gliela "spedì".

«Su, lasciami in pace», disse il ragazzo, parando la mano di Quilp con entrambi i gomiti alternativamente. «Se non lo fai ti darò qualcosa che non ti piacerà e te lo dico io».

«Cane», ringhiò Quilp, «ti picchierò con una sbarra di ferro, ti graffierò con un chiodo arrugginito, ti strapperò gli occhi se continui a parlarmi così - lo farò.»

Accompagnando queste minacce con un pugno chiuso e con una manovra abile,
scivolò tra i gomiti del ragazzo e, afferrandogli la testa mentre si muoveva da
una parte all'altra, gli assestò tre o quattro buoni colpi. Avendo ora ottenuto il suo scopo e insistito su di esso, smise.

«Non lo farai più», disse il ragazzo, annuendo e arretrando con i gomiti pronti nel caso peggiore; «ora, »

«Resta fermo, cane», disse Quilp. «Non lo farò più perché l'ho fatto tutte le volte che volevo. Ecco. Prendi la chiave».

«Perché non colpisci qualcuno della tua statura?» disse il ragazzo avvicinandosi molto lentamente.

«Dov'è qualcuno della mia taglia, cane?» rispose Quilp. «Prendi la chiave, o ti spacco il cranio con essa» -- in effetti gli diede un colpetto deciso sul manico mentre parlava. «Ora, apri l'ufficio contabile».

Il ragazzo obbedì malvolentieri, borbottando all'inizio, ma smise quando si guardò intorno e vide che Quilp lo stava seguendo con uno sguardo fisso. E qui si può osservare che tra questo ragazzo e il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]] esisteva una strana specie di reciproca simpatia. Come fosse nata o cresciuta, e se fosse stata nutrita da botte e minacce da un lato e risposte taglienti e sfide dall'altro, non è qui il caso di discuterne. Quilp avrebbe certamente permesso a nessun altro di contrattare con lui tranne il ragazzo, e il ragazzo non si sarebbe assolutamente sottomesso ad essere così malmenato da chiunque altro se non da Quilp, quando aveva la possibilità di scappare in qualsiasi [[motifs/time|momento]] lo desiderasse.

«Ora», disse Quilp entrando nella cassa di legno, «tu sorvegli il molo.
Stai di nuovo in piedi sulla testa e ti taglio un piede.»

Il ragazzo non rispose; ma appena Quilp si fu chiuso dentro, si mise a testa in giù davanti alla porta, poi camminò sulle mani fino al retro e lì rimase a testa in giù, quindi passò all'altro lato e ripeté la scena. La cassa di banca aveva infatti quattro lati, ma lui evitò quello dove c'era la [[motifs/window|finestra]], ritenendo probabile che Quilp potesse guardare fuori da lì. Fu prudente, perché in effetti il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]], conoscendone i modi, si era appostato a poca distanza dallo stipite armato di un grosso pezzo di legno che, essendo ruvido e frastagliato e munito qua e là di chiodi spezzati, avrebbe potuto ferirlo.

Era una sudicia casupola, questa bottega di cambiavalute, che non conteneva altro che un vecchio tavolo traballante e due sgabelli, un gancio per il cappello, un almanacco antico, un calamaio senza inchiostro, lo stelo di una penna e un orologio a otto giorni [[motifs/clock|orologio]] che non funzionava da almeno diciotto anni e del quale l'indice delle ore era stato piegato per farne uno stuzzicadenti. [[characters/daniel-quilp|Daniel Quilp]] si tirò il cappello sugli occhi, salì sul tavolo (che aveva un piano piatto) e distendendovi sopra la sua piccola figura vi si addormentò con l'agilità di un vecchio praticone; intendendo, senza [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], compensarsi della privazione del riposo della scorsa [[motifs/night|notte]] con un lungo e profondo pisolino.

Forse era un rumore, ma non durò molto, perché non aveva dormito da neanche quindici minuti quando il ragazzo aprì la porta e infilò dentro la testa, che sembrava un fascio di canapa scartata male. Quilp si svegliava facilmente e si rizzò subito a sedere.

«Ecco qualcuno per voi», disse il ragazzo.

'Chi?'

'Non lo so.'

«Chiedi!» disse Quilp, afferrando il pezzetto di legno sopra menzionato e lanciandolo verso di lui con tale destrezza che fu [[motifs/well|bene]] che il ragazzo scomparve prima che raggiungesse il punto in cui si era trovato. «Chiedi, cane.»

Non volendo più esporsi al rischio di quei proiettili, il ragazzo inviò con discrezione la prima causa dell'interruzione, che ora si presentava alla porta.

«Che cosa, Nell!» esclamò Quilp.

«Sì», disse il [[archetypes/child|bambino]], esitando se entrare o ritirarsi, perché il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]] appena svegliato, con i capelli arruffati che gli pendevano intorno e un fazzoletto giallo in testa, era una vista spaventosa; «sono solo io, signore».

«Entri», disse Quilp senza alzarsi dal banco. «Entri. Resti. Guardi solo nel cortile e veda se c'è un ragazzo che sta in piedi sulla testa».

'No, signore', rispose Nell. 'È in piedi.'

«Ne sei sicuro?» disse Quilp. «[[motifs/well|Bene]]. Ora, entra e chiudi la porta. Qual è il tuo messaggio, Nelly?»

Il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] gli porse una lettera. Il signor Quilp, senza cambiare posizione se non per girarsi un po' di più sul fianco e appoggiare il mento sulla mano, procedette a prendere conoscenza del contenuto.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_06--part_01" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 6 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 06" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/death,motif/hill,motif/home,motif/pain,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/well,concept/courage,concept/fear,concept/grotesque,character/dwarf,character/little_nell"></span>


CHAPTER 6

[[characters/little-nell|Little Nell]] stood timidly by, with her eyes raised to the countenance
of Mr Quilp as he read the letter, plainly showing by her looks that
while she entertained some [[concepts/fear|fear]] and distrust of the little man, she was
much inclined to laugh at his uncouth appearance and [[concepts/grotesque|grotesque]]
attitude. And yet there was visible on the part of the [[archetypes/child|child]] a painful
anxiety for his reply, and consciousness of his power to render it
disagreeable or distressing, which was strongly at variance with this
impulse and restrained it more effectually than she could possibly have
done by any efforts of her own.

That Mr Quilp was himself perplexed, and that in no small degree, by
the contents of the letter, was sufficiently obvious. Before he had got
through the first two or three lines he began to open his eyes very
wide and to frown most horribly, the next two or three caused him to
scratch his head in an uncommonly vicious manner, and when he came to
the conclusion he gave a long dismal whistle indicative of surprise and
dismay. After folding and laying it down beside him, he bit the nails
of all of his ten fingers with extreme voracity; and taking it up
sharply, read it again. The second perusal was to all appearance as
unsatisfactory as the first, and plunged him into a profound reverie
from which he awakened to another assault upon his nails and a long
stare at the [[archetypes/child|child]], who with her eyes turned towards the ground awaited
his further pleasure.

‘Halloa here!’ he said at length, in a voice, and with a suddenness,
which made the [[archetypes/child|child]] start as though a gun had been fired off at her
ear. ‘Nelly!’

‘Yes, sir.’

‘Do you know what’s inside this letter, Nell?’

‘No, sir!’

‘Are you sure, quite sure, quite certain, upon your [[motifs/soul|soul]]?’

‘Quite sure, sir.’

‘Do you wish you may die if you do know, hey?’ said the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]].

‘Indeed I don’t know,’ returned the [[archetypes/child|child]].

‘[[motifs/well|Well]]!’ muttered Quilp as he marked her earnest look. ‘I believe you.
Humph! Gone already? Gone in four-and-twenty hours! What the devil has
he done with it, that’s the mystery!’

This reflection set him scratching his head and biting his nails once
more. While he was thus employed his features gradually relaxed into
what was with him a cheerful smile, but which in any other man would
have been a ghastly grin of [[motifs/pain|pain]], and when the [[archetypes/child|child]] looked up again
she found that he was regarding her with extraordinary favour and
complacency.

‘You look very pretty to-day, Nelly, charmingly pretty. Are you tired,
Nelly?’

‘No, sir. I’m in a hurry to get back, for he will be anxious while I am
away.’

‘There’s no hurry, [[characters/little-nell|little Nell]], no hurry at all,’ said Quilp. ‘How
should you like to be my number two, Nelly?’

‘To be what, sir?’

‘My number two, Nelly, my second, my Mrs Quilp,’ said the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]].

The [[archetypes/child|child]] looked frightened, but seemed not to understand him, which Mr
Quilp observing, hastened to make his meaning more distinctly.

‘To be Mrs Quilp the second, when Mrs Quilp the first is dead, sweet
Nell,’ said Quilp, wrinkling up his eyes and luring her towards him
with his bent forefinger, ‘to be my wife, my little cherry-cheeked,
red-lipped wife. Say that Mrs Quilp lives five year, or only four,
you’ll be just the proper age for me. Ha ha! Be a good girl, Nelly, a
very good girl, and see if one of these days you don’t come to be Mrs
Quilp of Tower [[motifs/hill|Hill]].’

So far from being sustained and stimulated by this delightful prospect,
the [[archetypes/child|child]] shrank from him in great agitation, and trembled violently.
Mr Quilp, either because frightening anybody afforded him a
constitutional delight, or because it was pleasant to contemplate the
[[motifs/death|death]] of Mrs Quilp number one, and the elevation of Mrs Quilp number
two to her post and title, or because he was determined from purposes
of his own to be agreeable and good-humoured at that particular [[motifs/time|time]],
only laughed and feigned to take no heed of her alarm.

‘You shall come with me to Tower [[motifs/hill|Hill]] and see Mrs Quilp that is,
directly,’ said the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]]. ‘She’s very fond of you, Nell, though not so
fond as I am. You shall come [[motifs/home|home]] with me.’

‘I must go back indeed,’ said the [[archetypes/child|child]]. ‘He told me to return directly
I had the answer.’

‘But you haven’t it, Nelly,’ retorted the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]], ‘and won’t have it,
and can’t have it, until I have been [[motifs/home|home]], so you see that to do your
errand, you must go with me. Reach me yonder hat, my dear, and we’ll go
directly.’ With that, Mr Quilp suffered himself to roll gradually off
the desk until his short legs touched the ground, when he got upon them
and led the way from the counting-house to the wharf outside, when the
first objects that presented themselves were the boy who had stood on
his head and another young gentleman of about his own stature, rolling
in the mud together, locked in a tight embrace, and cuffing each other
with mutual heartiness.

‘It’s Kit!’ cried Nelly, clasping her hand, ‘poor Kit who came with me!
Oh, pray stop them, Mr Quilp!’

‘I’ll stop ‘em,’ cried Quilp, diving into the little counting-house and
returning with a thick stick, ‘I’ll stop ‘em. Now, my boys, fight away.
I’ll fight you both. I’ll take both of you, both together, both
together!’

With which defiances the [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]] flourished his cudgel, and dancing round
the combatants and treading upon them and skipping over them, in a kind
of frenzy, laid about him, now on one and now on the other, in a most
desperate manner, always aiming at their heads and dealing such blows
as none but the veriest little savage would have inflicted. This being
warmer work than they had calculated upon, speedily cooled the [[concepts/courage|courage]]
of the belligerents, who scrambled to their feet and called for quarter.

‘I’ll beat you to a pulp, you dogs,’ said Quilp, vainly endeavoring to
get near either of them for a parting blow. ‘I’ll bruise you until
you’re copper-coloured, I’ll break your faces till you haven’t a
profile between you, I will.’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 6

[[characters/little-nell|La piccola Nell]] stava timidamente in disparte, con gli occhi fissi sul volto del signor Quilp mentre leggeva la lettera, mostrando chiaramente dal suo sguardo che sebbene provasse un po' di [[concepts/fear|timore]] e diffidenza per l'uomo basso, era molto incline a ridere della sua apparenza goffa e dell'atteggiamento [[concepts/grotesque|grotesco]]. Eppure si poteva notare nel [[archetypes/child|bambino]] una dolorosa ansia per la risposta di lui, e la consapevolezza del suo potere di renderla spiacevole o angosciante, che era fortemente in contrasto con questo impulso e lo restringeva più efficacemente di quanto lei avrebbe potuto fare con qualsiasi sforzo.

Che il signor Quilp fosse lui stesso perplesso, e in non lieve misura,
per il contenuto della lettera era abbastanza evidente. Prima di averne letto le prime due o tre righe aveva cominciato ad aprire molto gli occhi e a corrugare la fronte in modo terribile; le successive due o tre lo spinsero a grattarsi la testa in maniera straordinariamente viziata, e quando giunse alla conclusione emise un lungo fischio lugubre che indicava sorpresa e sgomento. Dopo averla ripiegata e posata accanto a sé, si morse le unghie di tutte e dieci le dita con estrema voracità; e raccogliendola bruscamente la lesse di nuovo. Il secondo esame sembrò essere altrettanto insoddisfacente del primo e lo immerse in una profonda riflessione da cui si risvegliò per un altro assalto alle sue unghie e a lungo fissò il [[archetypes/child|bambino]], che con gli occhi rivolti verso terra attendeva i suoi ulteriori piaceri.

«Ehi là!», disse infine con una voce e con un'improvvisità che fecero sobbalzare la [[archetypes/child|bambina]] come se le avessero sparato un colpo di pistola all'orecchio. «Nelly!»

'Sì, signore.'

'Sai cosa c'è in questa lettera, Nell?'

'No, signore!'

«Ne siete sicuro, proprio sicuro, assolutamente certo, sulla vostra [[motifs/soul|anima]]?»

'Ne sono certo, signore.'

«Desideri di morire se lo sai, eh?» disse il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]].

«In verità non lo so», rispose il [[archetypes/child|bambino]].

«[[motifs/well|Bene]]!» borbottò Quilp mentre notava il suo sguardo serio. «Ti credo.
Humph! Già andato? Sparito in ventiquattro ore! Che diavolo ne ha fatto, ecco l'enigma!»

Questa riflessione lo portò di nuovo ad arruffarsi i capelli e a mordersi le unghie. Mentre era così impegnato, i suoi lineamenti si distesero gradualmente in quello che per lui era un sorriso allegro, ma che in qualsiasi altro uomo sarebbe stato un ghigno spettrale di [[motifs/pain|dolore]], e quando la [[archetypes/child|bambina]] alzò di nuovo lo sguardo scoprì che lui la stava osservando con straordinaria benevolenza e compiacimento.

'Oggi sei molto carina, Nelly, incantevolmente carina. Sei stanca, Nelly?'

'No, signore. Devo tornare subito, perché sarà preoccupato mentre sono via.'

«Non c'è fretta, [[characters/little-nell|piccola Nell]], non c'è fretta affatto», disse Quilp. «Che ne diresti di essere il mio numero due, Nelly?»

'Essere cosa, signore?'

«Il mio numero due, Nelly, la mia seconda moglie, la signora Quilp», disse il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]].

Il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] sembrava spaventato, ma non riusciva a capire cosa volesse dire il signor Quilp,
che quindi si affrettò a chiarire meglio le sue intenzioni.

«Essere la signora Quilp seconda, quando la signora Quilp prima è morta, dolce Nell», disse Quilp, strizzando gli occhi e attirandola verso di sé con il dito indice curvo, «essere mia moglie, la mia piccola moglie dalle guance di ciliegia e le labbra rosse. Diciamo che la signora Quilp viva cinque anni, o solo quattro, tu avrai proprio l'età giusta per me. Ah ah! Sii una brava ragazza, Nellina, una bravissima ragazza, e vediamo se un giorno non diventerai la signora Quilp di Tower [[motifs/hill|Hill]].»

Lontano dal sentirsi sostenuto e stimolato da questa deliziosa prospettiva,
il [[archetypes/child|bambino]] si ritrasse da lui in grande agitazione, tremando violentemente.
Il signor Quilp, o perché spaventare chiunque gli procurava un
piacere costituzionale, o perché era piacevole contemplare la
[[motifs/death|morte]] della signora Quilp numero uno e l'innalzamento della signora Quilp numero
due al suo posto e titolo, o perché era determinato per i suoi scopi
a essere affabile e di buon umore in quel particolare [[motifs/time|momento]],
si limitò a ridere e fingere di non badare al suo allarme.

«Verrai con me a Tower [[motifs/hill|Hill]] e vedrai la signora Quilp, cioè,
subito», disse il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]]. «È molto affezionata a te, Nell, anche se non tanto quanto lo sono io. Verrai a [[motifs/home|casa]] con me».

«Devo proprio tornare», disse il [[archetypes/child|bambino]]. «Mi ha detto di rientrare non appena avessi la risposta.»

«Ma non l'hai, Nelly», ribatté il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]], «e non l'avrai,
e non puoi averla, finché io non sarò stato a [[motifs/home|casa]], quindi vedi che per fare la tua
commissione, devi venire con me. Passami quel cappello laggiù, mia cara, e andremo
subito». Detto ciò, il signor Quilp si lasciò rotolare gradualmente dalla scrivania finché le sue gambe corte toccarono terra, quando si alzò in piedi e fece strada dal ufficio contabile fino al molo esterno, dove i primi oggetti che si presentarono furono il ragazzo che era rimasto in piedi sulla testa e un altro giovane signore della sua stessa statura, che si rotolavano
nel fango insieme, stretti in un abbraccio serrato, e si percuotevano a vicenda con reciproca cordialità.

«È Kit!» gridò Nelly stringendole la mano «Povero Kit che è venuto con me!
Oh, per favore fermateli, signor Quilp!»

«Li fermerò», gridò Quilp, tuffandosi nella piccola cassa di conteggio e
tornando con un bastone spesso, «li fermerò. Ora, miei ragazzi, combattete.
Combatterò entrambi voi. Vi prenderò tutti e due insieme!»

Con tali provocazioni il [[characters/dwarf|nanerottolo]] brandiva il suo bastone e danzando intorno ai combattenti, calpestandoli e saltellando sopra di loro in una specie di frenesia, colpiva ora l'uno ora l'altro con disperata ferocia, puntando sempre alle teste e infliggendo percosse che solo un piccolo selvaggio avrebbe potuto infliggere. Si trattava di un lavoro più duro del previsto, il che raffreddò ben presto il [[concepts/courage|coraggio]] dei contendenti, i quali si rimisero in piedi e chiesero quartiere.

«Vi ridurrò in poltiglia, cani», disse Quilp, cercando invano di avvicinarsi a uno dei due per un ultimo colpo. «Vi concerò così male che diventerete color rame, vi romperò il viso fino a non lasciarvi nemmeno un profilo tra tutti e due, lo farò».



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_06--part_02" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 6 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 06" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/child,archetype/fool,archetype/villain,motif/home,motif/lion,motif/love,motif/river,motif/secrets,motif/soul,motif/time,motif/water,motif/wind,concept/truth,character/dwarf"></span>


‘Come, you drop that stick or it’ll be worse for you,’ said his boy,
dodging round him and watching an opportunity to rush in; ‘you drop
that stick.’

‘Come a little nearer, and I’ll drop it on your skull, you dog,’ said
Quilp, with gleaming eyes; ‘a little nearer--nearer yet.’

But the boy declined the invitation until his master was apparently a
little off his guard, when he darted in and seizing the weapon tried to
wrest it from his grasp. Quilp, who was as strong as a [[motifs/lion|lion]], easily
kept his hold until the boy was tugging at it with his utmost power,
when he suddenly let it go and sent him reeling backwards, so that he
fell violently upon his head. The success of this manoeuvre tickled Mr
Quilp beyond description, and he laughed and stamped upon the ground as
at a most irresistible jest.

‘Never mind,’ said the boy, nodding his head and rubbing it at the same
[[motifs/time|time]]; ‘you see if ever I offer to strike anybody again because they say
you’re an uglier [[characters/dwarf|dwarf]] than can be seen anywheres for a penny, that’s
all.’

‘Do you mean to say, I’m not, you dog?’ returned Quilp.

‘No!’ retorted the boy.

‘Then what do you fight on my wharf for, you [[archetypes/villain|villain]]?’ said Quilp.

‘Because he said so,’ replied the boy, pointing to Kit, ‘not because you
an’t.’

‘Then why did he say,’ bawled Kit, ‘that Miss Nelly was ugly, and that
she and my master was obliged to do whatever his master liked?  Why did
he say that?’

‘He said what he did because he’s a [[archetypes/fool|fool]], and you said what you did
because you’re very wise and clever--almost too clever to live, unless
you’re very careful of yourself, Kit.’ said Quilp, with great suavity
in his manner, but still more of quiet malice about his eyes and mouth.
‘Here’s sixpence for you, Kit. Always speak the [[concepts/truth|truth]].  At all times,
Kit, speak the [[concepts/truth|truth]]. Lock the counting-house, you dog, and bring me
the key.’

The other boy, to whom this order was addressed, did as he was told,
and was rewarded for his partizanship in behalf of his master, by a
dexterous rap on the nose with the key, which brought the [[motifs/water|water]] into
his eyes. Then Mr Quilp departed with the [[archetypes/child|child]] and Kit in a boat, and
the boy revenged himself by dancing on his head at intervals on the
extreme verge of the wharf, during the whole [[motifs/time|time]] they crossed the
[[motifs/river|river]].

There was only Mrs Quilp at [[motifs/home|home]], and she, little expecting the return
of her lord, was just composing herself for a refreshing slumber when
the sound of his footsteps roused her. She had barely [[motifs/time|time]] to seem to
be occupied in some needle-work, when he entered, accompanied by the
[[archetypes/child|child]]; having left Kit downstairs.

‘Here’s Nelly Trent, dear Mrs Quilp,’ said her husband. ‘A glass of
wine, my dear, and a biscuit, for she has had a long walk. She’ll sit
with you, my [[motifs/soul|soul]], while I write a letter.’

Mrs Quilp looked tremblingly in her spouse’s face to know what this
unusual courtesy might portend, and obedient to the summons she saw in
his gesture, followed him into the next room.

‘Mind what I say to you,’ whispered Quilp. ‘See if you can get out of
her anything about her grandfather, or what they do, or how they live,
or what he tells her. I’ve my reasons for knowing, if I can. You women
talk more freely to one another than you do to us, and you have a soft,
mild way with you that’ll win upon her. Do you hear?’

‘Yes, Quilp.’

‘Go then. What’s the matter now?’

‘Dear Quilp,’ faltered his wife. ‘I [[motifs/love|love]] the [[archetypes/child|child]]--if you could do
without making me deceive her--’
