Avendo Kit solo, lo terrò impegnato in conversazione e metterò questa proprietà nel suo cappello. Farò in modo”, dice, “che il signor [[characters/richard|Richard]] la trovi lì e ne sia la testimonianza. E se questo non toglie Christopher di torno al signor Quilp e non soddisfa i rancori del signor Quilp”, dice, “allora ci deve essere il diavolo dentro”. La signorina Sally rise e disse che era il piano, e dato che sembravano voler andarsene, e io avevo paura di fermarmi più a lungo, sono tornato di sotto. --Ecco!»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_64--part_04" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 64 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 64" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/fire,motif/night,motif/time,character/marchioness,character/nurse,character/richard"></span>


The small servant had gradually worked herself into as much agitation
as Mr Swiveller, and therefore made no effort to restrain him when he
sat up in bed and hastily demanded whether this story had been told to
anybody.

‘How could it be?’ replied his [[characters/nurse|nurse]].  ‘I was almost afraid to think
about it, and hoped the young man would be let off.  When I heard ‘em
say they had found him guilty of what he didn’t do, you was gone, and
so was the lodger--though I think I should have been frightened to tell
him, even if he’d been there.  Ever since I come here, you’ve been out
of your senses, and what would have been the good of telling you then?’

‘[[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]],’ said Mr Swiveller, plucking off his nightcap and
flinging it to the other end of the room; ‘if you’ll do me the favour
to retire for a few minutes and see what sort of a [[motifs/night|night]] it is, I’ll
get up.’

‘You mustn’t think of such a thing,’ cried his [[characters/nurse|nurse]].

‘I must indeed,’ said the patient, looking round the room.
‘Whereabouts are my clothes?’

‘Oh, I’m so glad--you haven’t got any,’ replied the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]].

‘Ma’am!’ said Mr Swiveller, in great astonishment.

‘I’ve been obliged to sell them, every one, to get the things that was
ordered for you.  But don’t take on about that,’ urged the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]],
as Dick fell back upon his pillow.  ‘You’re too weak to stand, indeed.’

‘I am afraid,’ said [[characters/richard|Richard]] dolefully, ‘that you’re right.  What ought
I to do! what is to be done!’

It naturally occurred to him on very little reflection, that the first
step to take would be to communicate with one of the Mr Garlands
instantly.  It was very possible that Mr Abel had not yet left the
office.  In as little [[motifs/time|time]] as it takes to tell it, the small servant
had the address in pencil on a piece of paper; a verbal description of
father and son, which would enable her to recognise either, without
difficulty; and a special caution to be shy of Mr Chuckster, in
consequence of that gentleman’s known antipathy to Kit.  Armed with
these slender powers, she hurried away, commissioned to bring either
old Mr Garland or Mr Abel, bodily, to that apartment.

‘I suppose,’ said Dick, as she closed the door slowly, and peeped into
the room again, to make sure that he was comfortable, ‘I suppose
there’s nothing left--not so much as a waistcoat even?’

‘No, nothing.’

‘It’s embarrassing,’ said Mr Swiveller, ‘in case of [[motifs/fire|fire]]--even an
umbrella would be something--but you did quite right, dear [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]].
I should have died without you!’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

La piccola domestica si era gradualmente agitata quanto il signor Swiveller, e quindi non fece alcuno sforzo per trattenerlo quando si alzò a sedere sul letto e chiese in tutta fretta se questa storia fosse stata raccontata a qualcuno.

«Come sarebbe potuto essere?» rispose la sua [[characters/nurse|balia]]. «Avevo quasi paura di pensarci e speravo che il giovane sarebbe stato assolto. Quando ho sentito dire che lo avevano dichiarato colpevole di qualcosa che non aveva fatto, eri già andato via, e così era il pensionante, anche se credo che avrei avuto paura di dirglielo, anche se fosse stato lì. Da quando sono arrivata qui, sei stato fuori di te, e a che sarebbe servito dirtelo allora?»

«[[characters/marchioness|Marchesa]],» disse il signor Swiveller, strappandosi via il berretto da notte e
lanciandolo dall'altra parte della stanza; «se mi vuole fare il favore
di ritirarsi per qualche minuto e vedere che tipo di [[motifs/night|notte]] è, mi
alzerò.»

«Non dovete pensare a una cosa del genere», esclamò la sua [[characters/nurse|balia]].

"Devo proprio," disse il paziente, guardandosi intorno nella stanza. "Dove sono i miei vestiti?"

«Oh, sono così contenta, non ne hai», rispose la [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]].

«Signora!» esclamò il signor Swiveller, con grande stupore.

«Sono stato costretto a venderli, tutti quanti, per procurarmi le cose che erano state ordinate per te. Ma non ti agitare per questo», esortò la [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], mentre Dick ricadeva sul cuscino. «Sei troppo debole per alzarti, davvero.»

«Temo», disse [[characters/richard|Richard]] con tristezza, «che abbiate ragione.  Cosa dovrei fare! cosa si può fare!»

Naturalmente, dopo averci riflettuto solo un po', gli venne in mente che il primo passo da compiere sarebbe stato quello di mettersi subito in contatto con uno dei signori Garland. Era molto probabile che il signor Abel non avesse ancora lasciato l'ufficio. In un [[motifs/time|tempo]] brevissimo, la piccola serva aveva l'indirizzo scritto a matita su un pezzo di carta; una descrizione verbale di padre e figlio, che le avrebbe permesso di riconoscere l'uno o l'altro senza difficoltà; e un avvertimento speciale di stare alla larga dal signor Chuckster, a causa della nota antipatia di quel gentiluomo per Kit. Armata di questi modesti poteri, si affrettò a partire, incaricata di portare fisicamente in quell'appartamento il vecchio signor Garland o il signor Abel.

«Suppongo», disse Dick mentre lei chiudeva la porta lentamente e sbirciava di nuovo nella stanza per assicurarsi che fosse comodo, «suppongo che non sia rimasto nulla, nemmeno un panciotto?»

‘No, niente.’

«È imbarazzante», disse il signor Swiveller, «in caso di [[motifs/fire|incendio]] -- anche un ombrello sarebbe qualcosa -- ma hai fatto benissimo, cara [[characters/marchioness|marchesa]]. Sarei morto senza di te!»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_65" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 65" data-chapter="Chapter 65" data-kind="chapter" data-tags="archetype/child,motif/city,motif/fire,motif/home,motif/journey,motif/nature,motif/night,motif/road,motif/sleep,motif/tears,motif/time,motif/well,motif/window,concept/fear,concept/honour,concept/hope,concept/nature,concept/truth,character/marchioness,character/nurse,character/richard,character/sally_brass,character/speed"></span>


CHAPTER 65

It was [[motifs/well|well]] for the small servant that she was of a sharp, quick
[[concepts/nature|nature]], or the consequence of sending her out alone, from the very
neighbourhood in which it was most dangerous for her to appear, would
probably have been the restoration of Miss [[characters/sally-brass|Sally Brass]] to the supreme
authority over her person.  Not unmindful of the risk she ran, however,
the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] no sooner left the house than she dived into the first
dark by-way that presented itself, and, without any present reference
to the point to which her [[motifs/journey|journey]] tended, made it her first business to
put two good miles of brick and mortar between herself and Bevis Marks.

When she had accomplished this object, she began to shape her course
for the notary’s office, to which--shrewdly inquiring of apple-women
and oyster-sellers at street-corners, rather than in lighted shops or
of [[motifs/well|well]]-dressed people, at the hazard of attracting notice--she easily
procured a direction.  As carrier-pigeons, on being first let loose in
a strange place, beat the air at random for a short [[motifs/time|time]] before darting
off towards the spot for which they are designed, so did the
[[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] flutter round and round until she believed herself in
safety, and then bear swiftly down upon the port for which she was
bound.

She had no bonnet--nothing on her head but a great cap which, in some
old [[motifs/time|time]], had been worn by [[characters/sally-brass|Sally Brass]], whose taste in head-dresses
was, as we have seen, peculiar--and her [[characters/speed|speed]] was rather retarded than
assisted by her shoes, which, being extremely large and slipshod, flew
off every now and then, and were difficult to find again, among the
crowd of passengers.  Indeed, the poor little creature experienced so
much trouble and delay from having to grope for these articles of dress
in mud and kennel, and suffered in these researches so much jostling,
pushing, squeezing and bandying from hand to hand, that by the [[motifs/time|time]] she
reached the street in which the notary lived, she was fairly worn out
and exhausted, and could not refrain from [[motifs/tears|tears]].

But to have got there at last was a great comfort, especially as there
were lights still burning in the office [[motifs/window|window]], and therefore some [[concepts/hope|hope]]
that she was not too late.  So the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] dried her eyes with the
backs of her hands, and, stealing softly up the steps, peeped in
through the glass door.

Mr Chuckster was standing behind the lid of his desk, making such
preparations towards finishing off for the [[motifs/night|night]], as pulling down his
wristbands and pulling up his shirt-collar, settling his neck more
gracefully in his stock, and secretly arranging his whiskers by the aid
of a little triangular bit of looking glass.  Before the ashes of the
[[motifs/fire|fire]] stood two gentlemen, one of whom she rightly judged to be the
notary, and the other (who was buttoning his great-coat and was
evidently about to depart immediately) Mr Abel Garland.

Having made these observations, the small spy took counsel with
herself, and resolved to wait in the street until Mr Abel came out, as
there would be then no [[concepts/fear|fear]] of having to speak before Mr Chuckster, and
less difficulty in delivering her message.  With this purpose she
slipped out again, and crossing the [[motifs/road|road]], sat down upon a door-step
just opposite.

She had hardly taken this position, when there came dancing up the
street, with his legs all wrong, and his head everywhere by turns, a
pony.  This pony had a little phaeton behind him, and a man in it; but
neither man nor phaeton seemed to embarrass him in the least, as he
reared up on his hind legs, or stopped, or went on, or stood still
again, or backed, or went side-ways, without the smallest reference to
them--just as the fancy seized him, and as if he were the freest animal
in creation.  When they came to the notary’s door, the man called out
in a very respectful manner, ‘Woa then’--intimating that if he might
venture to express a wish, it would be that they stopped there.  The
pony made a moment’s pause; but, as if it occurred to him that to stop
when he was required might be to establish an inconvenient and
dangerous precedent, he immediately started off again, rattled at a
fast trot to the street corner, wheeled round, came back, and then
stopped of his own accord.

‘Oh! you’re a precious creatur!’ said the man--who didn’t venture by
the bye to come out in his true colours until he was safe on the
pavement.  ‘I wish I had the rewarding of you--I do.’

‘What has he been doing?’ said Mr Abel, tying a shawl round his neck as
he came down the steps.

‘He’s enough to fret a man’s heart out,’ replied the hostler.  ‘He is
the most wicious rascal--Woa then, will you?’

‘He’ll never stand still, if you call him names,’ said Mr Abel, getting
in, and taking the reins.  ‘He’s a very good fellow if you know how to
manage him.  This is the first [[motifs/time|time]] he has been out, this long while,
for he has lost his old driver and wouldn’t stir for anybody else, till
this morning.  The lamps are right, are they?  That’s [[motifs/well|well]].  Be here to
take him to-morrow, if you please.  Good [[motifs/night|night]]!’

And, after one or two strange plunges, quite of his own invention, the
pony yielded to Mr Abel’s mildness, and trotted gently off.

All this [[motifs/time|time]] Mr Chuckster had been standing at the door, and the small
servant had been afraid to approach.  She had nothing for it now,
therefore, but to run after the chaise, and to call to Mr Abel to stop.
Being out of breath when she came up with it, she was unable to make
him hear.  The case was desperate; for the pony was quickening his
pace.  The [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] hung on behind for a few moments, and, feeling
that she could go no farther, and must soon yield, clambered by a
vigorous effort into the hinder seat, and in so doing lost one of the
shoes for ever.

Mr Abel being in a thoughtful frame of mind, and having quite enough to
do to keep the pony going, went jogging on without looking round:
little dreaming of the strange figure that was close behind him, until
the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], having in some degree recovered her breath, and the
loss of her shoe, and the novelty of her position, uttered close into
his ear, the words--‘I say, Sir’--

He turned his head quickly enough then, and stopping the pony, cried,
with some trepidation, ‘God bless me, what is this!’

‘Don’t be frightened, Sir,’ replied the still panting messenger.  ‘Oh
I’ve run such a way after you!’

‘What do you want with me?’ said Mr Abel.  ‘How did you come here?’

‘I got in behind,’ replied the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]].  ‘Oh please drive on,
sir--don’t stop--and go towards the [[motifs/city|City]], will you?  And oh do please
make haste, because it’s of consequence.  There’s somebody wants to see
you there.  He sent me to say would you come directly, and that he
knowed all about Kit, and could save him yet, and prove his innocence.’

‘What do you tell me, [[archetypes/child|child]]?’

‘The [[concepts/truth|truth]], upon my word and [[concepts/honour|honour]] I do.  But please to drive on--
quick, please!  I’ve been such a [[motifs/time|time]] gone, he’ll think I’m lost.’

Mr Abel involuntarily urged the pony forward.  The pony, impelled by
some secret sympathy or some new caprice, burst into a great pace, and
neither slackened it, nor indulged in any eccentric performances, until
they arrived at the door of Mr Swiveller’s lodging, where, marvellous
to relate, he consented to stop when Mr Abel checked him.

‘See!  It’s the room up there,’ said the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], pointing to one
where there was a faint light.  ‘Come!’

Mr Abel, who was one of the simplest and most retiring creatures in
existence, and naturally timid withal, hesitated; for he had heard of
people being decoyed into strange places to be robbed and murdered,
under circumstances very like the present, and, for anything he knew to
the contrary, by guides very like the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]].  His regard for Kit,
however, overcame every other consideration.  So, entrusting Whisker to
the charge of a man who was lingering hard by in expectation of the
job, he suffered his companion to take his hand, and to lead him up the
dark and narrow stairs.

He was not a little surprised to find himself conducted into a
dimly-lighted sick chamber, where a man was sleeping tranquilly in bed.

‘An’t it nice to see him lying there so quiet?’ said his guide, in an
earnest whisper.  ‘Oh! you’d say it was, if you had only seen him two
or three days ago.’

Mr Abel made no answer, and, to say the [[concepts/truth|truth]], kept a long way from the
bed and very near the door.  His guide, who appeared to understand his
reluctance, trimmed the candle, and taking it in her hand, approached
the bed.  As she did so, the sleeper started up, and he recognised in
the wasted face the features of [[characters/richard|Richard]] Swiveller.

‘Why, how is this?’ said Mr Abel kindly, as he hurried towards him.
‘You have been ill?’

‘Very,’ replied Dick.  ‘Nearly dead.  You might have chanced to hear of
your [[characters/richard|Richard]] on his bier, but for the friend I sent to fetch you.
Another shake of the hand, [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], if you please.  Sit down, Sir.’

Mr Abel seemed rather astonished to hear of the quality of his guide,
and took a chair by the bedside.

‘I have sent for you, Sir,’ said Dick--‘but she told you on what
account?’

‘She did.  I am quite bewildered by all this.  I really don’t know what
to say or think,’ replied Mr Abel.

‘You’ll say that presently,’ retorted Dick.  ‘[[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], take a seat
on the bed, will you?  Now, tell this gentleman all that you told me;
and be particular.  Don’t you speak another word, Sir.’

The story was repeated; it was, in effect, exactly the same as before,
without any deviation or omission.  [[characters/richard|Richard]] Swiveller kept his eyes
fixed on his visitor during its narration, and directly it was
concluded, took the word again.

‘You have heard it all, and you’ll not forget it.  I’m too giddy and
too queer to suggest anything; but you and your friends will know what
to do.  After this long delay, every minute is an age.  If ever you
went [[motifs/home|home]] fast in your life, go [[motifs/home|home]] fast to-[[motifs/night|night]].  Don’t stop to say
one word to me, but go.  She will be found here, whenever she’s wanted;
and as to me, you’re pretty sure to find me at [[motifs/home|home]], for a week or two.
There are more reasons than one for that.  [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], a light!  If
you lose another minute in looking at me, sir, I’ll never forgive you!’

Mr Abel needed no more remonstrance or persuasion.  He was gone in an
instant; and the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], returning from lighting him down-stairs,
reported that the pony, without any preliminary objection whatever, had
dashed away at full gallop.

‘That’s right!’ said Dick; ‘and hearty of him; and I [[concepts/honour|honour]] him from
this [[motifs/time|time]].  But get some supper and a mug of beer, for I am sure you
must be tired.  Do have a mug of beer.  It will do me as much good to
see you take it as if I might drink it myself.’

Nothing but this assurance could have prevailed upon the small [[characters/nurse|nurse]] to
indulge in such a luxury.  Having eaten and drunk to Mr Swiveller’s
extreme contentment, given him his drink, and put everything in neat
order, she wrapped herself in an old coverlet and lay down upon the rug
before the [[motifs/fire|fire]].

Mr Swiveller was by that [[motifs/time|time]] murmuring in his [[motifs/sleep|sleep]], ‘Strew then, oh
strew, a bed of rushes.  Here will we stay, till morning blushes.  Good
[[motifs/night|night]], [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]]!’




<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_66--part_01" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 66 (part 1)" data-chapter="Chapter 66" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="topos/double,motif/dreams,motif/night,motif/time,motif/water,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/jealousy,concept/truth,character/marchioness,character/nurse,character/richard"></span>


CHAPTER 66

On awaking in the morning, [[characters/richard|Richard]] Swiveller became conscious, by slow
degrees, of whispering voices in his room.  Looking out between the
curtains, he espied Mr Garland, Mr Abel, the notary, and the single
gentleman, gathered round the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], and talking to her with
great earnestness but in very subdued tones--fearing, no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], to
disturb him.  He lost no [[motifs/time|time]] in letting them know that this precaution
was unnecessary, and all four gentlemen directly approached his
bedside.  Old Mr Garland was the first to stretch out his hand, and
inquire how he felt.

Dick was about to answer that he felt much better, though still as weak
as need be, when his little [[characters/nurse|nurse]], pushing the visitors aside and
pressing up to his pillow as if in [[concepts/jealousy|jealousy]] of their interference, set
his breakfast before him, and insisted on his taking it before he
underwent the fatigue of speaking or of being spoken to.  Mr Swiveller,
who was perfectly ravenous, and had had, all [[motifs/night|night]], amazingly distinct
and consistent [[motifs/dreams|dreams]] of mutton chops, [[topoi/double|double]] stout, and similar
delicacies, felt even the weak tea and dry toast such irresistible
temptations, that he consented to eat and drink on one condition.

‘And that is,’ said Dick, returning the pressure of Mr Garland’s hand,
‘that you answer me this question truly, before I take a bit or drop.
Is it too late?’

‘For completing the work you began so [[motifs/well|well]] last [[motifs/night|night]]?’ returned the
old gentleman.  ‘No.  Set your mind at rest on that point.  It is not,
I assure you.’

Comforted by this intelligence, the patient applied himself to his food
with a keen appetite, though evidently not with a greater zest in the
eating than his [[characters/nurse|nurse]] appeared to have in seeing him eat.  The manner
of this meal was this:--Mr Swiveller, holding the slice of toast or cup
of tea in his left hand, and taking a bite or drink, as the case might
be, constantly kept, in his right, one palm of the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] tight
locked; and to shake, or even to kiss this imprisoned hand, he would
stop every now and then, in the very act of swallowing, with perfect
seriousness of intention, and the utmost gravity.  As often as he put
anything into his mouth, whether for eating or drinking, the face of
the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] lighted up beyond all description; but whenever he gave
her one or other of these tokens of recognition, her countenance became
overshadowed, and she began to sob.  Now, whether she was in her
laughing joy, or in her crying one, the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] could not help
turning to the visitors with an appealing look, which seemed to say,
‘You see this fellow--can I help this?’--and they, being thus made, as
it were, parties to the scene, as regularly answered by another look,
‘No.  Certainly not.’  This dumb-show, taking place during the whole
[[motifs/time|time]] of the invalid’s breakfast, and the invalid himself, pale and
emaciated, performing no small part in the same, it may be fairly
questioned whether at any meal, where no word, good or bad, was spoken
from beginning to end, so much was expressed by gestures in themselves
so slight and unimportant.

At length--and to say the [[concepts/truth|truth]] before very long--Mr Swiveller had
despatched as much toast and tea as in that stage of his recovery it
was discreet to let him have.  But the cares of the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] did not
stop here; for, disappearing for an instant and presently returning
with a basin of fair [[motifs/water|water]], she laved his face and hands, brushed his
hair, and in short made him as spruce and smart as anybody under such
circumstances could be made; and all this, in as brisk and
business-like a manner, as if he were a very little boy, and she his
grown-up [[characters/nurse|nurse]].  To these various attentions, Mr Swiveller submitted in
a kind of grateful astonishment beyond the reach of language.  When
they were at last brought to an end, and the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] had withdrawn
into a distant corner to take her own poor breakfast (cold enough by
that [[motifs/time|time]]), he turned his face away for some few moments, and shook
hands heartily with the air.

‘Gentlemen,’ said Dick, rousing himself from this pause, and turning
round again, ‘you’ll excuse me.  Men who have been brought so low as I
have been, are easily fatigued.  I am fresh again now, and fit for
talking.  We’re short of chairs here, among other trifles, but if
you’ll do me the favour to sit upon the bed--’

‘What can we do for you?’ said Mr Garland, kindly.

‘If you could make the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] yonder, a [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]], in real,
sober earnest,’ returned Dick, ‘I’d thank you to get it done off-hand.
But as you can’t, and as the question is not what you will do for me,
but what you will do for somebody else who has a better claim upon you,
pray sir let me know what you intend doing.’

‘It’s chiefly on that account that we have come just now,’ said the
single gentleman, ‘for you will have another visitor presently.  We
feared you would be anxious unless you knew from ourselves what steps
we intended to take, and therefore came to you before we stirred in the
matter.’

‘Gentlemen,’ returned Dick, ‘I thank you.  Anybody in the helpless
state that you see me in, is naturally anxious.  Don’t let me interrupt
you, sir.’

‘Then, you see, my good fellow,’ said the single gentleman, ‘that while
we have no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] whatever of the [[concepts/truth|truth]] of this disclosure, which has so
providentially come to light--’

‘Meaning hers?’ said Dick, pointing towards the [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]].

‘--Meaning hers, of course.  While we have no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] of that, or that a
proper use of it would procure the poor lad’s immediate pardon and
liberation, we have a great [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] whether it would, by itself, enable
us to reach Quilp, the chief agent in this villany.  I should tell you
that this [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] has been confirmed into something very nearly
approaching certainty by the best opinions we have been enabled, in
this short space of [[motifs/time|time]], to take upon the subject.  You’ll agree with
us, that to give him even the most distant chance of escape, if we
could help it, would be monstrous.  You say with us, no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], if
somebody must escape, let it be any one but he.’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

CAPITOLO 66

Al risveglio del mattino, [[characters/richard|Richard]] Swiveller divenne consapevole, a poco a poco, di voci sussurrate nella sua stanza. Guardando tra le tende, scorse il signor Garland, il signor Abel, il notaio e il gentiluomo singolo, radunati intorno alla [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] e che le parlavano con grande serietà ma in toni molto sommessi, temendo, senza [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], di disturbarlo. Non perse [[motifs/time|tempo]] a far loro sapere che tale precauzione era inutile, e tutti e quattro gli signori si avvicinarono subito al suo letto. Il vecchio signor Garland fu il primo a tendere la mano e a chiedergli come si sentiva.

Dick stava per rispondere che si sentiva molto meglio, sebbene ancora debole
come era necessario, quando la sua piccola [[characters/nurse|infermiera]], spingendo da parte i visitatori
e avvicinandosi al suo cuscino come se fosse in [[concepts/jealousy|gelosia]] per la loro interferenza, gli mise
davanti la colazione e insistette affinché la consumasse prima di
affrontare la fatica di parlare o di essere ascoltato.  Il signor Swiveller,
che era perfettamente affamato, e aveva avuto, per tutta la [[motifs/night|notte]], [[motifs/dreams|sogni]]
incredibilmente distinti e coerenti di bistecca di agnello, birra [[topoi/double|doppia]] e simili
delizie, sentì che anche il tè debole e il pane tostato rappresentavano tentazioni
irresistibili, tanto che accettò di mangiare e bere a una condizione.

«E questa è», disse Dick, restituendo la pressione della mano del signor Garland,
«che mi rispondiate sinceramente a questa domanda, prima che io prenda un boccone o beva una goccia.
È troppo tardi?»

«Per completare il lavoro che hai iniziato così [[motifs/well|bene]] ieri [[motifs/night|sera]]?» rispose il vecchio signore. «No. Tranquillizzati su questo punto. Non è così, te lo assicuro.»

Consolato da questa notizia, il paziente si dedicò al suo cibo con un appetito vivace, sebbene evidentemente non con un gusto maggiore nel mangiare rispetto a quello che la sua [[characters/nurse|infermiera]] sembrava avere nel vederlo mangiare.  Il modo di questo pasto era questo:--Mr Swiveller, tenendo il pezzo di toast o la tazza di tè nella sua mano sinistra, e prendendo un morso o un sorso, a seconda dei casi, manteneva costantemente, nella sua destra, una mano della [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] stretta saldamente; e per scuotere, o anche per baciare questa mano imprigionata, si fermava di tanto in tanto, nel bel mezzo dell'atto di inghiottire, con perfetta serietà di intenti e la massima gravità.  Ogni volta che metteva qualcosa in bocca, sia per mangiare che per bere, il volto della [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] si illuminava oltre ogni descrizione; ma ogni volta che le dava uno di questi segni di riconoscimento, il suo volto si offuscava, e lei iniziava a singhiozzare.  Ora, che fosse nella sua gioia ridanciana, o in quella piangente, la [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] non poteva fare a meno di rivolgersi ai visitatori con uno sguardo di appello, che sembrava dire: ‘Vedete questo tizio--posso fare qualcosa?’--e loro, essendo così, per così dire, coinvolti nella scena, rispondevano regolarmente con un altro sguardo: ‘No.  Certo che no.’  Questo mimo, che aveva luogo durante tutto il [[motifs/time|tempo]] della colazione dell'invalido, e l'invalido stesso, pallido ed emaciato, che svolgeva una parte non piccola nella stessa, può essere giustamente messo in dubbio se in qualche pasto, dove non una parola, buona o cattiva, veniva pronunciata dall'inizio alla fine, tanto fosse espresso da gesti in sé così lievi e insignificanti.

Alla fine -- e per dire la [[concepts/truth|verità]] non molto tempo dopo -- il signor Swiveller aveva consumato una quantità di pane tostato e tè che, in quella fase della sua convalescenza, era prudente lasciargli avere. Ma le cure della [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] non si fermavano qui; infatti, scomparendo per un istante e tornando poco dopo con una bacinella d'[[motifs/water|acqua]] pulita, gli lavò il viso e le mani, gli spazzolò i capelli e, in breve, lo mise in ordine e lo fece apparire il più elegante e presentabile che si potesse sotto tali circostanze; e tutto ciò con una vivacità e una serietà d'affari, come se lui fosse un bambino molto piccolo e lei la sua [[characters/nurse|balia]] ormai cresciuta. A queste varie attenzioni, il signor Swiveller si sottomise in una specie di gratitudine e stupore al di là di ogni espressione. Quando queste furono finalmente terminate e la [[characters/marchioness|Marchioness]] si ritirò in un angolo lontano per fare la sua povera colazione (fredda ormai a quell'[[motifs/time|ora]]), egli volse il viso altrove per alcuni istanti e strinse calorosamente la mano all'aria.

«Signori», disse Dick, riprendendosi da questa pausa e girandosi di nuovo, «mi scuserete. Gli uomini che sono stati ridotti così in basso come me, si stancano facilmente. Ora sono di nuovo fresco e pronto a parlare. Qui ci mancano le sedie, tra le altre piccole cose, ma se vorrete farmi il favore di sedervi sul letto, »

«Cosa possiamo fare per voi?» disse gentilmente il signor Garland.

«Se poteste trasformare la [[characters/marchioness|marchesa]] là in una vera e propria [[characters/marchioness|marchesa]],» rispose Dick, «vi sarei grato se lo facessero subito.
Ma poiché non potete, e poiché la questione non è cosa farete per me,
ma cosa farete per qualcun altro che ha un diritto maggiore su di voi,
per favore, signore, fatemi sapere cosa intendete fare.»

«È principalmente per questo motivo che siamo venuti proprio ora», disse l'uomo solo, «perché fra poco avrete un altro visitatore.  Ci preoccupava che poteste essere ansiosi se non aveste saputo da noi quali provvedimenti intendevamo prendere, e per questo siamo venuti da voi prima di muoverci in proposito.»

«Signori», rispose Dick, «vi ringrazio. Chiunque si trovi in uno stato di impotenza come quello in cui mi vedete, è naturalmente ansioso. Non fate che vi interrompa, signore».

«Allora, vede, mio buon amico», disse il signore da solo, «che mentre
non abbiamo alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] sulla [[concepts/truth|verità]] di questa rivelazione, che è venuta a galla così
provvidenzialmente--»

«Vuol dire la sua?» disse Dick, indicando la [[characters/marchioness|marchesa]].

«--Intendiamo la sua, naturalmente.  Mentre non abbiamo alcun [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] al riguardo, né che un
uso appropriato di essa procurerebbe la immediata grazia e
liberazione del povero ragazzo, abbiamo un grande [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] se ciò, da solo, ci permetterebbe
di raggiungere Quilp, il principale responsabile di questa infamia.  Dovrei dirvi
che questo [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]] è stato confermato in qualcosa di molto vicino
alla certezza dalle migliori opinioni che siamo stati in grado, in
questo breve lasso di [[motifs/time|tempo]], di raccogliere sull'argomento.  Siete d'accordo con
noi, che dare anche la più remota possibilità di fuga, se potessimo evitarlo, sarebbe mostruoso.  Siete d'accordo con noi, senza [[concepts/doubt|dubbio]], se
qualcuno deve scappare, che sia chiunque tranne lui.»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_66--part_02" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 66 (part 2)" data-chapter="Chapter 66" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/leaves,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,motif/wind,concept/beauty,concept/guilt,character/richard,character/sally_brass"></span>


‘Yes,’ returned Dick, ‘certainly.  That is if somebody must--but upon
my word, I’m unwilling that anybody should.  Since laws were made for
every degree, to curb vice in others as [[motifs/well|well]] as in me--and so forth
you know--doesn’t it strike you in that light?’

The single gentleman smiled as if the light in which Mr Swiveller had
put the question were not the clearest in the world, and proceeded to
explain that they contemplated proceeding by stratagem in the first
instance; and that their design was to endeavour to extort a confession
from the gentle Sarah.

‘When she finds how much we know, and how we know it,’ he said, ‘and
that she is clearly compromised already, we are not without strong
hopes that we may be enabled through her means to punish the other two
effectually.  If we could do that, she might go scot-free for aught I
cared.’

Dick received this project in anything but a gracious manner,
representing with as much warmth as he was then capable of showing,
that they would find the old buck (meaning Sarah) more difficult to
manage than Quilp himself--that, for any tampering, terrifying, or
cajolery, she was a very unpromising and unyielding subject--that she
was of a kind of brass not easily melted or moulded into shape--in
short, that they were no match for her, and would be signally defeated.
But it was in vain to urge them to adopt some other course.  The single
gentleman has been described as explaining their joint intentions, but
it should have been written that they all spoke together; that if any
one of them by chance held his peace for a moment, he stood gasping and
panting for an opportunity to strike in again: in a word, that they had
reached that pitch of impatience and anxiety where men can neither be
persuaded nor reasoned with; and that it would have been as easy to
turn the most impetuous [[motifs/wind|wind]] that ever blew, as to prevail on them to
reconsider their determination.  So, after telling Mr Swiveller how
they had not lost sight of Kit’s mother and the children; how they had
never once even lost sight of Kit himself, but had been unremitting in
their endeavours to procure a mitigation of his sentence; how they had
been perfectly distracted between the strong proofs of his [[concepts/guilt|guilt]], and
their own fading hopes of his innocence; and how he, [[characters/richard|Richard]] Swiveller,
might keep his mind at rest, for everything should be happily adjusted
between that [[motifs/time|time]] and [[motifs/night|night]];--after telling him all this, and adding a
great many kind and cordial expressions, personal to himself, which it
is unnecessary to recite, Mr Garland, the notary, and the single
gentleman, took their [[motifs/leaves|leaves]] at a very critical [[motifs/time|time]], or [[characters/richard|Richard]]
Swiveller must assuredly have been driven into another fever, whereof
the results might have been fatal.

Mr Abel remained behind, very often looking at his watch and at the
room door, until Mr Swiveller was roused from a short nap, by the
setting-down on the landing-place outside, as from the shoulders of a
porter, of some giant load, which seemed to shake the house, and made
the little physic bottles on the mantel-shelf ring again.  Directly
this sound reached his ears, Mr Abel started up, and hobbled to the
door, and opened it; and behold! there stood a strong man, with a
mighty hamper, which, being hauled into the room and presently
unpacked, disgorged such treasures as tea, and coffee, and wine, and
rusks, and oranges, and grapes, and fowls ready trussed for boiling,
and calves’-foot jelly, and arrow-root, and sago, and other delicate
restoratives, that the small servant, who had never thought it possible
that such things could be, except in shops, stood rooted to the spot in
her one shoe, with her mouth and eyes watering in unison, and her power
of speech quite gone.  But, not so Mr Abel; or the strong man who
emptied the hamper, big as it was, in a twinkling; and not so the nice
old lady, who appeared so suddenly that she might have come out of the
hamper too (it was quite large enough), and who, bustling about on
tiptoe and without noise--now here, now there, now everywhere at
once--began to fill out the jelly in tea-cups, and to make chicken
broth in small saucepans, and to peel oranges for the sick man and to
cut them up in little pieces, and to ply the small servant with glasses
of wine and choice bits of everything until more substantial meat could
be prepared for her refreshment.  The whole of which appearances were
so unexpected and bewildering, that Mr Swiveller, when he had taken two
oranges and a little jelly, and had seen the strong man walk off with
the empty basket, plainly leaving all that abundance for his use and
benefit, was fain to lie down and fall asleep again, from sheer
inability to entertain such wonders in his mind.

Meanwhile, the single gentleman, the Notary, and Mr Garland, repaired
to a certain coffee-house, and from that place indited and sent a
letter to Miss [[characters/sally-brass|Sally Brass]], requesting her, in terms mysterious and
brief, to favour an unknown friend who wished to consult her, with her
company there, as speedily as possible.  The communication performed
its errand so [[motifs/well|well]], that within ten minutes of the messenger’s return
and report of its delivery, Miss Brass herself was announced.

‘Pray ma’am,’ said the single gentleman, whom she found alone in the
room, ‘take a chair.’

Miss Brass sat herself down, in a very stiff and frigid state, and
seemed--as indeed she was--not a little astonished to find that the
lodger and her mysterious correspondent were one and the same person.

‘You did not expect to see me?’ said the single gentleman.

‘I didn’t think much about it,’ returned the [[concepts/beauty|beauty]].  ‘I supposed it
was business of some kind or other.  If it’s about the apartments, of
course you’ll give my brother regular notice, you know--or money.
That’s very easily settled.  You’re a responsible party, and in such a
case lawful money and lawful notice are pretty much the same.’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

«Sì», rispose Dick, «certamente.  A meno che qualcuno debba--ma, a dire il vero, non voglio che nessuno lo faccia.  Poiché le leggi sono state fatte per ogni grado, per frenare il vizio negli altri così come in me--e così via, sapete--non vi sembra che sia così?»

Il signore scapolo sorrise come se la luce in cui il signor Swiveller aveva posto la domanda non fosse la più chiara del mondo, e proseguì spiegando che intendevano procedere per stratagemma in un primo momento; e che il loro piano era di cercare di estorcere una confessione dalla gentile Sarah.

«Quando scoprirà quanto sappiamo, e come lo sappiamo», disse, «e che è già chiaramente compromessa, non siamo senza forti speranze che possiamo essere messi in grado, attraverso i suoi mezzi, di punire efficacemente gli altri due. Se potessimo farlo, lei potrebbe andarsene senza pagare nulla, per quanto mi riguarda.»

Dick accolse il progetto in modo tutt’altro che cortese, sostenendo con tutto l’entusiasmo di cui era capace che avrebbero trovato la vecchia capra (intendendo Sarah) più difficile da gestire di Quilp in persona, che per quanto riguardava manipolazioni, intimidazioni o blandizie, lei era un soggetto davvero poco promettente e irremovibile, che era fatta di un genere di ottone non facile da fondere o modellare, insomma che non erano all’altezza di lei e sarebbero stati sconfitti in modo clamoroso. Ma fu inutile cercare di convincerli a seguire un altro piano. Il signorino è stato descritto mentre spiegava le loro intenzioni comuni, ma avrebbe dovuto essere scritto che parlavano tutti insieme, che se per caso uno di loro taceva per un momento, stava ansimando e cercando disperatamente un’occasione per intervenire di nuovo: insomma, avevano raggiunto un livello di impazienza e ansia tale che non si poteva né persuaderli né ragionare con loro, e sarebbe stato altrettanto facile deviare il più impetuoso [[motifs/wind|vento]] che mai soffiò, quanto convincerli a riconsiderare la loro decisione. Così, dopo aver detto a Mr Swiveller come non avessero perso di vista la madre di Kit e i bambini, come non avessero mai perso di vista nemmeno Kit stesso, ma avessero fatto ogni sforzo per ottenere una riduzione della sua pena, come fossero stati completamente disorientati tra le prove schiaccianti della sua [[concepts/guilt|colpevolezza]] e le loro speranze sempre più deboli della sua innocenza, e come lui, [[characters/richard|Richard]] Swiveller, potesse stare tranquillo perché tutto si sarebbe risolto felicemente tra quel [[motifs/time|momento]] e [[motifs/night|sera]]; dopo avergli detto tutto questo, e aggiunto molte altre espressioni gentili e cordiali, personali nei suoi confronti, che non è necessario riportare, Mr Garland, il notaio e il signorino presero congedo in un momento davvero critico, altrimenti [[characters/richard|Richard]] Swiveller sarebbe stato sicuramente costretto in un’altra febbre, i cui risultati avrebbero potuto essere fatali.

Il signor Abel rimase indietro, guardando spesso l'orologio e la porta della stanza, finché il signor Swiveller fu svegliato da un breve pisolino dal posizionamento su un luogo esterno, come sulle spalle di un facchino, di un carico gigantesco, che sembrò scuotere la casa e fece tintinnare di nuovo le piccole bottiglie di medicina sullo scaffale del caminetto. Non appena questo suono raggiunse le sue orecchie, il signor Abel si alzò di scatto, zoppicò fino alla porta e la aprì; ed ecco! c'era un uomo robusto con un enorme cesto, che, una volta trascinato nella stanza e subito svuotato, riversò tesori come tè, caffè, vino, biscotti, arance, uva, polli già spennati per bollire, gelatina di piede di vitello, fecola di maranta, sago e altri delicati rinforzi, che la piccola serva, che non aveva mai pensato che tali cose potessero esistere, se non nei negozi, rimase radicata al posto con un solo scarpa, con la bocca e gli occhi che le colavano all'unisono, e la capacità di parlare completamente persa. Ma non così il signor Abel; o l'uomo robusto che svuotò il cesto, grande com'era, in un attimo; e nemmeno la gentile vecchia signora, che apparve così all'improvviso che avrebbe potuto uscire anche lei dal cesto (era abbastanza grande), e che, affaccendandosi in punta di piedi e senza fare rumore--ora qui, ora là, ora dappertutto contemporaneamente--cominciò a riempire le tazze da tè con la gelatina, a fare brodo di pollo in piccole pentole, a sbucciare arance per l'uomo malato e a tagliarle a pezzetti, e a offrire alla piccola serva bicchieri di vino e bocconi prelibati di tutto finché non si potesse preparare per lei un pasto più sostanzioso. Tutte queste apparizioni erano così inaspettate e sconcertanti, che il signor Swiveller, dopo aver preso due arance e un po' di gelatina, e aver visto l'uomo robusto andarsene con il cesto vuoto, lasciando chiaramente tutta quell'abbondanza per il suo uso e beneficio, fu costretto a sdraiarsi e a riaddormentarsi, per pura incapacità di accogliere tali meraviglie nella sua mente.

Nel frattempo, il signore single, il notaio e il signor Garland si recarono in un certo caffè e da quel luogo scrissero e inviarono una lettera a Miss [[characters/sally-brass|Sally Brass]], chiedendole, in termini misteriosi e brevi, di favorire un amico sconosciuto che desiderava consultarla, con la sua compagnia lì, il più rapidamente possibile. La comunicazione svolse il suo compito così [[motifs/well|bene]], che entro dieci minuti dal ritorno del messaggero e dalla notizia della sua consegna, fu annunciata la stessa Miss Brass.

«Per favore, signora», disse l'unico gentiluomo, che lei trovò solo nella stanza, «si prega di prendere una sedia.»

La signorina Brass si sedette, in uno stato di grande rigidità e freddezza, e sembrò - come infatti era - non poco sorpresa di scoprire che l'inquilino e il suo misterioso corrispondente erano una sola e stessa persona.

«Non vi aspettavate di vedermi?» disse il signore.

«Non ci ho pensato molto», rispose la [[concepts/beauty|bellezza]]. «Supponevo che fosse una faccenda di qualche tipo. Se riguarda gli appartamenti, naturalmente darai a mio fratello un preavviso regolare, lo sai, oppure dei soldi. È una cosa molto facile da risolvere. Sei una persona responsabile, e in un caso del genere il denaro legale e il preavviso legale sono praticamente la stessa cosa.»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_66--part_03" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 66 (part 3)" data-chapter="Chapter 66" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/innocent,archetype/villain,motif/death,motif/dust,motif/grave,motif/night,motif/time,motif/well,concept/history,concept/honour,concept/hope,concept/imagination,concept/mercy,concept/truth,form/history,character/sampson_brass"></span>


‘I am obliged to you for your good opinion,’ retorted the single
gentleman, ‘and quite concur in these sentiments.  But that is not the
subject on which I wish to speak with you.’

‘Oh!’ said Sally.  ‘Then just state the particulars, will you?  I
suppose it’s professional business?’

‘Why, it is connected with the law, certainly.’

‘Very [[motifs/well|well]],’ returned Miss Brass.  ‘My brother and I are just the same.
I can take any instructions, or give you any advice.’

‘As there are other parties interested besides myself,’ said the single
gentleman, rising and opening the door of an inner room, ‘we had better
confer together.  Miss Brass is here, gentlemen.’

Mr Garland and the Notary walked in, looking very [[motifs/grave|grave]]; and, drawing up
two chairs, one on each side of the single gentleman, formed a kind of
fence round the gentle Sarah, and penned her into a corner.  Her brother
Sampson under such circumstances would certainly have evinced some
confusion or anxiety, but she--all composure--pulled out the tin box,
and calmly took a pinch of snuff.

‘Miss Brass,’ said the Notary, taking the word at this crisis, ‘we
professional people understand each other, and, when we choose, can say
what we have to say, in very few words.  You advertised a runaway
servant, the other day?’

‘[[motifs/well|Well]],’ returned Miss Sally, with a sudden flush overspreading her
features, ‘what of that?’

‘She is found, ma’am,’ said the Notary, pulling out his
pocket-handkerchief with a flourish.  ‘She is found.’

‘Who found her?’ demanded Sarah hastily.

‘We did, ma’am--we three.  Only last [[motifs/night|night]], or you would have heard
from us before.’

‘And now I have heard from you,’ said Miss Brass, folding her arms as
though she were about to deny something to the [[motifs/death|death]], ‘what have you
got to say?  Something you have got into your heads about her, of
course.  Prove it, will you--that’s all.  Prove it.  You have found
her, you say.  I can tell you (if you don’t know it) that you have
found the most artful, lying, pilfering, devilish little minx that was
ever born.--Have you got her here?’ she added, looking sharply round.

‘No, she is not here at present,’ returned the Notary.  ‘But she is
quite safe.’

‘Ha!’ cried Sally, twitching a pinch of snuff out of her box, as
spitefully as if she were in the very act of wrenching off the small
servant’s nose; ‘she shall be safe enough from this [[motifs/time|time]], I warrant
you.’

‘I [[concepts/hope|hope]] so,’ replied the Notary.  ‘Did it occur to you for the first
[[motifs/time|time]], when you found she had run away, that there were two keys to your
kitchen door?’

Miss Sally took another pinch, and putting her head on one side, looked
at her questioner, with a curious kind of spasm about her mouth, but
with a cunning aspect of immense expression.

‘Two keys,’ repeated the Notary; ‘one of which gave her the
opportunities of roaming through the house at nights when you supposed
her fast locked up, and of overhearing confidential
consultations--among others, that particular conference, to be
described to-day before a justice, which you will have an opportunity
of hearing her relate; that conference which you and Mr Brass held
together, on the [[motifs/night|night]] before that most unfortunate and [[archetypes/innocent|innocent]] young
man was accused of robbery, by a horrible device of which I will only
say that it may be characterised by the epithets which you have applied
to this wretched little witness, and by a few stronger ones besides.’

Sally took another pinch.  Although her face was wonderfully composed,
it was apparent that she was wholly taken by surprise, and that what
she had expected to be taxed with, in connection with her small
servant, was something very different from this.

‘Come, come, Miss Brass,’ said the Notary, ‘you have great command of
feature, but you feel, I see, that by a chance which never entered your
[[concepts/imagination|imagination]], this base design is revealed, and two of its plotters must
be brought to justice.  Now, you know the pains and penalties you are
liable to, and so I need not dilate upon them, but I have a proposal to
make to you.  You have the [[concepts/honour|honour]] of being sister to one of the
greatest scoundrels unhung; and, if I may venture to say so to a lady,
you are in every respect quite worthy of him.  But connected with you
two is a third party, a [[archetypes/villain|villain]] of the name of Quilp, the prime mover
of the whole diabolical device, who I believe to be worse than either.
For his sake, Miss Brass, do us the favour to reveal the whole [[concepts/history|history]]
of this affair.  Let me remind you that your doing so, at our instance,
will place you in a safe and comfortable position--your present one is
not desirable--and cannot injure your brother; for against him and you
we have quite sufficient evidence (as you hear) already.  I will not
say to you that we suggest this course in [[concepts/mercy|mercy]] (for, to tell you the
[[concepts/truth|truth]], we do not entertain any regard for you), but it is a necessity
to which we are reduced, and I recommend it to you as a matter of the
very best policy.  [[motifs/time|Time]],’ said Mr Witherden, pulling out his watch, ‘in
a business like this, is exceedingly precious.  Favour us with your
decision as speedily as possible, ma’am.’

With a smile upon her face, and looking at each of the three by turns,
Miss Brass took two or three more pinches of snuff, and having by this
[[motifs/time|time]] very little left, travelled round and round the box with her
forefinger and thumb, scraping up another.  Having disposed of this
likewise and put the box carefully in her pocket, she said,--

‘I am to accept or reject at once, am I?’

‘Yes,’ said Mr Witherden.

The charming creature was opening her lips to speak in reply, when the
door was hastily opened too, and the head of [[characters/sampson-brass|Sampson Brass]] was thrust
into the room.

‘Excuse me,’ said the gentleman hastily.  ‘Wait a bit!’

So saying, and quite indifferent to the astonishment his presence
occasioned, he crept in, shut the door, kissed his greasy glove as
servilely as if it were the [[motifs/dust|dust]], and made a most abject bow.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

«Sono in debito con voi per la vostra buona opinione», ribatté il gentiluomo scapolo, «e concordo pienamente con questi sentimenti. Ma questo non è l'argomento di cui desidero parlare con voi.»

«Oh!» disse Sally. «Allora dica pure i particolari, per favore. Immagino che si tratti di una faccenda professionale?»

'Beh, è collegato alla legge, certamente.'

«Molto [[motifs/well|bene]]», rispose Miss Brass. «Mio fratello ed io siamo esattamente uguali.
Posso ricevere istruzioni o darle consigli.»

«Poiché ci sono altri interessati oltre a me», disse il signore scapolo, alzandosi e aprendo la porta di una stanza interna, «è meglio che ci consultiamo insieme. La signorina Brass è qui, signori.»

Il signor Garland e il notaio entrarono, con un'aria molto [[motifs/grave|grave]]; e, avvicinando due sedie, una per parte del signore solo, formarono una specie di recinto intorno alla gentile Sarah, e la spinsero in un angolo.  Suo fratello Sampson in circostanze simili avrebbe certamente mostrato un po' di confusione o ansia, ma lei -- tutta calma -- tirò fuori la scatola di latta e prese tranquillamente un pizzico di tabacco da fiuto.

«Signorina Brass», disse il notaio, prendendo la parola in quel momento, «noi professionisti ci intendiamo e, quando vogliamo, possiamo dire ciò che abbiamo da dire in pochissime parole. Avete dato un annuncio per una serva fuggita, l'altro giorno?»

«[[motifs/well|Beh]],» rispose Miss Sally, con un'improvvisa vampata di rossore che le si diffuse sul viso, «che c'è di male?»

«È stata trovata, signora», disse il notaio, tirando fuori il fazzoletto con un gesto teatrale. «È stata trovata.»

«Chi l'ha trovata?» chiese Sarah in fretta.

«L'abbiamo fatto, signora, noi tre. Proprio la [[motifs/night|scorsa]] notte, altrimenti avrebbe già ricevuto nostre notizie.»

«E ora ho sentito quello che avete da dire», disse Miss Brass, incrociando le braccia come se fosse sul punto di negare qualcosa fino alla [[motifs/death|morte]], «e allora, che cosa avete da dire?  Qualcosa che vi siete messi in testa riguardo a lei, naturalmente.  Provatele, allora -- questo è tutto.  Provatele.  Dite di averla trovata.  Posso dirvi (se non lo sapete) che avete trovato la più astuta, bugiarda, furtiva, diabolica piccola sgualdrina che sia mai nata. -- L'avete portata qui?», aggiunse, guardandosi intorno con attenzione.

"No, al momento non è qui," rispose il notaio. "Ma sta benissimo."

«Ah!» esclamò Sally, tirando fuori un pizzico di tabacco da fiuto dalla sua scatola, con la stessa cattiveria con cui avrebbe potuto staccare il naso alla piccola servetta; «da questo [[motifs/time|momento]] starà al sicuro, ve lo garantisco.»

«Lo [[concepts/hope|spero]],» rispose il notaio. «Le è venuto in mente per la prima [[motifs/time|volta]], quando ha scoperto che era fuggita, che c'erano due chiavi della porta della sua cucina?»

Miss Sally prese un'altra presa e, inclinando la testa da un lato, guardò
chi le faceva la domanda, con una specie di spasmo curioso intorno alla bocca, ma
con un'aria astuta di immensa espressività.

«Due chiavi», ripeté il notaio, «di cui una le dava la possibilità di girare per la casa di notte, quando lei pensava che fosse chiusa a chiave, e di ascoltare conversazioni riservate, tra cui quella particolare riunione che oggi sarà descritta davanti a un giudice, e che lei avrà l'opportunità di sentirla raccontare; quella riunione che lei e il signor Brass avete tenuto insieme la [[motifs/night|notte]] prima che quel giovane così sfortunato e [[archetypes/innocent|innocente]] venisse accusato di furto, a causa di un orribile stratagemma di cui dirò solo che può essere descritto con gli stessi epiteti che lei ha applicato a questo misero piccolo testimone, e con alcuni altri ancora più forti».

Sally prese un'altra presa.  Anche se il suo viso era meravigliosamente composto,
era evidente che era stata completamente colta di sorpresa, e che ciò
che si aspettava di dover ammettere, in relazione alla sua piccola
serva, era qualcosa di molto diverso da questo.

«Dai, dai, Miss Brass», disse il notaio, «avete un grande controllo delle vostre espressioni, ma vedo che sentite che, per un caso che non avreste mai [[concepts/imagination|immaginato]], questo vile piano è stato svelato e due dei suoi artefici devono essere portati davanti alla giustizia. Ora, conoscete le pene e le sanzioni a cui siete soggetta, quindi non è necessario che mi dilunghi su di esse, ma ho una proposta da farvi. Avete l'[[concepts/honour|onore]] di essere la sorella di uno dei più grandi furfanti non ancora impiccati; e, se posso permettermi di dirlo a una signora, siete in ogni aspetto del tutto degna di lui. Ma legati a voi due c'è una terza persona, un [[archetypes/villain|villano]] di nome Quilp, il principale artefice di tutto questo diabolico piano, che credo sia peggiore di entrambi. Per il suo bene, Miss Brass, fateci il favore di rivelare tutta la [[concepts/history|storia]] di questa faccenda. Lasciate che vi ricordi che farlo, su nostra istanza, vi metterà in una posizione sicura e confortevole - la vostra attuale non è desiderabile - e non potrà nuocere a vostro fratello; poiché contro di lui e voi abbiamo già prove più che sufficienti (come sentite). Non vi dirò che suggeriamo questa linea d'azione per [[concepts/mercy|pietà]] (perché, per dirvi la [[concepts/truth|verità]], non nutriamo alcun riguardo per voi), ma è una necessità a cui siamo ridotti, e ve la raccomando come la cosa più saggia da fare. [[motifs/time|Il tempo]]», disse il signor Witherden, tirando fuori il suo orologio, «in una faccenda come questa, è estremamente prezioso. Ci fate l'onore di comunicarci la vostra decisione il più rapidamente possibile, signora».

Con un sorriso sul volto e guardando a turno ciascuno dei tre, Miss Brass prese altri due o tre pizzichi di tabacco da fiuto, e avendo ormai [[motifs/time|poco]] da spremere, viaggiò intorno e intorno alla scatola con il pollice e l'indice, raccogliendo un altro pizzico.  Dopo averlo consumato anche questo e riposto con cura la scatola in tasca, disse:

‘Devo accettare o rifiutare subito, vero?’

«Sì», disse il signor Witherden.

La graziosa creatura stava aprendo le labbra per rispondere, quando
la porta si aprì di scatto e la testa di [[characters/sampson-brass|Sampson Brass]] fu spinta
dentro la stanza.

"Scusatemi", disse l'uomo in fretta. "Aspettate un attimo!"

Detto ciò, e del tutto indifferente allo stupore che la sua presenza
provocava, si insinuò dentro, chiuse la porta, baciò il suo guanto unto
con la stessa servilità con cui avrebbe baciato la [[motifs/dust|polvere]], e fece un inchino davvero abietto.



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_66--part_04" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 66 (part 4)" data-chapter="Chapter 66" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="motif/fire,motif/love,motif/time,motif/well,concept/honour,concept/sublime,concept/truth,concept/wonder"></span>


‘Sarah,’ said Brass, ‘hold your tongue if you please, and let me speak.
Gentlemen, if I could express the pleasure it gives me to see three
such men in a happy unity of feeling and concord of sentiment, I think
you would hardly believe me.  But though I am unfortunate--nay,
gentlemen, criminal, if we are to use harsh expressions in a company
like this--still, I have my feelings like other men.  I have heard of a
poet, who remarked that feelings were the common lot of all.  If he
could have been a pig, gentlemen, and have uttered that sentiment, he
would still have been immortal.’

‘If you’re not an idiot,’ said Miss Brass harshly, ‘hold your peace.’

‘Sarah, my dear,’ returned her brother, ‘thank you.  But I know what I
am about, my [[motifs/love|love]], and will take the liberty of expressing myself
accordingly.  Mr Witherden, Sir, your handkerchief is hanging out of
your pocket--would you allow me to--,

As Mr Brass advanced to remedy this accident, the Notary shrunk from
him with an air of disgust.  Brass, who over and above his usual
prepossessing qualities, had a scratched face, a green shade over one
eye, and a hat grievously crushed, stopped short, and looked round with
a pitiful smile.

‘He shuns me,’ said Sampson, ‘even when I would, as I may say, heap
coals of [[motifs/fire|fire]] upon his head.  [[motifs/well|Well]]!  Ah! But I am a falling house, and
the rats (if I may be allowed the expression in reference to a
gentleman I respect and [[motifs/love|love]] beyond everything) fly from me!
Gentlemen--regarding your conversation just now, I happened to see my
sister on her way here, and, wondering where she could be going to, and
being--may I venture to say?--naturally of a suspicious turn, followed
her.  Since then, I have been listening.’

‘If you’re not mad,’ interposed Miss Sally, ‘stop there, and say no
more.’

‘Sarah, my dear,’ rejoined Brass with undiminished politeness, ‘I thank
you kindly, but will still proceed.  Mr Witherden, sir, as we have the
[[concepts/honour|honour]] to be members of the same profession--to say nothing of that
other gentleman having been my lodger, and having partaken, as one may
say, of the hospitality of my roof--I think you might have given me the
refusal of this offer in the first instance.  I do indeed.  Now, my
dear Sir,’ cried Brass, seeing that the Notary was about to interrupt
him, ‘suffer me to speak, I beg.’

Mr Witherden was silent, and Brass went on.

‘If you will do me the favour,’ he said, holding up the green shade,
and revealing an eye most horribly discoloured, ‘to look at this, you
will naturally inquire, in your own minds, how did I get it.  If you
look from that, to my face, you will [[concepts/wonder|wonder]] what could have been the
cause of all these scratches.  And if from them to my hat, how it came
into the state in which you see it.  Gentlemen,’ said Brass, striking
the hat fiercely with his clenched hand, ‘to all these questions I
answer--Quilp!’

The three gentlemen looked at each other, but said nothing.

‘I say,’ pursued Brass, glancing aside at his sister, as though he were
talking for her information, and speaking with a snarling malignity, in
violent contrast to his usual smoothness, ‘that I answer to all these
questions,--Quilp--Quilp, who deludes me into his infernal den, and
takes a delight in looking on and chuckling while I scorch, and burn,
and bruise, and maim myself--Quilp, who never once, no never once, in
all our communications together, has treated me otherwise than as a
dog--Quilp, whom I have always hated with my whole heart, but never so
much as lately.  He gives me the cold shoulder on this very matter as
if he had had nothing to do with it, instead of being the first to
propose it.  I can’t trust him.  In one of his howling, raving, blazing
humours, I believe he’d let it out, if it was murder, and never think
of himself so long as he could terrify me.  Now,’ said Brass, picking
up his hat again and replacing the shade over his eye, and actually
crouching down, in the excess of his servility, ‘what does all this
lead to?--what should you say it led me to, gentlemen?--could you guess
at all near the mark?’

Nobody spoke.  Brass stood smirking for a little while, as if he had
propounded some choice conundrum; and then said:

‘To be short with you, then, it leads me to this.  If the [[concepts/truth|truth]] has
come out, as it plainly has in a manner that there’s no standing up
against--and a very [[concepts/sublime|sublime]] and grand thing is [[concepts/truth|Truth]], gentlemen, in its
way, though like other [[concepts/sublime|sublime]] and grand things, such as thunder-storms
and that, we’re not always over and above glad to see it--I had better
turn upon this man than let this man turn upon me.  It’s clear to me
that I am done for.  Therefore, if anybody is to split, I had better be
the person and have the advantage of it.  Sarah, my dear, comparatively
speaking you’re safe.  I relate these circumstances for my own profit.’

With that, Mr Brass, in a great hurry, revealed the whole story;
bearing as heavily as possible on his amiable employer, and making
himself out to be rather a saint-like and holy character, though
subject--he acknowledged--to human weaknesses.  He concluded thus:

‘Now, gentlemen, I am not a man who does things by halves.  Being in
for a penny, I am ready, as the saying is, to be in for a pound.  You
must do with me what you please, and take me where you please.  If you
wish to have this in writing, we’ll reduce it into manuscript
immediately.  You will be tender with me, I am sure.  I am quite
confident you will be tender with me.  You are men of [[concepts/honour|honour]], and have
feeling hearts.  I yielded from necessity to Quilp, for though
necessity has no law, she has her lawyers.  I yield to you from
necessity too; from policy besides; and because of feelings that have
been a pretty long [[motifs/time|time]] working within me.  Punish Quilp, gentlemen.
Weigh heavily upon him.  Grind him down.  Tread him under foot.  He has
done as much by me, for many and many a day.’


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

«Sarah», disse Brass, «tieni la lingua a freno, se non ti dispiace, e lascia parlare me.
Signori, se potessi esprimere il piacere che mi dà vedere tre
uomini come voi in una felice unità di sentimenti e concordia di pensiero, credo
che a malapena mi credereste. Ma sebbene io sia sfortunato - anzi,
signori, criminale, se dobbiamo usare espressioni dure in una compagnia
come questa - tuttavia, ho i miei sentimenti come tutti gli altri. Ho sentito parlare di un
poeta, che osservava che i sentimenti sono il comune destino di tutti. Se avesse potuto essere un maiale, signori, e aver espresso quel pensiero, sarebbe stato comunque immortale.»

"Se non sei un idiota," disse bruscamente Miss Brass, "tieni la bocca chiusa."

«Sarah, mia cara», rispose suo fratello, «grazie. Ma so quel che faccio, mia [[motifs/love|cara]], e mi prenderò la libertà di esprimermi di conseguenza. Signor Witherden, la sua sciarpa le sta uscendo di tasca -- mi permette di --,

Mentre il signor Brass si avvicinava per rimediare a questo incidente, il notaio si ritrasse da lui con aria di disgusto.  Brass, che oltre alle sue solite qualità pregevoli, aveva il viso graffiato, un occhio coperto da una benda verde e un cappello gravemente schiacciato, si fermò di colpo e guardò intorno con un sorriso pietoso.

«Mi evita», disse Sampson, «anche quando io vorrei, come si suol dire, accumulare carboni di [[motifs/fire|fuoco]] sulla sua testa. [[motifs/well|Bene]]! Ah! Ma io sono una casa in rovina, e i topi (se mi è consentito usare questa espressione parlando di un gentiluomo che io rispetto e [[motifs/love|amo]] più di ogni altra cosa) mi abbandonano! Signori, riguardo alla vostra conversazione di poco fa, mi è capitato di vedere mia sorella mentre veniva qui, e, chiedendomi dove potesse andare, e essendo io, se posso permettermi di dirlo, di natura sospettosa, l'ho seguita. Da allora, ho ascoltato.»

"Se non sei pazza," intervenne Miss Sally, "fermati qui e non dire altro."

«Sarah, mia cara», riprese Brass con la stessa cortesia, «ti ringrazio
moltissimo, ma continuerò.  Signor Witherden, signore, poiché abbiamo
l'[[concepts/honour|onore]] di essere membri della stessa professione--per non parlare del
fatto che quell'altro signore è stato mio inquilino e ha goduto, come si
suol dire, dell'ospitalità del mio tetto--credo che avreste potuto darmi
la possibilità di rifiutare questa offerta in prima istanza.  Lo credo
davvero.  Ora, mio caro signore», esclamò Brass, vedendo che il notaio stava per interromperlo, «permettetemi di parlare, ve ne prego.»

Il signor Witherden rimase in silenzio, e Brass continuò.

«Se vorrete farmi il favore», disse, alzando la visiera verde
e rivelando un occhio terribilmente ammaccato, «di dare un'occhiata a questo, vi
verrà naturalmente da chiedervi, tra voi, come l'ho preso.  Se poi
guardate da quello al mio viso, vi [[concepts/wonder|chiederete]] quale possa essere stata
la causa di tutti questi graffi.  E se poi dai graffi al mio cappello, come sia
finito nello stato in cui lo vedete.  Signori», disse Brass, colpendo
il cappello con violenza con la mano chiusa a pugno, «a tutte queste domande io
rispondo: Quilp!»

I tre signori si guardarono l'un l'altro, ma non dissero nulla.

«Voglio dire», continuò Brass, lanciando un'occhiata di lato a sua sorella, come se stesse parlando per informarla, e con una malignità ringhiosa, in violento contrasto con la sua solita dolcezza, «che rispondo a tutte queste domande,--Quilp--Quilp, che mi inganna nel suo infernale covo, e si diverte a guardare e a ridere mentre mi scotto, e brucio, e mi ferisco, e mi mutilo--Quilp, che mai una volta, no mai una volta, in tutte le nostre comunicazioni insieme, mi ha trattato diversamente che come un cane--Quilp, che ho sempre odiato con tutto il cuore, ma mai tanto come di recente.  Mi dà il freddo spalla su questa stessa faccenda come se non ci avesse avuto nulla a che fare, invece di essere il primo a proporla.  Non posso fidarmi di lui.  In uno dei suoi umori urlanti, rabbiosi, ardenti, credo che lo farebbe uscire, se fosse un omicidio, e non penserebbe a se stesso finché potesse terrorizzarmi.  Ora», disse Brass, raccogliendo di nuovo il cappello e riposizionando l'ombra sul suo occhio, e addirittura accovacciandosi, nell'eccesso della sua servilità, «a cosa porta tutto questo?--a cosa pensate che mi porti, signori?--potreste indovinare anche solo lontanamente?»

Nessuno parlò. Brass rimase lì a sogghignare per un po', come se avesse proposto un indovinello davvero raffinato; e poi disse:

«Per essere breve con voi, allora, mi porta a questo. Se la [[concepts/truth|verità]] è
venuta fuori, come è chiaramente successo in un modo che non c’è modo di
resistere--e la [[concepts/truth|Verità]] è una cosa molto [[concepts/sublime|sublime]] e grandiosa, signori, a suo
modo, anche se come altre cose [[concepts/sublime|sublime]] e grandiose, come i temporali
e cose del genere, non siamo sempre felici di vederla--è meglio che io
mi rivolti contro quest'uomo piuttosto che lasciare che quest'uomo si
rivolti contro di me. È chiaro a me che sono spacciato. Pertanto, se
qualcuno deve tradire, è meglio che sia io a farlo e trarne vantaggio.
Sarah, mia cara, relativamente parlando sei al sicuro. Racconto queste
circostanze per il mio profitto.»

Con ciò, il signor Brass, in gran fretta, rivelò tutta la storia,
caricando il più possibile il suo amabile datore di lavoro, e dipingendosi
come un personaggio piuttosto santo e pio, sebbene soggetto -- ammise -- a
debolezze umane.  Concluse così:

«Ora, signori, non sono un uomo che faccia le cose a metà.  Essendo
entrato per un penny, sono pronto, come si suol dire, a entrare per una sterlina.  Dovete fare con me ciò che vi piace, e portarmi dove vi piace.  Se
desiderate avere questo per iscritto, lo ridurremo in manoscritto
immediatamente.  Sarà tenero con me, ne sono sicuro.  Sono
del tutto
fiducioso che sarete teneri con me.  Siete uomini di [[concepts/honour|onore]], e avete
cuori sensibili.  Ho ceduto per necessità a Quilp, perché sebbene
la necessità non abbia legge, ha i suoi avvocati.  Cedo anche a voi per
necessità; per politica inoltre; e a causa di sentimenti che sono stati a lungo [[motifs/time|tempo]] a lavorare dentro di me.  Punite Quilp, signori.
Pesate pesantemente su di lui.  Schiacciatelo.  Calpestatelo.  Ha
fatto altrettanto con me, per molti e molti giorni.»



<span class="atom-split" data-atom="chapter_66--part_05" data-title="The Old Curiosity Shop — Chapter 66 (part 5)" data-chapter="Chapter 66" data-kind="excerpt" data-tags="archetype/damsel,archetype/innocent,motif/sleep,motif/time,motif/well,concept/doubt,concept/humility,concept/jealousy,concept/melancholy"></span>


Having now arrived at the conclusion of his discourse, Sampson checked
the current of his wrath, kissed his glove again, and smiled as only
parasites and cowards can.

‘And this,’ said Miss Brass, raising her head, with which she had
hitherto sat resting on her hands, and surveying him from head to foot
with a bitter sneer, ‘this is my brother, is it!  This is my brother,
that I have worked and toiled for, and believed to have had something
of the man in him!’

‘Sarah, my dear,’ returned Sampson, rubbing his hands feebly; ‘you
disturb our friends.  Besides you--you’re disappointed, Sarah, and, not
knowing what you say, expose yourself.’

‘Yes, you pitiful dastard,’ retorted the lovely [[archetypes/damsel|damsel]], ‘I understand
you.  You feared that I should be beforehand with you.  But do you
think that I would have been enticed to say a word!  I’d have scorned
it, if they had tried and tempted me for twenty years.’

‘He he!’ simpered Brass, who, in his deep debasement, really seemed to
have changed sexes with his sister, and to have made over to her any
spark of manliness he might have possessed.  ‘You think so, Sarah, you
think so perhaps; but you would have acted quite different, my good
fellow.  You will not have forgotten that it was a maxim with
Foxey--our revered father, gentlemen--“Always suspect everybody.”
That’s the maxim to go through life with!  If you were not actually
about to purchase your own safety when I showed myself, I suspect you’d
have done it by this [[motifs/time|time]].  And therefore I’ve done it myself, and
spared you the trouble as [[motifs/well|well]] as the shame.  The shame, gentlemen,’
added Brass, allowing himself to be slightly overcome, ‘if there is
any, is mine.  It’s better that a female should be spared it.’

With deference to the better opinion of Mr Brass, and more particularly
to the authority of his Great Ancestor, it may be doubted, with
[[concepts/humility|humility]], whether the elevating principle laid down by the latter
gentleman, and acted upon by his descendant, is always a prudent one,
or attended in practice with the desired results.  This is, beyond
question, a bold and presumptuous [[concepts/doubt|doubt]], inasmuch as many distinguished
characters, called men of the world, long-headed customers, knowing
dogs, shrewd fellows, capital hands at business, and the like, have
made, and do daily make, this axiom their polar star and compass.
Still, the [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] may be gently insinuated.  And in illustration it may
be observed, that if Mr Brass, not being over-suspicious, had, without
prying and listening, left his sister to manage the conference on their
joint behalf, or prying and listening, had not been in such a mighty
hurry to anticipate her (which he would not have been, but for his
distrust and [[concepts/jealousy|jealousy]]), he would probably have found himself much
better off in the end.  Thus, it will always happen that these men of
the world, who go through it in armour, defend themselves from quite as
much good as evil; to say nothing of the inconvenience and absurdity of
mounting guard with a microscope at all times, and of wearing a coat of
mail on the most [[archetypes/innocent|innocent]] occasions.

The three gentlemen spoke together apart, for a few moments.  At the
end of their consultation, which was very brief, the Notary pointed to
the writing materials on the table, and informed Mr Brass that if he
wished to make any statement in writing, he had the opportunity of
doing so.  At the same [[motifs/time|time]] he felt bound to tell him that they would
require his attendance, presently, before a justice of the peace, and
that in what he did or said, he was guided entirely by his own
discretion.

‘Gentlemen,’ said Brass, drawing off his glove, and crawling in spirit
upon the ground before them, ‘I will justify the tenderness with which
I know I shall be treated; and as, without tenderness, I should, now
that this discovery has been made, stand in the worst position of the
three, you may depend upon it I will make a clean breast.  Mr
Witherden, sir, a kind of faintness is upon my spirits--if you would
do me the favour to ring the bell and order up a glass of something
warm and spicy, I shall, notwithstanding what has passed, have a
[[concepts/melancholy|melancholy]] pleasure in drinking your good health.  I had hoped,’ said
Brass, looking round with a mournful smile, ‘to have seen you three
gentlemen, one day or another, with your legs under the mahogany in my
humble parlour in the Marks.  But hopes are fleeting.  Dear me!’

Mr Brass found himself so exceedingly affected, at this point, that he
could say or do nothing more until some refreshment arrived.  Having
partaken of it, pretty freely for one in his agitated state, he sat
down to write.

The lovely Sarah, now with her arms folded, and now with her hands
clasped behind her, paced the room with manly strides while her brother
was thus employed, and sometimes stopped to pull out her snuff-box and
bite the lid.  She continued to pace up and down until she was quite
tired, and then fell asleep on a chair near the door.

It has been since supposed, with some reason, that this slumber was a
sham or feint, as she contrived to slip away unobserved in the dusk of
the afternoon.  Whether this was an intentional and waking departure,
or a somnambulistic leave-taking and walking in her [[motifs/sleep|sleep]], may remain a
subject of contention; but, on one point (and indeed the main one) all
parties are agreed.  In whatever state she walked away, she certainly
did not walk back again.

Mention having been made of the dusk of the afternoon, it will be
inferred that Mr Brass’s task occupied some [[motifs/time|time]] in the completion.  It
was not finished until evening; but, being done at last, that worthy
person and the three friends adjourned in a hackney-coach to the
private office of a justice, who, giving Mr Brass a warm reception and
detaining him in a secure place that he might insure to himself the
pleasure of seeing him on the morrow, dismissed the others with the
cheering assurance that a warrant could not fail to be granted next day
for the apprehension of Mr Quilp, and that a proper application and
statement of all the circumstances to the secretary of state (who was
fortunately in town), would no [[concepts/doubt|doubt]] procure Kit’s free pardon and
liberation without delay.


<span class="qlang-split" data-lang="it"></span>

Avendo ora raggiunto la conclusione del suo discorso, Sampson frenò la corrente della sua ira, baciò di nuovo il guanto e sorrise come possono fare solo i parassiti e i codardi.

«E questo», disse Miss Brass, alzando la testa, che fino a quel momento aveva appoggiato sulle mani, e scrutandolo dalla testa ai piedi con un ghigno amaro, «questo è mio fratello, dunque! Questo è mio fratello, per il quale ho lavorato e mi sono affaticata, e per il quale credevo che ci fosse qualcosa di umano in lui!»
